\vspace*{154pt}
\begingroup
\noindent For Julie, and for my dad.

\vspace{28pt}
\noindent Julie,

Three years ago, a few months into the rendering engine, I came out of my office and told you I
thought I was onto something. You said okay. You didn't ask what it was, or what it was for, or
when it would be done, and you didn't ask me for anything I could have shown you, because there
was nothing to show. There was a program that had done something it shouldn't have been able to
do, and a man who didn't yet know what a Turing machine was.

You gave me the three years anyway. The nights after the lot closed. The weekends. The hours I
was in the house and not in the house, because my head was in a wall I couldn't get past. Every
dead end, and there were more of those than there are pages here. You never once asked me to
stop, and you never once said it was fine when it wasn't. You just kept giving me the next
evening.

This book is what I did with them. It's the one thing I've built from nothing that I'm sure of,
because I threw out every piece of it I couldn't prove, and what's left holds. I know that isn't
what you gave the years for. You gave them for me. But it's what I have to show, and I wanted it
to be worth showing.

\vspace{14pt}
\noindent Dad,

The name on the cover was yours first. I asked you before I used it and you said go ahead. You
and Mom taught me that nothing is true just because somebody says it is. This book is that
lesson, six hundred pages long. I put our name on it because I wanted one thing in the world
with that name on it that nobody handed me, that I couldn't have faked, and that I can stand
behind in front of anyone. Here it is.

Julie carries the name now too. So the machine has it third. This is for the two of you who had
it first.
\endgroup

%===========================================================================
\phantomsection\section*{The point}
\label{sec:point}
%===========================================================================

The whole book is four steps, and I'll set them out first so you know what you're carrying. Each step is motivated by the one
before it, and the book goes up them in order.

\emph{One: nothing becomes something for free.} Take a blank cell: a square of paper with nothing
on it, a bead that could sit in either of two dips, a bit of memory nobody has set. Now make it a
0, and keep it a 0. Something is the case now that wasn't a moment ago. For a total deterministic rule, a reading newly raised and then held requires
a merge somewhere in the run or endlessly fresh states. Physical dissipation
requires a separate model; the thermal models discussed below impose further
costs under their own hypotheses.

\emph{Two: so the machine is the thing that steps, with the price in the move.} A Thiele machine
is a state, some thing; a reading of each state into an order, so that of two states you can ask
whether the second reads at or below the first, and higher means more is settled; moves, each a
direction that transforms the state into the next state; and a price on each move. One rule, which
I call the toll: a move that carries the reading somewhere not at or below where it stood is never
free. That is the whole definition, and everything in this book is a consequence of it or an
instance of it. I named it after myself, on purpose: I wanted to call it the meta machine, a
company took that word in 2021, and I went one level up, half a joke and half a stake in the
ground; the afterword has the rest. The step that raises a reading that stays is the step that's charged. A machine
whose moves never climb its order is the \emph{flat case}, and the toll has nothing to say to it: a
clock is one, a reversible process is one, and so is every ordinary model of computation, the Turing
machine included, with its price column torn off and its record forgotten. Computer science charges
a computation for how long it runs and how much space it takes, and the bits it erases have been
counted too. What no model I found charges is the moment a reading goes up and stays. Those steps
are a few events in a run, not the billions of overwrites a computer makes every second; what they
write doesn't stay, and the toll leaves them to the erasure count and to physics. Put a window over
the machine that shows only the flat part, and through it you can watch the computing while missing
what the machine kept about it. I will have to earn that picture by giving the window and the moves
precise rules; calling something a window is not enough.

To show the definition can be met, Part~III builds one example and takes it apart: two counters
and a line number for the flat part, and a record whose moves check a claim, commit to a passed
check and certify it. Its working states can look alike while the full states differ in what was
kept. The Thiele Machine is the definition, not the example.

The counting underneath needs its own conditions too: states, a next-state
rule, and a reading that stays. Once those are given, what follows is a
theorem. Whether a physical process fits that description is the further
question stated in the Conclusion.

\emph{Three: the structure a computation makes is made of exactly this.} Structure in general is a
relation kept under the changes you choose; Part~II takes that word from the people who wrestled
with it. The part a computation makes, and can't take back, is a distinction held in its state, and
a 0 is the smallest one there is: the ways a cell could be, sorted into piles, and one pile held. A
grouping, an order, a relation a later move leans on, a fact somebody found out and wrote down:
each is a distinction that stays, paid for the same way as the 0. Insight, in the sense this book can
price, is a kept distinction. The toll charges the moment it's raised; holding it up afterward adds nothing to the cost. That's what the book's other name, No Free Insight, means.

\emph{Four: established is the sharpest case.} Two computers can end with the same answer, and only
one of them checked it. The difference between them is a distinction one of them never kept. A
record that a claim was checked and closed is a 0 that stays, with a check in front of it, and it's
paid for the same way. I build a machine for that case, all the way down, because it's the one where
you can point at the kept 0 and at what it cost. It's the sharpest case of what keeping takes, but it isn't the
point. The point is the 0.

Step one is where the toll gets its reason. If it breaks, the toll goes back to being only my
choice, though the latch, the window, the diagonal and the earned record are proved without it and
would stand. So that's where I start: the blank
cell, taken apart as far down as I can get before I hit something that holds or something I can't
get under. I'll tell you which.

One warning about how this went, because it explains the shape of everything after it. Most of the
time I had the hunch first and found the names later. Over and over, somebody had been here before
me. Sometimes that made my day. Sometimes it pissed me off. You'll see both.

\subsection*{Where a 0 comes from}

Before any machine comes the cell. What does it take for there to be a 0 at all?

It takes three things. First, something that can be more than one way: a bead in a dish of
water, a speck of magnetised metal, a charge on a tiny capacitor, a square of paper. Nature hands
you that much, and it isn't a 0 yet. It's stuff that can sit in a lot of arrangements.

Second, a sorting: somebody says which arrangements count as 0, which count as 1, and which count
as blank. The sorting is the first piece of structure Part~II gets to: the ways a thing could be, cut into
piles. Without it there's no 0, just a bead somewhere. A 0 and a 1 aren't things; they're the two
sides of a line somebody drew across the ways a thing can be.

Third, something that keeps the chosen arrangement readable for the time you
need it. In the bead experiment below, that something is a hill between two wells.
A high hill makes escape rare; it does not make escape impossible. At a barrier
of about eight times the thermal energy, the paper estimates a characteristic
escape time of roughly fifty minutes. Lower the barrier to about twice that
energy and the estimate is about ten seconds. Those are waiting-time scales,
not appointments at which the bead must jump. The barrier height is not a bill
for heat already given off.

A latch, a refreshed charge or a written mark needs its own account of how it
holds. The common question is simple: which later changes are allowed, and do
they leave the answer readable? In the mathematical examples I can require a
yes to stay yes under every allowed move. The bead is a physical example of
retention for a time, with a chance of failure.

Now for the moment itself: the cell is blank and you write a 0. Everything that step can take comes next, in Part~I, and
the rest of the book only ever adds detail to it.

\subsection*{Why it has to cost}

Now what it takes to keep that 0, made exact, and it's the part I'm proudest of, because once something
stays, the choosing stops and the counting takes over. And the counting is the one behind musical chairs.

Do it with chairs when the room runs out. Draw a box on the floor, three chairs inside, one chair
outside by the door. Four people, one per chair: the four states the machine could be in. The
three inside already read yes. One step moves everybody at once, each to the chair the rule sends
them to. Nobody inside may leave, because yes is permanent. The person by the door has to come in,
because this is the step that flips them to yes. Now finish the move, one person per chair. You
can't. Four people, three inside chairs: somebody shares. Maybe the newcomer ends up on a lap,
maybe two insiders squeeze onto one chair; either way, two starting places share a destination.
Somebody secretly picks a starting chair, the rule moves them, and you're told only where they
ended up: at a shared chair, you can't say where they started. That's the pigeonhole principle,
which is old and not mine, and the chapter ``Why the toll isn't arbitrary''
(Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}) proves it with exactly three conditions on a rule that gives every state a next one: finitely many states that read yes, a yes that stays, and one flip. There's no physics
in it anywhere, only counting.

So, the deepest thing I can say about keeping: not every forgetting keeps anything, and
wiping a scratch pad keeps nothing. But every keeping pays. On a finite machine that keeps running, keeping pays by forgetting: the step that makes something stay for good lands two states on one,
somewhere, maybe not where you happen to be standing, and afterward nothing can tell which one it
was. With endless fresh states it can dodge the merge only by spending fresh states it never gets back. A verdict
keeps the decision and lets go of the arguing.

Part~I proves the count on any machine, prices it on finite ones, and keeps the heat floor as an
assumption with its name on it. I never let those two swap places.

An ordinary computational model keeps no account of what it made the case. It is the flat
case: moves that never climb, so the toll never speaks. The Thiele Machine is the general
thing, a state with an order read off it and a price in every move, and the computer is what
is left of one when the order is taken flat.

\subsection*{What the usual models don't count}

That's step one, and step two is what it means for the machines people already count with.

Computer science has always counted what a computation costs. How many steps it takes is time.
How many cells it needs is space. The bits a computation erases have been counted too, by Ming Li
and Paul Vitányi (1996) and by Erik Demaine and his coauthors (2016). Every one of those models is
a flat case. Its states carry no order, so no move of it ever climbs, and nothing in it can charge
for the moment a reading goes up and stays. Now look again at what step one found keeping takes.
Every time a computation makes something the case and keeps it, a bit set, a list left in order,
an answer written down, it pays, in a merge or in fresh states. What it pays isn't the time count:
a slow step and a fast one can keep the same thing. It isn't the space count either, though fresh
states are one of the two ways to pay it: a machine with a fixed memory pays it by merging, over
and over, in the same cells, and its space count never moves. What none of the usual counts
charges, as far as I found, is the moment a chosen reading goes up and stays, whichever way keeping
it is paid. That's a third thing a computation does, and it's what this model counts.

So here is the Thiele Machine, all of it, math you can reason about, the way Turing's machine is.
A set of states, each with a reading into an order: for any two readings you can ask whether one
sits at or below the other, and higher means more is settled. A set of moves, each a direction
that transforms a state into the next state. A step that takes a state and a move to the next
state. A price on each move, a whole number of units of cost. And one rule, which I call the toll:
a move that carries the reading somewhere not at or below where it stood costs at least one unit.
A machine whose moves never climb is the flat case, and the toll never charges it; every ordinary
computer is one. The smallest case that isn't flat has a reading with two places, blank and
written, nothing and a 0, and I write them no and yes. There the toll says that turning no into
yes costs at least one, and most of Part~I is told with that record, because it is the one you
can point at. The toll sits on the raise, not on the merge, so it charges for keeping something
whichever way that's paid, in a merge or in fresh states. Two more pieces come in when a result
needs them: a counter in the state that adds up the costs and only climbs, which is the ledger,
and a window, what an outside observer gets to see. The toll's first name, the one I gave it
before I understood it, is No Free Insight.

Put a dial with four positions beside a slider with three stops. ROTATE
moves the dial one position around for free and leaves the slider alone.
ADVANCE moves the slider toward its last stop, leaves the dial alone and
costs one. At the last stop the reading is yes; at the other two it is no.
ADVANCE pays when it first reaches yes and still costs one when pressed
at the last stop. The price belongs to the button. Look only at the dial:
ROTATE moves the picture and ADVANCE leaves it alone. Those are the
horizontal and vertical moves of the sliced definition below. There are
twelve full configurations, four dial positions for each slider stop.
We have met the rules without introducing a checker or a claim.

It computes nothing new; its flat case already computes everything a Turing machine can. What it adds is a place, in the
step itself, for what a computation made the case and what that cost. The reading can be any
reading into an order at all; the toll charges every step that climbs. The readings this book cares about are
the ones that, once up, stay up, because those are the kept distinctions and keeping is what the merge or the fresh states pay for. A cell's ``it's a 0 now'' stays only if the later moves preserve that value.
Likewise, a sorted list can be scrambled by the next write. A flag saying
``this list was sorted earlier'' answers a different question.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[thiele]
\node[pipe,text width=2.9cm,minimum width=0pt] (a) at (0,0)
  {Tiles: 2, 1\\Sorted now: no\\Ever sorted: no};
\node[pipe,text width=2.9cm,minimum width=0pt] (b) at (4.2,0)
  {Tiles: 1, 2\\Sorted now: yes\\Ever sorted: yes};
\node[pipe,text width=2.9cm,minimum width=0pt] (c) at (8.4,0)
  {Tiles: 2, 1\\Sorted now: no\\Ever sorted: yes};
\draw[pipearrow] (a) -- node[above=28pt]{sort} (b);
\draw[pipearrow] (b) -- node[above=28pt]{swap} (c);
\end{tikzpicture}

\small The tiles can lose their order. A separate history flag can keep the fact
that they were ordered earlier. Read one, and you have not read the other.
\end{center}

``This claim was checked and closed'' can be a historical reading of that kind. The model doesn't care which, and for readings that
stay, Part~I derives the toll from what keeping takes, on stated premises. A reading that flips back and forth does not by itself retain whether an event ever happened: Part~II calls it a toggle and proves it's the latch of no event
(Section~\ref{sec:latch}).

The one in the toll is one unit of cost, in the model's own count, and it's one because that's the least a
whole-number count can charge and still not be free, and the toll only says \emph{not free}. A unit of cost
isn't a joule. What ties it to heat is Landauer's principle, named, through the merge a raise has to make when only finitely many states read yes, and nothing else.

And there's one thing to hold on to through the whole book, because it's where readers go wrong and
where I went wrong for a long time. \emph{The ledger is a count, not a lock.} It doesn't stop
anybody from doing anything. It adds up the prices you chose for the moves that ran, writes the
sum down where the machine can't lose it, and the toll makes each raise of the reading you chose
cost at least one. It doesn't measure merges, fresh states or heat: a merge that keeps nothing can cost
nothing, fresh states are taken at every step and the toll asks for a unit only at the raise, and where a merge raises nothing, a cost of one unit per raise leaves that merge out. What ties the count to what keeping takes is a
theorem, not a reading of a dial: on a machine with finitely many states reading yes, any price list
that charges merges has to charge each raise of a reading that stays at least one. What a kept reading \emph{means}, whether
a reading that's up stands for anything, is a separate question with a separate answer, and Part~III
gives it for one case: an order the step enforces, which is the lock. A lock would work at a price of
zero. The price isn't there to make the lock work. It's there because, on a machine where every
state has a next one, the raise of a reading that stays merges or takes fresh states, whether anybody writes
it down or not.

\subsection*{What I found, what I assumed and what I chose}

I didn't invent a machine. I found one. That's how I see this work, and I'll be straight
about the difference between that conviction and a theorem before I do anything else. A proof
doesn't settle it: showing what follows from the premises doesn't decide whether you found the
theorem or made it. That's why it's labelled a conviction. What it changes is how I hold the
thing, like something that was already there, which means I can be wrong about its shape and
the shape won't care. And to be exact about what ``found'' covers, it covers the parts the
counting forces on you, the order and the merge or the fresh states. The event to record, the
price list, and putting the count inside the step are choices, mine, and the three lists below
say which is which.

The three lists draw the line between what nothing let me choose, what I had to assume, and what I did choose,
because everything after this depends on where it falls. Read the first list as the ground, the
second as what the ground is taken to stand on, and the third as the model built on it.

\emph{Found: what counting forces on any machine.}
\begin{itemize}
\item Run a machine that gives each state exactly one next state. It takes fresh states until it
first comes back to one it has used; that return lands on its start or is a merge, two states with
one next state; and after it the run only repeats steps it already took. There's no fourth thing a
step can do, and a run merges at most once (Theorem~\ref{thm:step-law}).
\item So any run that never comes back to its start merges somewhere or takes a fresh state at every
step. A reading that goes from no to yes and never comes back rules the return out, so every run that
raises it merges or takes fresh states (Proposition~\ref{prop:heat-or-room}). The sharper fact is
about the move: when only finitely many states read yes, the move that raises the reading merges two
states (Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges} for a finite machine,
Proposition~\ref{prop:raise-needs-room} when only the yes-states are finitely many). A machine that
can stop, with a state that has no next state at all, slips past this, and Part~I says exactly how
(Theorem~\ref{thm:halting-hole}). All of that is counting, with no physics in it.
\item Over any machine at all, a record that the computation drives and that never comes down is a
latch on one event: it switches on the first time something happens and nothing switches it off
(Observation~\ref{thm:u11-latch}). That's counting too, given the two conditions in it.
\end{itemize}

\emph{Assumed: what the found list is taken to stand on, in the world.}
\begin{itemize}
\item A merge of states the machine really could have been in, done in surroundings at some temperature, has a floor under its heat, on average, however slowly it's done, in a memory whose states are alike apart from what they record.
That's Landauer's principle, the premise from thermodynamics, named and assumed and never proved
here, with its critics named.
\item A real device can tell apart only finitely many states in any bounded place, so its fresh states run out.
Nobody has measured where that ceiling sits.
\item The clean start: a raised record means the event happened only because the record was down at
the start, and that start is put in by hand. It's a past hypothesis in miniature. The past
hypothesis, the philosopher David Albert's name (2000) for an assumed low-entropy beginning of the
universe, is an idea that goes back to Boltzmann; several accounts of why records point to the past
lean on it, and every theorem here about records gets its arrow from an assumed clean start
(Section~\ref{sec:latch}).
\end{itemize}

\emph{Chosen: what the model adds, each of which could have gone another way.}
\begin{itemize}
\item To put the account inside the step, as part of what a step is. Two things go there. That the record stays and the computing can't reach it has to: the record is one of the five parts, a reading of the state, and a rule about the state kept by the step holds of every program, where a log a program keeps holds of that program only.
\item The toll itself: a whole unit, at least one, on the step that raises a reading, whichever way
keeping is paid. On a machine with finitely many states reading yes, for a reading that stays, it follows from a price on merging, and that price is a choice too.
\item Which readings matter: the ones that never come down. The toll charges any reading's rise;
permanence is what makes the rise a case of keeping, and permanence is a choice. So is one next state for every state,
the condition the stopping hole gets around.
\item Which event gets a record, and what price list the record pays. The latch leaves both unforced.
And on a machine that pays in fresh states, where the write merges nothing, the record stays up because I
declare that it does (Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-reversible}).
\item On the machine of Part~III, where its flat part ends and its record begins, and that its step never reads the flag: the rest of the state moves by its own rule and the ledger adds the instruction's price, whichever way the flag reads.
\end{itemize}

The machine Part~III builds is one worked demonstration of the third list, on one reading. Nothing
in the first list needs it.

\subsection*{What structure is made of}

Step three says that a 0 is the smallest structure that sorts, and that the rest of structure is the same thing at a bigger size.

A sorting of a pile into groups is a distinction: these go together, those don't. Keep it and
it's a distinction that stays, paid for the same way. An ordering is every pair compared and the
answers kept. A fact somebody found out and wrote down is a distinction between the ways things could
have been and the way they were, kept. A machine can carry any of those in its state and in its
rules, and each one it keeps is paid for the way the 0 is. Part~II takes the word
\emph{structure} from the people who wrestled with it, and comes out at that:
structure is distinctions held in a state.

That gives \emph{insight} an exact meaning, a narrower one than you'd like, and I'll be honest
about how narrow. Finding something out doesn't have to pay the merge. Bennett
showed that you can write down what you see on a blank page without merging anything, so Landauer's
floor isn't owed; the page is what you spend, and it can be handed back while the original is still
there. Making it stay is what pays. Learning borrows, committing pays. The insight the toll prices
is the committed kind, a distinction made to stay. Whether that narrower thing deserves the word is
a fair thing to argue about, and Part~I argues it, where learning and committing get pulled apart.

Then Part~II asks what follows, on any machine, once a distinction is kept and the keeping is
charged. The ledger is itself a distinction that stays: a number that only climbs takes a fresh value for every unit it counts.
A window that shows only part of a state can hide the very distinction that was paid for, and when it shows a step that paid and one that didn't the same, before and after, no price read off the window can be exact. A later step can be entitled to something
because a distinction stayed, and the entitlement has an exact count. Over any machine at all, a
reading the machine's own steps turn on and nothing turns off is a latch, the blank cell's 0 one
level up. And there's a wall no level gets past: no state codes every question about the states.

\subsection*{Established}

Step four is the sharpest case, and it's the one I build a machine for.

Give two workers the same messy list. The first sorts it, then runs a separate
test that compares each neighbouring pair and reports whether the order is right.
The test passes. The second copies in that same sorted list and runs no test.
Ask only for the final list. The bytes agree. Reading them can tell you whether
they are sorted now; it cannot tell you whether the earlier test ran.

I have specified the output being compared, not every register and every line
of program memory. If those retain the difference, the full machine can still
tell the histories apart. If a cleanup makes the full endpoints agree too,
then nothing in those endpoints can answer which history occurred. An ordinary
computer can retain that evidence when its program and interface require it.
The question is what this task asks it to keep.

\emph{Established} is the name for the difference. An answer is established when a check that could
have said no said yes, about that very answer, and the result was made to stay. That last part is a
kept distinction, a 0 in some cell that says ``checked,'' and it's paid for the same way as every other 0.
Part~III opens by taking that apart (Section~\ref{sec:established}): what ``could have said no'' means, what settling a question is, and why
the people who thought hardest about knowledge kept landing near it.

How far the example reaches, to other models of computation and to universal machines that run it
as a guest and earn its flag again, is proved too; Part~III states it (Section~\ref{sec:reach}) and the
appendices build it. That's the reach of the case, not what the book is about.

\subsection*{How the book goes}

Part~I is what keeping costs. It covers a distinction that stays, and what every step of every machine does to the states it has used;
the machine, stated once, with the smallest record that can carry a charge, and the toll written into its step as one rule; whether the rule is
forced, and on which premises; the record anywhere in an order; and why finding out only borrows, where committing pays.

Part~II is structure, as kept distinctions: the word itself, and
then what follows on any machine once a distinction is kept and the keeping charged: the ledger, the
window, entitlement, the latch, the shadow, and the wall no level gets past.

Part~III is the sharpest case: what established means, the machine that keeps it, how far the
machine reaches, five real systems that keep records and whether they price the write, the thesis about which kept
distinction is worth paying for, and what its ledger has to do with heat.

Part~IV brings the results together: what each establishes, which conditions it uses, and how
the constructions fit. After that comes how I got here, for anyone who wants the story, and then
the appendices, which carry the universal machines and the machines built from parts.

\clearpage

\part{What keeping costs}
\clearpage

Part~I is step one, and the rule step two needs. It starts at the smallest structure that sorts: a cell that's blank, and then a 0. First comes what keeping takes, before any price list: what a distinction that stays is, what
every step of every machine does to the states it has used, and what it costs for something to go from
nothing to something and stay. Then the smallest machine that writes what keeping takes into its own step, as
one rule, the toll. Then whether the rule is forced, and on which premises. Then the one thing that
looks like it ought to pay a merge and doesn't have to: finding out, which borrows fresh states instead.

%===========================================================================
\section{A distinction that stays}
\label{sec:what-a-chair-is}
%===========================================================================

A cell can be blank, or 0,
or 1, and somebody has drawn the lines between those. Write a 0 in it and it stays a 0, and that's
the event this whole book is about, nothing becoming something; this chapter is what it takes,
before any machine and before any price list.

What this chapter counts is a distinction that stays. A cell on a tape that reads 0, and not 1, and not blank, is one; a
bead sitting in the left well and not the right is one; a flag that is up is one. Anything the world can
tell apart from something else and keeps telling apart counts. It needs distinguishable arrangements, a reading that groups them, and rules or a physical mechanism that retain the chosen answer. The bead uses a hill for the last part. \hyperref[sec:point]{The point} said so in pictures (``Where a 0 comes from''). Here I want two things exactly:
what every step of every machine does to the states it has used, and what it costs for a state to be
taken at all. Both answers are proofs, and every one of them is short enough to follow on the
page. Nothing in this chapter needs a price list, and the toll, named up front, is stated exactly only in the next chapter,
which writes what keeping takes into a machine's step; the one after asks whether it had to.

\subsection{Every step does one of three things}

Forget the cell for a moment, and forget finiteness. Take any machine at all, with any number of
states and any rule that gives each state exactly one next state, and watch it run from any
start. Keep a list of every state it has been in. Now look at the next step. There are exactly three things it
can do.

It can land on a state the run has not used yet, which uses up a fresh state on this
step. The only way to stop using up fresh states is to come back to a state the run has used: to the start, and a run that does that has kept nothing, or to another one, which is the next thing a step can do.

It can come back, for the first time in the run, to a state the run has used before, and not
the state it started from. Then it came from a different state than the one that first got
there, so two different states have led to the same place, and that is what I mean by a merge: a literal collision,
two different states with the same next state. Under Landauer's premise a merge of states that
were really possible carries a floor of heat, and no amount of going slowly lowers it.

Or it can land back on the very state it started from, or take a step the run has already
taken. Then the machine is going round a loop, and this is certain: a machine with one rule for the next state, once it stands where it stood before, does again what it did before, forever. Every
later state is one it already had, and every later step is one it already took, and it is computing nothing new.

There is no fourth thing a step can do, and every run has the same shape: fresh
states, then at most one return, and after it nothing but steps already taken. The proof is one
line: the first time a run comes back to a state it has used, either it came back to its very first state,
which is a pure loop from the start, or the step that brought it back lands on the same state as the
step that first got there, which is a merge. So a run reveals at most one pair of distinct visited sources with a shared successor. Later laps can visit that same landing again; they reveal no additional pair.

\begin{theorem}[The step law]\label{thm:step-law}
Let a step give every state of a set exactly one next state, where the states can be told
apart, and run it from any start $x_0$, writing $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots$ for the run. Either every
step is fresh, landing on a state the run has not visited, or there is a first step that lands on
a visited state, from $x_n$ to $x_{n+1} = x_j$ with $j \le n$, and then: every step before it is
fresh; it lands on the start ($j = 0$), or it is a merge, coming from a different state than the
one that first reached $x_j$, so that two distinct states share a next state; and from $x_j$ on
the run is periodic, so every later state is one the run already had and every later step, from
$x_k$ to $x_{k+1}$ with $k > n$, is a step the run already took. In a run at most one pair of
distinct states shares a next state, $x_{j-1}$ and $x_n$, when $j>0$. Later laps may revisit the shared destination, but introduce no further pair of distinct visited sources with a shared successor.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If no state repeats, every step is fresh. Otherwise take the first step that lands on a visited
state, from $x_n$ to $x_{n+1}$, and the position $j \le n$ with $x_j = x_{n+1}$; it is unique,
because $x_0, \ldots, x_n$ are all different. Every earlier step is fresh, by the choice of $n$.
If $j > 0$, compare $x_{j-1}$, which first reached $x_j$, with $x_n$: both land on $x_j$. They
differ, because $x_n = x_{j-1}$ with $j - 1 < n$ would be an earlier repeat. So two distinct
states share a next state: a merge. Either way, since one rule gives the next state,
$x_{n+1} = x_j$ gives $x_{n+1+k} = x_{j+k}$ for every $k$, so the run repeats with period
$p = n + 1 - j$ from position $j$ on. For $k > n$ the step from $x_k$ to $x_{k+1}$ is then the
step from $x_{k-p}$ to $x_{k-p+1}$, taken earlier, and every later state is one of
$x_j, \ldots, x_n$. No later step introduces a new such pair: it repeats a transition already seen. If $j>0$, the only two distinct states with a shared next state in the run are $x_{j-1}$ and $x_n$; if $j=0$, there is no such pair.
\end{proof}

The step law is ``nothing is kept for free'' as a theorem with two hypotheses: you can tell states
apart, and each state has one next state. The only step that neither uses up a fresh state nor merges is a step on a
loop, and a loop makes nothing new. Anything new is a state never used before or one that two states have led to, and that's
what keeping takes. Physical dissipation is a separate question, answered here only under the
specified thermal dynamics and distributional premises. That one is
heat against time: I prove it below for Bennett's walker, and the cited physicists prove related bounds for specified thermal stochastic dynamics. The
reading that stays up is the way to force ``new'': a reading that was no and is now yes can
never come back to the state it started on, so the run can't be a loop through its start. Its first return to any state it has
used, if it ever has one, is a merge; if it never has one, every state it takes is fresh. Two
chapters on, that's the first part of Proposition~\ref{prop:heat-or-room}, where the fresh states get
counted exactly. (After a merge the
run can settle onto a loop among states that read yes and idle there, making nothing new. The
keeping was paid for at the merge.)

There is one hole, and it's worth seeing exactly. Take a machine that stops, with two states. The first reads no,
the step takes it to the second, which reads yes, and the second has no next step at all.
The reading is raised, there is no merge, no fresh state after that, nothing. The step law assumed every state
has a next state, and a machine that stops its clock dodges it. Close the hole either way and
what keeping takes comes back. Say the halted state's next state is itself, which is the usual way to
give a stopped machine a step, and the halt is a merge: the moving state and the halted
state both land on the halted state. A physical device can also hold a reading through its
storage arrangement. What that arrangement costs is a question about the device; the
partial transition rule has not answered it. Here I can settle the state-counting question
once holding is included in a total next-state rule.

\begin{theorem}[Halting]\label{thm:halting-hole}
A partial step, one that may have no next state, can raise a permanent reading on two states
with no two states sharing a next state. Totalising it, with the halted state stepping to
itself, makes the raise a merge: the halted state and the state that steps onto it share a next
state. In general, once every halted state steps to itself, any other state that steps onto a
halted state shares that landing with it.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
States $a$ and $b$, reading no on $a$ and yes on $b$; $a$ steps to $b$ and $b$ has no next
state. No two states step to the same state, because only $a$ steps at all. Totalise: $b$
steps to $b$, and now $a$ and $b$ both step to $b$, a merge of two distinct states. The general
case is the same two lines: if $c \ne h$ steps to the halted state $h$ and $h$ steps to $h$,
then $c$ and $h$ share a next state.
\end{proof}

Stepping the halted state to itself is one way to totalise. Step it to a fresh sink state instead and the merge only moves: the sink steps to itself, and the halted state lands there too. On finitely many states reading yes, every way to totalise that keeps the reading up merges somewhere (Proposition~\ref{prop:raise-needs-room}, two chapters on). An endless counter offers another arrangement: the reading stays put while the full state keeps changing. I want to count that arrangement now, because the screen and the box are doing different things.

\subsubsection*{The camera stops; the box keeps ticking}

At three o'clock the screen says 42. The program is finished. Stop filming and you have
the computation from start to finish. Leave the camera running and the box is still on
the desk. At 3:01 it says 42. At 3:02 it says 42.

Let the box's next-state rule keep ticking. It can stay exactly where it is, or change
something behind that screen. Imagine a wheel inside it, turning from ``first holding
state'' to ``second holding state'' while the display never moves. The screen gives you
42 each time. Open the box and the wheel may tell you which tick you are looking at.

Start the count one tick before completion. That unfinished state is $u$. Call the total
next-state rule $F$, so $F(u)$ is the first completed state and $F^2(u)$ is the next one.
Gather the full states that keep the answer into a set $H$, and require the rule to stay
in that set once it enters. Give $H$ room for $K$ configurations. Two bits can have four
configurations; these are the arrangements of the box I am counting.

Now ask it to hold for $L$ samples while every distinct source in that stretch, including
$u$, has a distinct successor. Suppose two holding samples repeated the same full state.
Follow their equal successors backwards. Each cancellation takes one step off both sides,
until the unfinished state equals a state already holding the answer. That is impossible.
Every holding sample needs its own full configuration.

\begin{theorem}[Room to hold an answer]\label{thm:host-holding-capacity}
Let $F:X\to X$ be total, with distinguishable states, and let $H\subseteq X$ have $K$
elements. Suppose $u\notin H$, $F(u)\in H$, and $F(H)\subseteq H$. For $L\ge0$, put
\[
D_L=\{u,F(u),\ldots,F^{L-1}(u)\},\qquad D_0=\varnothing.
\]
If $F$ is one-to-one on $D_L$, then the $L$ held states $F(u),\ldots,F^L(u)$ are distinct,
and $L\le K$. In particular, among $u,F(u),\ldots,F^K(u)$ there are two distinct states
with the same successor. If instead $F$ is one-to-one everywhere and the held region is
allowed to be infinite, the orbit from $u$ never repeats.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose the same full state occurs twice in the displayed stretch, first
at position $i$ and later at position $j$. If the earlier position is the
start, I have already equated the unfinished state $u$ with a held state,
which is impossible.

Otherwise look one tick behind both occurrences. Those two predecessors
belong to $D_L$, and they have the same successor. The one-to-one rule on
$D_L$ says that the predecessors must therefore be equal. Move back another
tick on both sides and repeat. You eventually reach position zero on the
earlier side and position $j-i>0$ on the later side. In symbols, the repeated
backward comparison has given $u=F^{j-i}(u)$. The left side is unfinished;
the right side has entered $H$ and stayed there. That is the contradiction.

So all $L$ held samples are distinct. There are only $K$ states available
in $H$, giving $L\le K$. If the sources through $F^K(u)$ had no shared
successor, use $L=K+1$: you would need $K+1$ held states where only $K$ exist.
Finally, when the step is one-to-one everywhere, the backward comparison
works for any two finite positions in the run. No repetition is possible,
no matter how long you keep watching.
\end{proof}

Draw the smallest delayed example:
\[
u\longrightarrow h_1\longrightarrow h_2\longrightarrow h_2.
\]
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[thiele]
\node[pipe,text width=2.6cm,minimum width=0pt] (u) at (0,0)
  {Unfinished\\Reading: no};
\node[pipe,text width=2.6cm,minimum width=0pt] (a) at (4,0)
  {First\\holding state\\Screen: 42};
\node[pipe,text width=2.6cm,minimum width=0pt] (b) at (8,0)
  {Second\\holding state\\Screen: 42};
\draw[pipearrow] (u) -- node[above=28pt]{finish} (a);
\draw[pipearrow] (a) -- node[above=28pt]{hold} (b);
\draw[pipearrow] (b) edge[loop below] node[below]{hold again} (b);
\end{tikzpicture}

\small Only the unfinished state enters the first holding state. The two
holding states share a successor. The collision is later than the raise.
\end{center}

The screen says 42 at both $h_1$ and $h_2$. Only $u$ leads to $h_1$; the entry is clear.
The two arrows meet a tick later, when $h_1$ and $h_2$ both lead to $h_2$.
With $K$ holding configurations, the run exposes a collision within its first $K+1$
transitions from $u$.

You can reach the bound exactly. Hand me a guest run that halts after $T\ge1$ steps,
and let me use $K\ge1$ holding states. Line them up:
\[
\mathrm{prep}\longrightarrow a_0\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow a_{T-1}
\longrightarrow h_1\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow h_K\longrightarrow h_K.
\]
The preparation state shows nothing yet. Each $a_j$ shows that step of the guest run.
Every $h_j$ shows its final answer. There are $1+T+K$ full states. Starting at the last
running state, the first $K$ sources have different successors. Add the next source
and the arrows meet. The box uses every holding state before exposing the collision.

The camera can stop at 42. The box that keeps showing it still has a next step. Include
those steps and you can count exactly how long it can keep its full states apart.
\footnote{This is a state-capacity count. A ledger price requires a pricing rule;
a heat bound requires physical premises.}

\subsection{What a kept distinction is}

Now I turn to the cell. Blank is one of its logical states, alongside zero
and one. Give it a write-once rule: write zero when blank, and leave either
written value alone. That is what ``stays'' means in this example. The same
rule sends blank and zero to zero, so it has a collision. Whether that
collision removes uncertainty depends on which inputs were possible in the
preparation. Its physical heat needs the device and protocol as well.

And the cell isn't the lowest level. Describe whatever holds it, a bead in two dips, the molecules that
jostle the bead, whatever holds those, and you've described states that can be told apart and a way
they change: a machine of the same kind, charged the same way, because a merge one level up forces, one level down, either a merge or a state never used before, as long as the level above is exact about the level below and the level below stays among the states the one above describes (Theorem~\ref{thm:every-scale}). Every level you can describe is one of these. Under all
of them there's nothing told apart at all, and that's the nothing a blank cell stands for.

Preparation is a resource assumption too. A supplied known blank is a specified
initial condition, not evidence that a positive heat cost was paid earlier.
If an apparatus must reset an unknown input distribution for reuse, its reset
can incur an entropy-loss bound under Landauer's premises. Reeb and Wolf's
precise finite-dimensional formulation, for example, assumes an initially
thermal reservoir uncorrelated with the system and joint unitary evolution;
its heat bound is conditional on that setup. Inferring a past
or future payment from a known state alone would need more assumptions about
preparation, correlations, reuse and the thermal protocol.

The cell has three states: blank, zero, one. The reading is ``the cell is definite,'' no on blank and yes on
the other two, and a written cell stays written, so the reading is permanent. The move is
``write a 0,'' which takes blank to zero and leaves a written cell alone. Now look at where each state lands. Blank lands
on zero, and zero lands on zero, so two different states have led to the same place, and writing a 0 on nothing is, by itself,
a merge. For an input distribution with positive uncertainty between blank and 0,
this map removes entropy. Landauer's thermal premises then give a heat bound
for that loss. For a known blank, the input entropy is zero and this argument
gives no positive bound; it also implies no earlier payment for knowing. The history in which the cell was blank and the history in which it already held a 0
are now the same history. This is not an analogy to the step law; it's the step law with
three states filled in.

The obvious way round it is a fourth state that remembers: ``0, and it was blank before.'' Now
blank lands on a state nothing else has landed on. But the remembering state has to go somewhere on the next write
too, and it's written, so it has to stay written. Every written state already has something landing on it: zero
and one land on themselves, and the remembering state is where blank landed. So the remembering state has to share. In
the smallest version it lands on itself, and then blank and the remembering state land on the same
state. No finite extension of the cell gets out of the merge, and the reason is counting
(Proposition~\ref{prop:raise-needs-room}, two chapters on), not bad luck. The only way to write
with no merge, once every state has a next one, is a supply of fresh states that never runs out: a state never used before for every write, forever, such as a new cell of an endless
tape for each one (it comes back two chapters on, as the first of three ways out of a theorem). That isn't getting
out of what keeping takes. It dodges the floor by taking a state it has never used, at every write, without limit, and each write can dissipate under the stated thermal-model assumptions. Or, in a form I need below, a tape
that stretches both ways with the machine stepping one cell along it. Every cell has one before
it and one after it, nothing ever shares a landing, the reading ``past the start'' goes up on the first
step and never comes down, and the machine never returns. This is the bilateral shift, and it
pays at every step by taking a cell it has never used.

\begin{theorem}[The write of a 0 merges, and only fresh states avoid it]\label{thm:write-merge}
(1) On the three states blank, zero, one, with reading ``definite,'' writing a 0 is permanent,
raises the reading from blank, and merges blank with zero. (2) Adding a fourth state that
remembers the cell was blank, with written cells staying written, does not avoid the merge: on
the four states the write still merges two distinct states. The same holds on any finite set of
states. (3) On an endless tape, writing adds one cell and is one-to-one; on the integers, the
step ``one cell along'' is a bijection, raises ``past the start'' on the first step, keeps it
up, and after any positive number of steps is away from where it started.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(1) Blank and zero both step to zero, and blank is not zero; zero and one step to themselves,
so a written cell stays written. (2) Blank steps to the remembering state, and permanence sends
each of the three written states, zero, one and the remembering state, to a written state. So
four states land among the three written ones, and two of them share a landing. Whenever only finitely many states are written the same count works: permanence sends the finitely many written states
among themselves, blank lands among them too, so one more state lands among them than there are,
and two share a landing (Proposition~\ref{prop:raise-needs-room}, two chapters on, states it in
general). (3) ``Add
one'' on the counting numbers is one-to-one and never returns to zero; ``add one'' on the
integers is one-to-one and onto, sends 0 to 1, sends every number that is at least 1 to one that is at least 1, and
after $k>0$ steps has moved by $k$.
\end{proof}

The theorem leans on one thing, and I want it in the open. The write is a move defined on every
state of the cell, written ones included, and a written cell stays written, so the state blank merges
with is a cell that was already written. A write defined only on blank, with the machine simply
stopping when it meets a written cell, merges nothing. That's the stopping hole from above
(Theorem~\ref{thm:halting-hole}): it buys the 0 by having no next step at all.

The theorem buys this: a fact is a distinction that stays, and a kept distinction is a state the run has used and
can't give back. The machine is the thing whose own state includes the used states it can't give back.

It doesn't stop at the cell. The tape is a set of distinctions that stayed. So is the rule for
the next state, and so is the question you ask of a state. Each of the five parts of the model
is itself a definite thing where there could have been anything; the model doesn't charge for
them, but they're the same kind of thing it charges for. And the model can run itself: a host that obeys the toll and runs a guest move for move, carrying the guest's prices on its own ledger, pays at least one unit there for every step where the guest's record went up, and Part~III states
one (Section~\ref{sec:reach}; Appendix~\ref{sec:universal-machines} builds it). The tower is the same kind of machine above and below. What no level does is hold all the questions you can ask of it: for any way of coding
readings as states, there's a reading no state codes, the one that answers each state with the
opposite of what that state's own coded reading says of it. That's Cantor's diagonal, the shape
of Russell's 1902 letter to Frege (Section~\ref{sec:structure}), and the subject of Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}. Put the
two together and you have the regress exactly: every level runs the one below that way and pays again, in its own ledger, for every rise of the lower level's record, and no level ever holds every
question about itself.

\begin{theorem}[No level holds its own questions]\label{thm:no-self-containment}
For any set of states and any assignment of a yes/no reading to each state, some yes/no
reading on the states is assigned to no state.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Take the reading that says, of each state, the opposite of what that state's assigned reading
says of the state itself. If some state were assigned it, that state would answer itself both
ways.
\end{proof}

Write a 0 on a cell known to be blank and the entropy-loss premise sets
no positive floor: the input and output entropies are both zero
(Theorem~\ref{thm:known-state}). The thermal implementation can still have a
finite-time cost under the specified dynamical assumptions. A writer that
must handle both blank and 0 with one protocol faces a different question:
under the uniform two-input distribution its logical map removes one bit,
so Landauer's premises give an average heat bound. This does not charge
that average to every particular input.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[thiele]
\node[pipe,text width=3.5cm,minimum width=0pt] (known) at (0,0)
  {Supplied start: blank\\Chance one};
\node[pipe,text width=3.5cm,minimum width=0pt] (knownend) at (6,0)
  {End: zero\\Chance one};
\draw[pipearrow] (known) -- node[above=7pt]{write} (knownend);
\node[pipe,text width=3.5cm,minimum width=0pt] (spread) at (0,-2)
  {Possible starts: blank or zero\\Half the chance on each};
\node[pipe,text width=3.5cm,minimum width=0pt] (spreadend) at (6,-2)
  {End: zero\\Chance one};
\draw[pipearrow] (spread) -- node[above=7pt]{same write} (spreadend);
\end{tikzpicture}

\small The first preparation loses no uncertainty. The second loses one bit.
The transition rule is the same; the input preparation is different.
\end{center}

Keeping an exact answer among $N$ independently possible alternatives needs
at least $N$ representational states, or $\lceil\log_2 N\rceil$ bits in a
fixed-length binary encoding. That is a capacity bound. Identifying an
arbitrary one of three possibilities can require two binary questions in
the worst case; testing just ``is this cell blank?'' is a different, binary
task. Neither count proves that a known blank was prepared by an erasure or
that a heat bill has already been paid.

\subsection{A reversible machine keeps nothing}

Bennett's reversible machine never lets two of its states lead to the same next state; that's
what reversible means. Put one on finitely many states and watch it. By the pigeonhole it has to
revisit a state within as many steps as there are states. The step law says the first revisit is
a merge or a return to the start, and a merge is impossible for it, so it returns to its start,
and once it's back at its start it does everything again. Any reading it raised has come back
down. A reversible finite machine with a next state for every state keeps nothing, and that's
a theorem, not a slogan. One that stops slips past, as the stopping hole above says, and keeps
what it halted on. It is the recurrence Zermelo threw at
Boltzmann (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} tells that story), in its finite form, proved from the step law and the pigeonhole and nothing else.
What Bennett's machine keeps is the fresh states it's handed: on an endless tape it can keep its
whole history and never come back, taking a state it has never used at every step, and the tape
was paid for before the first step by whoever built it. A reversible machine dodges the merge and
its floor. For a specified thermal implementation, a finite-time change of distribution
can also require entropy production. Fresh states and physical dissipation are
different quantities; contact with surroundings alone supplies no numerical bound.

\begin{theorem}[Reversible keeps nothing]\label{thm:reversible-keeps-nothing}
Let a one-to-one step act on finitely many states. From any start the run returns to the start within as many steps as there are states, and any reading that is no at the start and never
goes from yes to no is no at every step.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Among the first (number of states) plus one states of the run, two are equal, by the
pigeonhole. Take two equal positions and cancel the one-to-one step back from both the same
number of times, until the earlier one reaches the start; the later one then equals the start.
So the run returns to the start after at most that many steps, and from then on repeats. If
the reading were yes at some step, it would stay yes from there, in particular at a later
multiple of the period, where the state is the start, which reads no.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Noisy steps}

Real states are noisy. The bead hops on its own. So take the step to be a table of chances:
from each state, the chance of landing on each state next, every row adding to one. A
permanent reading is a set of states you never leave once you're in it. And ``no merge'' has
an exact noisy meaning: the step preserves the even spread. Start with everybody spread evenly
over the states, take one step, and they're still spread evenly; which is to say every column
of the table adds to one as well as every row. Such a step squeezes nothing on average.

Then the cell's count goes through with chances in place of people. A step that preserves the even spread cannot raise
a permanent reading from any state outside it, and not merely with small chance but with none. Count the
chance flowing into the yes-states from everywhere. Column by column that's one per yes-state,
so it equals the number of yes-states. The yes-states alone already send exactly that much,
because they never leave. What's left over for the outside states is zero, and it's a sum of chances, so each is zero. The count never used that the spread was even, only that every state had some chance and the step gave the spread back. A lopsided memory that keeps its own lopsided spread can't raise a reading that stays either: weight each state by its chance and the same sum comes out.

And it runs the other way too. A step that can raise a permanent reading does not preserve the
even spread, so after one step from the even spread the crowd is more bunched up than it was.
Here is a way to measure that bunching. Draw a state twice, independently,
using the same spread of chances. Ask whether the two draws match. For two
equally likely states, the matching pairs have chances one quarter and one
quarter, so a match occurs half the time. Put three quarters of the chance
on one state and one quarter on the other: the matching chances are now nine
sixteenths and one sixteenth, adding to ten sixteenths. Bunching has made a
match more likely.

In general, a state with chance $q$ contributes $q^2$ to this matching chance:
$q$ for the first draw, times $q$ for the independent second draw. Add those
squares over all states. I call that total the \emph{collision weight}. The
step just described raises it above the value for an even spread.

There is another measure of the same change, Shannon entropy, which measures
uncertainty in the spread. It is largest when all states are equally likely,
so leaving that even spread lowers it. This is the quantity that enters the
heat bound under Landauer's premise. Section~\ref{sec:bits-zero} works through
its meaning in bits; the proof here establishes the drop. Finally, when a
step preserves the even spread, it cannot increase the collision weight of
\emph{any} starting spread. That last claim needs a calculation too.

\begin{theorem}[Noisy steps]\label{thm:noisy-chairs}
Let a step on finitely many states be a table of chances with rows adding to one, and let a
set of states be closed: from inside, the chance of leaving is zero. (1) If every column also
adds to one, the chance of entering the closed set from any state outside it is zero. (2) If
some state outside can enter the closed set with positive chance, then some column does not
add to one, and one step from the even spread strictly raises the collision weight, the sum of
the squared chances, which is least for the even spread, and it leaves a Shannon entropy
strictly below the logarithm of the number of states. (3) If every column adds to one, one step never raises the collision weight of any spread. \end{theorem} Part (1) needs only the closed set to be finite, the rest as large as you like, and part (3) needs no finiteness at all; part (2) needs the even spread, so it needs finitely many states.
\begin{proof}
(1) Count the total chance sent into the closed set. Each of its columns
sums to one, so the total equals the number of states in that set. The rows
belonging to states already inside send all their chance inside, and they
already supply that entire total. Nothing remains for an outside row to
contribute. Because every contribution is nonnegative, each outside
contribution is zero.

(2) Suppose instead that an outside state contributes a positive chance of
entry. Then the conclusion of (1) fails, so its column-sum condition cannot
hold: at least one column sum differs from one. Call the number of states
$N$ and the sum of column $j$ $c_j$. Starting evenly puts chance $1/N$ at
each source, so the chance at destination $j$ after the step is $c_j/N$.
The column sums themselves add to $N$, because the $N$ rows each add to one.
Expand the following squares and use that total:
\[
\sum_j(c_j-1)^2=\sum_j c_j^2-2\sum_j c_j+N
                 =\sum_j c_j^2-N.
\]
At least one square is positive. Thus $\sum_j c_j^2>N$. Dividing by $N^2$
says that the new collision weight is greater than $1/N$, the old even
spread's collision weight. Now compare the uncertainty before and after. Write $q_j=c_j/N$ for the new
chances. At least one differs from $1/N$. Shannon's entropy weights each
possible state's logarithmic uncertainty by its chance. Using the natural
logarithm, written $\ln$, its value is
\[
H(q)=-\sum_{j:q_j>0}q_j\ln q_j.
\]
The sum leaves out states with zero chance; they contribute nothing. An even
spread has $N$ equal terms, giving $H=\ln N$. Subtract the new entropy from
that value. Since the chances add to one, you can put $\ln N$ inside the sum:
\[
\ln N-H(q)=\sum_{j:q_j>0}q_j\ln(Nq_j).
\]
I need to show that this difference is positive, even though some individual
terms may be negative.

Use the elementary logarithm inequality $\ln y\le y-1$, with equality only
at $y=1$. One way to see it is to look at $y-1-\ln y$: its slope is
$1-1/y$, negative below one and positive above one, so its least value is
zero at one. Apply the inequality with $y=1/(Nq_j)$ and multiply by $q_j$.
Rearranging gives
\[
q_j\ln(Nq_j)\ge q_j-1/N,
\]
with equality only when $q_j=1/N$. A zero chance contributes zero to the
entropy difference, which is strictly greater than its comparison term
$-1/N$. Add the comparisons over all $N$ states. Their right sides sum to
$1-N/N=0$. At least one comparison is strict because the new spread is not
even, so the entropy difference is positive.

(3) Fix a destination column. Because its entries add to one, its new chance
is an average of the old chances, with those entries as weights. An average
of squares is never less than the square of the average. To see why, call
the weights $w_i$, the old chances $p_i$, and their weighted average $m$.
Expanding gives
\[
\sum_i w_i(p_i-m)^2=\sum_i w_i p_i^2-m^2\ge0,
\qquad \sum_i w_i=1,\quad m=\sum_i w_i p_i.
\]
So the new chance squared is at most the weighted sum of the old chances
squared. Add this comparison over all destination columns. Each old chance
squared gets weights from its whole row, whose sum is one. The result is
exactly the old collision weight, bounding the new one from above.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Unitary steps}

The quantum version needs a different picture. Draw a sheet through the centre of
a room. Call every direction along the sheet YES, and the direction straight
through it NO. Turn the whole arrangement without stretching it. Can the sheet
stay within its old plane while the direction through it turns into that plane?
No. The turn keeps right angles. If the sheet still fills that plane, the direction
that was at right angles to the whole sheet is still at right angles to it.

Here is what carries from that picture into the quantum statement. A quantum
state is described by a vector. A reversible quantum step preserves lengths
and overlaps between vectors; such a step is called \emph{unitary}. The YES
part is a \emph{subspace}: a collection of directions that also contains their
linear combinations. The directions with zero overlap with every YES direction
make up its \emph{orthogonal complement}. These are the NO states in this argument.
Permanence means that a vector in the YES subspace stays in it after the step.

There is one detail to settle before the right-angle argument works. The old
YES directions must fill the whole YES subspace after the step, leaving no
missing direction. Choose a finite list of directions from which every YES vector can be
assembled, with none of the listed directions assembled from the others.
Such a list is called an independent spanning list, or a basis. A unitary step keeps the
list independent, since any relation between its images could be reversed to
give the same relation before the step. The images are still inside the YES
subspace, and there are just as many independent directions as before. They
therefore still span it. That is why the step fills the YES subspace, rather
than merely landing somewhere inside it.

Now take a NO vector. Before the step it has zero overlap with every YES
vector. After the step those overlaps are still zero, and the stepped YES
vectors still fill the whole YES subspace. The stepped NO vector is therefore
still NO. Repeat the step and the same argument applies again.

Finite dimension was used exactly once: a full finite list of independent
YES directions still fills the YES subspace after the step. Drop it and the bilateral
shift, which is unitary on an endless ladder of states, raises ``past the start'' on the first
step and keeps it forever, taking a state it has never used every time. A reading that stays,
which no unitary step can raise in finite dimension, is paid for either by fresh states, a ladder
of states that never comes back around, or by a step that squeezes the even spread, which, when
the squeezed states were really possible, owes Landauer's floor. Not every step that fails to be
unitary squeezes: one that keeps the even spread, as pure dephasing and an unread projective measurement do,
can't raise a reading that stays either. The balance argument is the same one used for noisy steps. Choose a complete
set of mutually perpendicular directions, some filling the YES subspace and
the rest filling its orthogonal complement. Spread the chances equally over
those directions. This is the fully mixed state: choosing a different complete
perpendicular set gives the same mixture.

Suppose there are $N$ directions altogether and $m$ of them are YES. The
mixture has chance $m/N$ of YES. A step that preserves this mixture must leave
that chance at $m/N$. But the YES part already supplies all of it: it started
with weight $m/N$, and permanence keeps that whole weight inside YES. Every
contribution from the other directions is nonnegative, so none can contribute
any chance of entering YES. You can include any chosen NO vector among the
perpendicular directions of the complement. The same balance then rules out
entry from that vector. That is why the outside cannot get in. In finite dimension nothing is kept without
one of the two. Which way a quantum measurement pays when its outcome is kept isn't settled
here. The collapse models people test keep the even spread too, so the heat the experiments look
for is the heat of the noise those models add, not a Landauer price on a kept outcome; I come
back to them below.

\begin{theorem}[Unitary steps]\label{thm:quantum-chairs}
Let a unitary map a finite-dimensional subspace into itself. Then it maps the
orthogonal complement into itself: a state orthogonal to the subspace remains orthogonal after
every step.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Call the step $U$ and the YES subspace $Y$. Choose a basis of $Y$, meaning an
independent list from which every vector in $Y$ can be assembled. The step sends
that list to an equally long independent list inside $Y$, so its images are
another basis of $Y$.

Take any vector $x$ orthogonal to $Y$. To test whether $Ux$ is still orthogonal,
choose any vector $y$ in $Y$. Because the images fill $Y$, there is a vector
$z$ in $Y$ with $Uz=y$. Unitarity preserves the overlap, written with angle
brackets, so
\[
\langle Ux,y\rangle=\langle Ux,Uz\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle=0.
\]
The last equality holds because $x$ is orthogonal to every vector in $Y$,
including $z$. The choice of $y$ was arbitrary, so $Ux$ is orthogonal to all
of $Y$. This is the same condition I started with, and it survives every
further step.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Going faster gives off more heat}

Everything so far was what keeping takes. What comes next is a dissipation result for a particular stochastic model.
Bennett's Brownian computer is a walker on a line that is pushed forward a little: at
each tick it steps forward with some chance and back with the rest. Its speed is the
difference between the two. A forward translation is one-to-one, and so is a backward translation. The random choice between them is a stochastic rule, not one deterministic translation; the deterministic merge count does not apply to it as though it were. The entropy
it gives off per tick is Schnakenberg's formula for a biased walk, the speed times the logarithm
of the forward-to-backward ratio, and that number is strictly positive at any speed other than
zero, because both factors have the same sign. The only walker that gives off nothing is the one
with no drift, as likely to step back as forward. This is the point that going slower doesn't get you out of paying, now as a theorem: at any speed you actually run it,
every tick gives off heat on average.

The exchange rate has a floor as well. Heat per net step forward, counted in units of $kT$, is the
logarithm of the forward-to-backward ratio, and that logarithm is at least the speed. So walking
a distance costs at least distance times speed in heat and takes distance over speed in time,
and heat times time is at least the distance squared. At low speed, halve the speed and the
heat roughly halves while the time doubles; the product never drops below the square of how far
you went. Going slowly makes the mean heat for a specified amount of directed progress
smaller and its drift time longer. These are averages. With no bias, the
walker still moves, and it can reach a nearby target on the first tick.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[thiele]
\node[pipe,text width=2.6cm,minimum width=0pt] (start) at (0,0)
  {Start at zero};
\node[pipe,text width=3.8cm,minimum width=0pt] (back) at (6,1.3)
  {One place back\\Half the chance};
\node[pipe,text width=3.8cm,minimum width=0pt] (forward) at (6,-1.3)
  {Target: one place ahead\\Half the chance};
\draw[pipearrow] (start.east) -- (back.west);
\draw[pipearrow] (start.east) -- (forward.west);
\end{tikzpicture}

\small The mean displacement is zero. Half the paths reach this target on
the first tick. Zero drift does not mean no movement or no completed paths.
\end{center}

Below, distance divided by speed is the time scale for the mean displacement
to advance that distance. It is not the duration of every path that happens
to finish.

\begin{theorem}[Heat against time]\label{thm:time-bill}
For a walker stepping forward with chance $p$ and back with chance $1-p$, with $0<p<1$, the
entropy it hands to its surroundings per tick, $(2p-1)\ln\frac{p}{1-p}$, is zero at $p=\tfrac12$
and strictly positive otherwise. With speed $v = 2p-1$ in $(0,1)$ and distance $N \ge 0$, the mean heat in units
of $kT$ for drift progress $N$, $N\ln\frac{1+v}{1-v}$, times the drift time $N/v$ is at least $N^2$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $p > \tfrac12$ both factors are positive and for $p < \tfrac12$ both are negative, by the
monotonicity of the logarithm; at $p=\tfrac12$ the first factor is zero. For the floor,
$\ln(1+v) \ge 0$ and $\ln(1-v) \le -v$ since $\ln y \le y - 1$, so
$\ln\frac{1+v}{1-v} \ge v$, and the product is $N^2$ times that logarithm divided by $v$.
\end{proof}

That is the surroundings' share of the entropy production. The whole of it adds the change in
the walker's own spread, which on a line keeps growing but ever more slowly, so per tick that
share goes to zero and the long-run rate is the heat's.

The sharp floor is twice that. The difference $\ln\frac{1+v}{1-v} - 2v$ is zero at $v = 0$ and
its derivative, $\frac{2}{1-v^2} - 2$, is never negative on $(0,1)$, so the logarithm is at least
$2v$ and the product is at least $2N^2$. I state $N^2$ because the one-line bound gives it, and
what matters is the square, not the factor in front of it.

Keeping something costs, on top of that, either a merge, which under Landauer's premise owes a floor of
$kT\ln 2$ per bit that no slowness removes, or a state the device has never used before. Taking a
fresh state escapes the floor and does not settle the implementation's finite-time dissipation. And a finite set of states,
where every state has a next one, forces the merge.

\subsection{Every scale pays the same way}

One more question, and it's the one that decides whether any of this is about the world or
only about my pictures. A state is a description. The dial on a lab bench is a state, and so
is each atom in it, and so is each atom together with the light it gave off. Describe the same
thing coarser or finer and you get different states. Does what keeping takes change with the zoom?

It doesn't, and the reason fits in one picture. Draw the fine states, and draw a fence around each
group of them that counts as one coarse state. Say the coarse picture merges: two coarse states
step to one coarse state. Then, when the fine states are finitely many, the fine step can't keep
them all apart either. Count them. If the fine step sent different fine states to different fine states
and none of them stepped out of the fenced set, it would be a reshuffle of the fine states, with every
fine state landed on exactly once afterwards. But some fenced group is now landed on by nothing, because the coarse step
missed a coarse state (two coarse states went to one, so on a finite set some coarse state
is stepped to by nothing), and so nothing lands on any fine state in that group. A reshuffle leaves no state out. So
something gave: the fine step merges too, or some fine state stepped out of the fenced set, or the
fenced set has no end. The three ways come back one level down, though stepping out of the fenced set isn't taking a fresh state; it's
where the coarse picture stops tracking the fine one.

\begin{theorem}[Every scale pays the same way]\label{thm:every-scale}
Let a fine machine have one rule $F$ on a set $X$ of states, let $A$ be a set of its states, and
let a coarse description be a map $\pi$ from $X$ to a set $S$ of coarse states that takes $A$
onto $S$, with a coarse rule $f$ on $S$ such that $\pi(F(x)) = f(\pi(x))$ for every $x$ in $A$.
If the coarse rule merges two coarse states, then at least one of these holds: $F$ merges two
states of $A$; $F$ takes some state of $A$ outside $A$; or some run of $F$ from a state of $A$ stays in $A$ and never comes back to a state it has visited. \end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose the fine machine avoids all three ways out. It stays inside $A$, keeps different
states apart, and every run eventually visits a state it has visited before. Follow one
run to its first repeat. The two visits have the same state, so their predecessors must
agree too: different predecessors are never allowed to land together. Walk backwards
like that until the earlier visit reaches the start. The later visit has reached the
same start. The run is a loop from the start, with no loose approach leading into it.

Now watch that loop through the coarse window. Every fine step gives the coarse step
specified by $f$. When the fine state returns to its start, its picture returns too.
Every coarse state has a fine state above it, because $\pi$ takes $A$ onto $S$.
So every coarse state also lies on a loop.

That rules out a coarse merge. Suppose two different coarse starts had the same next
state. Call the lengths of their loops $L_1$ and $L_2$. Wait $L_1L_2$ steps from the
starts: that is a whole number of circuits for both loops, so each must be back at its
own start. But after their first step they were together. The same rule cannot separate
them afterwards, so at the end of that wait they are still together. Their starts must
have been the same after all.

The coarse rule does merge, by hypothesis. The fine machine therefore cannot avoid
all three alternatives. In the last alternative, every tick visits another state of
$A$, so no finite collection can hold the run.
\end{proof}

When I say a coarse description is exact about a set of fine states, I mean what the theorem asks: it follows the fine step on the set, and every coarse state describes some state in it. Put it next to the permanent flip. On a finite coarse picture, a reading that goes up and stays
up is raised by a merge (the cell above, on three states; Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges}, two
chapters on, in general). By this theorem, at every finer
description that the coarse one is exact about, keeping that reading is again a merge, though not always where the reading rose, or a step off the described states, or a run that takes a fresh described state at every step. The dial and its
light are the example. In the dial's own picture, two blends of readings decay to one
either-or, a merge (Section~\ref{sec:pointer}). In the picture of dial and light together, the
step is one-to-one, and it's the second case: the light starts blank and leaves carrying the
copy, so the fine step leaves the set of states where the light is still blank. At the fine scale
nothing merges; the step leaves the states the coarse picture describes. And the heat floor sits where the merge
really is. Landauer's premise charges the scale whose step merges states that were really
possible; a description that merges only because it stopped looking at the light owes that
floor nowhere merely because of that projection. Leaving the set where the light is blank is not the
same as visiting a fresh full state at every later tick. To infer an endless
fresh-state run, the theorem needs its third alternative. To infer heat,
specify the physical preparation and what happens to the light or reservoir.

\subsection{What keeping takes, and where the toll comes in}

So that's the whole of what keeping takes, set out before anybody writes a price on anything. The toll, which the
next chapter states, is what keeping takes, written into a step. It's the price of something being the case: a reading that goes from no
to yes and stays is a distinction that stays, and a distinction that stays is a state the run has used and can't
give back. Anything whose state includes distinctions it can't give back pays what the toll prices:
the bead, the cell, the memory bit, a world with a past. Give one a price list that obeys the toll
and it's a Thiele machine, and when the cell could have held anything, Landauer's premise puts a
heat floor under that raise, because on a finite cell the raise is a merge. The toll keeps its
shape there, charged in heat instead of units of cost. And what keeping takes, deterministic or noisy or
