forgetting isn't a second kind of price beside the toll. What the premise chooses is which
readings the toll answers to: the flag alone, or every reading a move keeps.

There is one more way to see the same thing, and I give it because it answers a rival I'd otherwise owe you. The
rival says: leave certification alone. Price \emph{erasure}, and keep an honest flag that reports
when something was erased. Fine; but a system can set its certificate at cost zero with its
erasure flag reporting nothing, exactly because the certifying move merged two states and
the flag didn't say so. Make the erasure
flag honest, so that it reports every move that forgets, and on a finite machine with a
flag that stays up the erasure law charges the same cost the toll does. The toll isn't a rival to
honest erasure accounting; it's what honest erasure accounting says about the certifying
move.

So, is the toll arbitrary? The honest answer is that the toll is a consequence of three
things: finitely many states that read yes (a finite memory is plenty), a flag that stays up,
and a charge on forgetting. If you accept all three, you don't get to refuse the toll; it's
forced. If you refuse any one of them, the toll on my ledger goes back to being my preference.
The cost stays where it was; what's gone is the proof that my ledger has to charge it. So the question ``did I have to pick it'' has turned into
three smaller questions, which is what progress usually looks like: a better set of things to argue about. Let me take the three ways out in order, and for each one
build the machine that leaves through it, because a premise you can't see the counterexample
to is a premise you're taking on faith.

\subsection{The first way out: keep everything, and pay by taking fresh states}

Take a strip of paper that never runs out of boxes. The machine's whole state is the strip.
Each move writes a 1 in the next empty box, and the flag is up as soon as any box has a 1 in
it.
Check the three premises. It is permanent: once there's a 1, there's always a 1. It flips: the empty
strip reads NO, and after one move it reads YES. It forgets nothing: every move can be undone by
erasing the last 1, so two different strips never become the same strip. So this is a machine
that raises a flag, keeps it up, and never merges anything. The theorem that a permanent flip on a finite machine merges has no grip on
it, and a price list that charges only merges doesn't charge it. But look at what each move does:
it writes in a box nobody has written in before. The raise takes a fresh box, and so does every
step after it, forever. It hasn't got out of paying. It's paying in the other column, by taking a state it has never used, and
a price list that only charges merges isn't looking at that column. (Each physical write may incur a model-dependent finite-time cost; what the strip dodges is the
floor a merge would add on top.) In the exact form its state is a row of 1s of any length, which is how you say the strip has no end.

If the endless strip feels like a cheat, it's a famous one. David Hilbert, in a lecture course in the winter of 1924--25, told a story about a hotel with infinitely many rooms, every one of them taken,
where a new guest still gets a room: everybody moves from room $n$ to room $n+1$, and room 1 is left empty. The hotel is that other column, the fresh states, told as a joke about a front desk: nobody shares, and every
guest in the building packs up and moves one room along, into a room that's occupied as he moves,
by a guest who's moving on at the same moment, so that one room at the front is left empty. The guests go one-to-one into a part of the hotel, with
a gap left over.
The part worth checking is that Hilbert never published it. The hotel became famous
because George Gamow put it in a popular book in 1947, and for a long time it wasn't clear Hilbert had told it at all. The historian of science Helge
Kragh first guessed that Gamow had made it up. Then Tilman Sauer, a historian of science who
had co-edited a volume of Hilbert's lectures on the foundations of physics, pointed him to Hilbert's lecture
notes, which had just been printed in 2013, and in 2014 Kragh took his guess back in a paper called
``The True (?) Story of Hilbert's Infinite Hotel.'' Keep the question mark. Even Kragh's own paper
puts the lecture in January 1924 in one place and January 1925 in another. Still, this time a story
everybody repeated turned out to have a real lecture behind it. I've learned not to count on that
happening. Bring it back to the table. In the closed room, the person from the door had nowhere to sit because the chairs ran out. In Hilbert's hotel they never do, so everybody shifts one
over and nobody has to share. The strip machine is that hotel. The argument stays the same.
What the hotel shows you is that the whole argument was about running out of states all along.

What walked out is the finiteness premise. Now cut the strip to eight boxes.
Keep the same rule: fill the next blank box from the left, leaving every
earlier mark alone. There are nine possible strips, including the blank one.
After eight moves the strip is full. What should the ninth move do?
If a full strip stays full, the seven-mark strip and the full strip both
go to the full strip. That is the collision. If the machine stops instead,
its next-step rule is partial. If it clears the strip, its YES reading
comes down. Each escape changes a premise.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}cll@{}}
Marks so far & Strip & Next strip under the stay-full rule \\ \hline
0 & \texttt{00000000} & \texttt{10000000} \\
1 & \texttt{10000000} & \texttt{11000000} \\
$\vdots$ & $\vdots$ & $\vdots$ \\
7 & \texttt{11111110} & \texttt{11111111} \\
8 & \texttt{11111111} & \texttt{11111111} \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Eight unrestricted bits have 256 configurations. These nine are the ones
this particular prefix-filling rule permits. A fresh configuration need
not use a fresh physical box; changing a pattern can reach one too.
Keeping the whole history is exactly the move Bennett made in 1973, when he showed
that any computation can be done without forgetting if you let it keep a copy of everything it
did; Landauer, back in 1961, had already written that for a machine able to run a program that doesn't stop, the
space to hold every intermediate result ``cannot be there.'' Keeping the history is a real way
to pay. It costs a memory that never fills, and every machine you can buy has a memory that fills.

Bennett wasn't the first there, or the last. Yves Lecerf, in a short note to the French
Academy of Sciences in 1963, had already shown that reversible Turing machines can simulate
arbitrary ones, and the note went largely unnoticed. The computer scientist Tommaso Toffoli
(1980), and Edward Fredkin and Toffoli together (1982), both then at MIT, built reversible logic:
gates and circuits that compute any function and lose nothing, by carrying constant inputs in and
extra outputs out. Their basic gate wasn't new even then. Landauer's own 1961 paper writes down a
three-bit device that replaces $r$ by $p \cdot q$ when $r$ is 0 and by the negation of $p \cdot q$
when $r$ is 1,
calls it logically reversible and capable of an AND, and says each AND then needs its own supplied
ZERO and leaves its extra outputs behind. He doubted such a machine could be useful. What Toffoli
added was the proof that it computes everything. And the computer scientist Kenichi Morita (1996) proved that reversible
two-counter machines are universal, so even a machine as small as the one Section~\ref{sec:smallest} builds, handed its input encoded, can compute everything with every move one-to-one. Every one of them keeps what it doesn't forget somewhere:
a history, garbage outputs, a counter that codes the past. The strip is one of those: it keeps the whole history, box by box.

There are three separate claims here, and I need to keep them apart. The
strip machine is permanent and forgets nothing. It also has infinitely many states:
no finite list holds every finite strip. Neither of those involves a cost. The third does: the
strip can raise its reading at zero cost. Count the strip's length as a whole number and let each move add one at a price of zero.
Nothing merges, merge pricing holds, and the toll fails. This is what a price list that charges
merges and nothing else looks like on a machine with endlessly many states to take: the raised reading shows up at no
charge on the ledger because the column it's paid in is one the price list doesn't charge.

The same thing holds for one move instead of a run, and in that form it says exactly how many states the move needs.

\begin{proposition}[A raise with no merge takes endlessly many states]\label{prop:raise-needs-room}
Let a move never turn a reading from yes to no, let it raise the reading at some state $s$ (no
at $s$, yes where the move sends $s$), and let it send no two different states to the same
state. Then it sends the states that read yes one-to-one into a part of themselves that leaves
at least one of them out: the state the move sends $s$ to. So there are infinitely many states
that read yes. With finitely many, the raising move merges two states.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The move sends every yes-state to a yes-state, because it never turns yes to no, and it sends
different states to different states. It sends $s$ to a yes-state. If some yes-state $c$ were
also sent there, the move would send $s$ and $c$ to one state, so $s = c$; but $s$ reads no and
$c$ reads yes. So the yes-states are sent one-to-one into the yes-states with that one left out.
If there were only $n$ yes-states, that would put $n$ things one-to-one into $n - 1$ places,
which the pigeonhole forbids. So there are infinitely many.
\end{proof}

The proposition is Hilbert's front desk as a theorem, and it's also exactly how Richard Dedekind
defined an infinite collection in 1888: one that can be matched one-to-one with a part of itself
that leaves something out. So with no merge, every raise has to send the kept things one-to-one
into a part of themselves with a gap left over, and only endlessly many of them have a gap to
spare.
Taking a fresh state isn't the absence of what keeping takes but the other way of paying it, and only a machine with endlessly many states
can keep paying that way.

\emph{Which state is being counted.} Whether a move merges depends on what the state keeps. The
strip keeps its history, so nothing merges; cut it to eight boxes and the stay-full rule merges.
Section~\ref{sec:landauer} proves the general form (Theorem~\ref{thm:u24-history}): keep the
list of every earlier state alongside the current one and every fixed-instruction step is
one-to-one. (Keeping only the one state before isn't enough: two states that differ only in what
came before them still land together.) So a merge
price is a fact about a move on a stated state space. Each price derived in this book is derived
on the whole state its definition gives, and three things go with it: which state that is, what
lies outside it (nothing outside it is charged), and whether the move is one primitive instruction
or a composite run of several. Relabelling the states one-to-one changes no price, since it sends
merges to merges and one-to-one moves to one-to-one moves. Adding history to the state, or
projecting part of the state away, changes the machine being modelled, and the price can change
with it.

The first way out deserves a number, because ``a memory that never fills'' is doing all the work and
I'd rather see what keeping takes than take it on trust.

\begin{proposition}[Merge, or a fresh state every step]\label{prop:heat-or-room}
(1) Let a machine run by one rule, so that every state has exactly one next state, and let its
reading never go from yes back to no. Take any run in which the reading goes from no to yes.
Then either some step of the run merges two of its states (two different states of the run
have the same next state), or the run never visits the same state twice. So on a machine with $M$ states, a run that keeps a record
and never merges has fewer than $M$ steps. (2) Let an operation send every value to one fixed
value and leave that value alone. Take a machine with $M$ states run by one rule, a reading of
its states, and $N$ different starting states, exactly one of which already reads the fixed
value, such that from every start each of the next $T$ states reads the fixed value. If no two
different states among those the runs sit in at steps $0$ to $T-1$ have the same next state
(the operation is carried out through $T$ repetitions without merging), then
$M \ge 1 + (T+1)(N-1)$. When $N \ge 2$, a bounded memory delays the merge and does not avoid it; with only the resting start there need be no merge.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(1) Suppose no two different states of the run share a next state, and suppose the run still
visits some state twice, once early and once later. Walk the two visits back together, one step
at a time: two equal states whose predecessors are both in the run had equal predecessors,
because nothing merged. The early visit gets back to the start first, and the later visit is
then at the start too. So the run comes back to its start after some number $p$ of
steps, and since one rule gives the next state, it comes back again after $2p$, $3p$, and so on
forever. The start reads no: a yes there would stay yes all along, and the reading does go from
no to yes. Some of those returns come after the raise, where the reading is yes and stays yes,
and each of them is the start, which reads no. So the repeat was impossible. A run that never
merges takes a state it hasn't used at every step, and with $M$ states that's at most $M - 1$
steps.
(2) Count the states along paths. Walking two equal states back together, as in (1), is allowed
at any step from $1$ to $T$, because the states one step earlier are at steps $0$ to $T-1$.
Each of the $N - 1$ starts not already in the fixed reading, followed through $T$ repetitions,
occupies $T + 1$ states, and none twice: a repeat would walk back to the start equalling a later
state of its own path, and every later state reads the fixed value while the start does not. Two
of those paths cannot share a state either: walk back to the earlier time, and either two
different starts are one state, or a start is a state that reads the fixed value. That
is $(T+1)(N-1)$ states. The start that already reads the fixed value, followed through $T$
repetitions, ends in one more: if that state were on one of the paths, walking back would again
put a start at a state that reads the fixed value. One more is all that start is owed, not
$T + 1$: every state on its own path reads the fixed value, so walking back along it finds no
contradiction, and the path may fold onto one state, as it does in the machine built below.
\end{proof}

The number is exact, not only a floor, and you can build the machine that reaches it. One
state for the start that already reads the fixed way; the operation leaves it there.
For every other start, lay out a row of states, one state longer than the number of
repetitions you want to survive. The first state in the row reads the way that start reads,
the rest read the fixed way, and the operation walks the row, sending its last state to
the common fixed state. This also works for zero requested repetitions, when a row
contains only its start. Count the states: one, plus a row for each of the other starts.
For as many repetitions as you asked for, no two distinct visited source states land on
one. If there is at least one other start, the next repetition merges its row's last state
with the fixed state: both go to the fixed state. With no other start, the one fixed state
idles forever and no finite retention horizon follows. A single fixed reading isn't
needed either. If the operation sends every state to one of a few resting states and leaves each
resting state alone, and every resting state is one of the starts, the same walking back counts the same rows
inside each resting state's own catchment, the starts that end at it. The total comes to one state per start, plus, for every
repetition, one more state for each start that isn't a resting state. With one resting state that is the
bound in the proposition, and the same rows in each catchment show it exact.
In the exact form: $N$ starts, $L$ of them resting states, $T$ repetitions, at least $N + T(N - L)$ states,
and that many are enough. In bits: a memory of $B$ bits has at most $2^B$ states, so surviving $T$
repetitions with one resting state takes $B \ge \log_2\bigl(1 + (T+1)(N-1)\bigr)$. The memory grows with the
logarithm of how long the history is kept; a fresh state at every step isn't a fresh cell at every
step.

So the strip uses fresh configurations for as long as its record stays up
without a collision. Cut its permitted state space to a finite size and
the counting bound applies. A configuration is a pattern, not a newly
allocated cell. Bennett's 1989 construction saves storage by undoing and
redoing intermediate work while retaining enough to recover it. Those
extra transitions buy a time--space tradeoff. They do not let a fixed
autonomous run under this fresh-state premise reuse a configuration.

Bennett's Brownian model supplies a separate tradeoff: reducing its bias
reduces its mean forward speed and its heat per net forward step. At zero
bias its mean drift is zero, although individual random walks still move.
Theorem~\ref{thm:time-bill} concerns that model, not every physical step.
There are two accounts: configurations in the structural argument, and
entropy production under specified thermal dynamics. The total autonomous
run just counted, after a new permanent raise, must have a collision
somewhere in its continued orbit or take endlessly fresh states. The
collision need not be on the entry arrow. Counting gives that alternative;
a physical implementation determines its resource costs.

\subsubsection*{Two levers, and whether their hidden moves commute}

Put two reset levers on the box. Pull left then right, and look at the tabletop.
Now start over and pull right then left. The picture agrees. Open the box as well:
are all its hidden parts in the same places? That is the extra demand in this example.
The order of the levers must leave the whole machine the same.

Use three tabletop values, $0,1,2$. The first lever wipes only $1$ to $0$. The second
wipes only $2$ to $0$. They commute on the tabletop. Choose one starting full state above
each value and allow every word of at most $T$ lever pulls. Call everything reached by
depth $t$ $R_t$. Through the promised horizon, each lever must give different successors
to different states in $R_{T-1}$, even if those states were reached at different times.
You know which lever was pulled, so the two levers may reuse a landing state.

\begin{proposition}[The exact room for exclusive resets]\label{prop:exclusive-room}
For $T\ge1$, the minimum finite installed carrier has $T+3$ states without a commutation
requirement, and $2T+2$ with commuting hidden levers. These are also the respective
minimum sizes of $R_T$ when larger carriers are allowed. With commuting levers that are
one-to-one on their \emph{whole} domain, the minimum $|R_T|$ is $2T+3$, attained for every
$T$ by one infinite machine. At $T=0$ the reachable minimum is three in each class.
\end{proposition}

Count the zero states first. Write $F,G$ for the hidden levers and $z,a,b$ for the starts
reading $0,1,2$. At depth $t$, let $Z_t$ contain the states reading zero. The first lever
takes every state in $Z_t$, and also $a$, into $Z_{t+1}$. Their successors must be distinct.
So $|Z_t|\ge t+1$. Add $a$ and $b$ and there are at least $T+3$ states.

A single line of zero states reaches that number. Use $z_0,\ldots,z_T$, advance the line
with either lever, and fix its last state. Put $F(a)=z_0$, $G(b)=z_0$, $G(a)=a$ and
$F(b)=b$. The final zero state stays outside $R_{T-1}$. Try the levers in opposite orders
at $a$, though, and the hidden states disagree. To make them commute, count again.

\begin{proof}[Counting when the hidden levers commute]
Start above $1$ and pull only the lever that leaves $1$ alone on the tabletop.
The hidden box can still move. Watch its first $T+1$ states,
$a,G(a),\ldots,G^T(a)$. Do the matching experiment above $2$, watching
$b,F(b),\ldots,F^T(b)$. The first list reads $1$ throughout; the second reads $2$.
If either list never repeats, its $T+1$ states, the at least $T+1$ zero states already
counted, and the other starting state give $2T+3$. There is enough room already.

So suppose both lists repeat. A deterministic run first follows an approach and then
enters a loop. Let the first approach take $r$ pulls and its loop take $p$ pulls;
let the second take $s$ and $q$. The loop lengths $p,q$ are at least one.
Call their first loop states $\alpha=G^r(a)$ and $\beta=F^s(b)$.
There are $r+p$ different states on the first approach and loop, and $s+q$ on the second.
All have been reached within the promised horizon.

At those loop states, switch levers. From $\alpha$, the first $F$ pull changes the
reading from $1$ to zero. From $\beta$, the first $G$ pull changes $2$ to zero.
There are $L=T-r$ pulls left in the first experiment and $M=T-s$ in the second.
Write the resulting two rows of zero states as
\[
A=\{F(\alpha),\ldots,F^L(\alpha)\},\qquad
C=\{G(\beta),\ldots,G^M(\beta)\}.
\]
Neither row repeats. If two entries agreed, walk their predecessors backwards together.
All those predecessors occur by depth $T-1$, where the lever keeps sources apart.
Eventually the earlier entry would reach the nonzero seed while the later one still
read zero. That is impossible. The rows therefore contain $L$ and $M$ states.

Can the rows cross? Suppose their $i$th and $j$th entries are the same state.
Pull $F$ another $q$ times. Seen from the second row, commutation lets you do those
pulls at $\beta$ before its $j$ pulls of $G$. They take $\beta$ once around its loop
and bring it back. So the shared state returns to itself after those $q$ pulls of $F$.
The same argument, exchanging the levers, returns it after $p$ pulls of $G$:
\[
F^{i+q}(\alpha)=F^i(\alpha),\qquad
G^{j+p}(\beta)=G^j(\beta).
\]
I have just proved there are no repeats within either displayed row. The returns must
therefore lie beyond their ends: $i+q>L$ and $j+p>M$. Only the last $q$ entries
of the first row and the last $p$ of the second can be shared. There are at most
$\min(p,q)$ shared states.

Now add the two nonzero lists and both zero rows, subtracting the shared entries once:
\[
|R_T|\ge(r+p)+(s+q)+L+M-\min(p,q)=2T+\max(p,q).
\]
The approach lengths disappear because every pull spent on an approach leaves one fewer
pull for its zero row. If either loop has length at least two, the count is at least $2T+2$.

Only two one-state loops remain: $p=q=1$. If the zero rows do not meet, adding them
without a subtraction gives $2T+2$. If they meet, the crossing restriction puts their
only shared state at both ends. Call it $c$. It is fixed by both levers.
The initial zero state $z$ must now supply another place. To see why, suppose it lay on
one of the rows. Starting there would reach $c$ in at most $T-1$ pulls. The state just
before $c$ on the first row is also reachable by then, and is different from $c$.
The first lever sends both to $c$, violating its promise on $R_{T-1}$.
Thus $z$ lies outside both rows. Count it, and the total is $2T+2$ again.

Finally strengthen the promise: each lever keeps different sources apart everywhere,
even beyond the horizon. A crossing would give the return
$F^{i+q}(\alpha)=F^i(\alpha)$ above. Now you may walk backwards all $i$ steps,
without a horizon restriction, giving $F^q(\alpha)=\alpha$. The left side reads zero
and the right side reads $1$. So in this case the rows cannot cross at all.
Their count with the nonzero lists is $2T+p+q$, which is at least $2T+3$ unless
both loop lengths are one.

In that last case you need one more state. If $z$ is outside the rows, it is the extra
state. If it lies at $F^i(\alpha)$ on the first row, pull $F$ from $z$ another $T$
times. This is allowed from an initial state and reaches $F^{T+i}(\alpha)$.
The whole zero row can never repeat under the global promise, by the same backward
argument used earlier. This new state lies past its displayed end. It cannot be on
the other row either, because the crossing argument still applies, however far you go.
Its zero reading also keeps it off the two nonzero lists. If $z$ lies on the second
row, pull $G$ instead and make the same count. Every case gives at least $2T+3$.
\end{proof}

Build the finite box with two arms and a shared endpoint. The $F$-arm has
$a_0,\ldots,a_{T-1}$; the $G$-arm has $b_0,\ldots,b_T$. Each lever advances its own arm
and fixes the opposite arm. Both fix the common end. Read $a_0$ as $1$, $b_0$ as $2$,
and everything else as zero. Start at those two heads and at $z=b_1$.

At horizon one, there are just four places. Write every arrow down:
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}ccccc@{}}
State & Tabletop & Pull $F$ & Pull $G$ & Start? \\ \hline
$a_0$ & 1 & end & $a_0$ & yes \\
$b_0$ & 2 & $b_0$ & $b_1$ & yes \\
$b_1$ & 0 & $b_1$ & end & yes \\
end & 0 & end & end & no \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
On the three starts each column has three different destinations.
On the whole four-state carrier each column has a repeated destination.
The horizon promise and the everywhere promise are different. Try both
orders at $b_0$: either order ends at $b_1$. The other three rows also
agree in both orders.
The endpoint first appears at depth $T$. By then every one of the $2T+2$ states has been
reached, and until then each lever keeps its sources apart.

For one-to-one levers on the whole machine, keep the two arms disjoint and let them run
forever. Give them a separate fixed zero state, and start at that state and the two heads.
After $T$ pulls the reachable population is exactly $2T+3$. The same box works at every
horizon.

Change the tabletop and the chairs can fit differently. Give it two bits, with one lever
clearing the first and the other clearing the second. Lay out an infinite grid with
nonnegative integer coordinates $(i,j)$ and a separate blank state. One lever adds one to $i$, the other to
$j$, and both fix blank. Read a grid point as $([i=0],[j=0])$ and blank as $(0,0)$.
Start at blank and the three grid points $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)$.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth, every node/.style={align=center,font=\small}]
\node (a) at (0,0) {grid $(0,0)$\\reads $(1,1)$};
\node (b) at (4,0) {grid $(1,0)$\\reads $(0,1)$};
\node (c) at (0,-2.7) {grid $(0,1)$\\reads $(1,0)$};
\node (d) at (4,-2.7) {grid $(1,1)$\\reads $(0,0)$};
\draw[->] (a)--node[above] {first lever}(b);
\draw[->] (a)--node[left] {second}(c);
\draw[->] (b)--node[right] {second}(d);
\draw[->] (c)--node[below] {first lever}(d);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
Both orders reach the very same grid point, not just the same reading.
The separate blank state also reads $(0,0)$ but is fixed by both levers;
it is not the grid's origin.

A pull adds one to $i+j$. The three grid starts have sums zero or one, so no word
of length at most $t$ can go beyond $i+j=t+1$. Conversely, the origin is a start. For any
other point in that triangle, start at $(1,0)$ if $i>0$, and at $(0,1)$ otherwise.
Exactly $i+j-1\le t$ pulls reach it. That gives the whole triangle. Its rows have
$1,2,\ldots,t+2$ points. Pair the first row with the last and count, then add blank:
\[
|R_t|=1+\frac{(t+2)(t+3)}2.
\]
Adding to one coordinate is one-to-one on the grid, and neither grid shift reaches
blank. Adding to different coordinates in either order gives $(i+1,j+1)$, so the levers
commute on the whole carrier. The reading follows the two clears because incrementing
a coordinate makes its zero-test false and leaves the other zero-test alone.

This count also meets the lower bound. Each one-cleared fibre starts with one state.
The appropriate clear sends that fibre and at least one $(1,1)$ state into it injectively,
so its population increases by at least one per depth: at depth $t$ it needs $t+1$.
The $(0,0)$ fibre also starts with one. At depth $j+1$, one clear sends both its $j$-depth
population and a one-cleared fibre of at least $j+1$ states into $(0,0)$ injectively.
Its population therefore increases by at least $j+1$. Summing from $j=0$ to $t-1$
gives $1+t(t+1)/2$. Add the one $(1,1)$ state and the two one-cleared populations:
$1+2(t+1)+1+t(t+1)/2=1+(t+2)(t+3)/2$. The three-value box needed extra room for commutation. This two-bit box fits
its best count while keeping commutation intact.

\subsection{The second way out: let the flag come back down}

Take one coin. The rule is: turn it over. Heads is YES, tails is NO. Every move is undoable
(turn it over again), so nothing is forgotten. Tails goes to heads, which is a flip, NO to YES,
and heads goes to tails, so the same move takes the flag back down somewhere else. There are
two states, as finite as it gets, and the move that raises the flag forgets nothing, so a
schedule that charges only for forgetting is allowed to charge it nothing. The move is
injective and can switch the reading both on and off. Pricing the turn at zero
meets merge pricing, since no move merges, and fails the toll.
The premise dropped on this way out is permanence.

There's a fact here sharper than the premise it replaces, and it was the thing
in this section that surprised me. Drop permanence entirely and keep only finiteness, and take
any move that raises the flag anywhere. Then one of two things is true: the move forgets
something, or the same move lowers the flag somewhere else. There's no third option, and the
proof below is a search: go through the finitely many YES states looking for one this move
turns to NO. Find one, and that's the revocation; find none, and the move is permanent at
least for itself, which is all the argument from fresh states needs. So a flag that goes up
without a merge is a flag the same move can take back. A flag that nothing takes back is paid
for. You can't have a raise at zero cost that stays raised, not on any finite machine, not
with any price schedule that charges for forgetting. The sentence is narrower than ``every
certificate costs.'' It's true, and I'll take it.
The broad one would only be mine.

\begin{theorem}[Merge or revoke]\label{thm:merge-or-revoke}
On a machine with finitely many states reading yes (no permanence assumed), if $\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{no}$ and
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(s, i)) = \mathrm{yes}$, then either $i$ merges, or there is a
state $t$ with $\mathrm{cert}(t) = \mathrm{yes}$ and $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(t, i)) =
\mathrm{no}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Check every yes-state on the finite list for one that $i$ sends to no. If there is one, that
is the second alternative. If there is none, then $i$ keeps every yes-state at yes, which is
permanence for the single move $i$; the argument of Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges} uses
permanence only for the move it is about, so it applies, and $i$ merges.
\end{proof}

I'll give you the three-card version too, because it shows that a move can
be forced to be priced without writing anything permanent, and I don't want you to think the
picture is tidier than it is. There are three cards, T0, T1, T2, with a star on T1.
The rule is that T0 goes to T1, T1 goes to T2, and T2 goes to T1. T0 gains the star (a flip).
T1 loses it (a revocation). T0 and T2 both land on T1 (a merge). So this move is priced, by
the forgetting rule, and yet it writes nothing permanent; it takes a star away in the same
breath. ``The priced moves are exactly the permanent records'' is false, as the three cards
just showed. What's true is one direction: on a finite machine, every permanent raise is a
priced move. The other direction has the three cards standing in it. And ``priced'' here has
an exact meaning worth one sentence: a move is \emph{forced to be priced} when every schedule
that charges for forgetting charges it, and that holds exactly when the move forgets
something, with no finiteness needed at all.

\begin{definition}[Forced to be priced]\label{def:forced-priced}
A move $i$ is \emph{forced to be priced} when every cost function satisfying merge pricing
(Premise~\ref{prem:merge-pricing}) charges $i$ at least one.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Forced price is merging]\label{thm:forced-iff-merge}
A move is forced to be priced exactly when it merges. No finiteness is needed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $i$ merges, merge pricing charges it at least one, whatever the cost function. If $i$
does not merge, define the cost that is $0$ on $i$ and $1$ on every other move. It satisfies merge pricing, since every merging move is some move other than $i$ and costs one, and it charges $i$ nothing, so $i$ is not forced. \end{proof} A cost here is any rule from move names to whole numbers, so that one is there whether or not anything can tell $i$ from the other names. A test that tells them apart comes in only when a cost has to be computed by a program, and then the program needs it to tell $i$ from the rest.

\begin{corollary}[Permanent records are forced]\label{cor:permanent-forced}
On a finite machine, a move that never turns the reading off and turns it on somewhere is forced to be priced. (By Theorem~\ref{thm:merge-or-revoke} it merges, and merge pricing charges every move that merges, whatever the cost function.) The converse fails: the three cards are
forced, because they merge, and they revoke.\proofclosed
\end{corollary}

\subsection{The third way out: don't charge for forgetting}

The third way out is the easiest to describe and the hardest to argue about, so I'll
describe it and then spend the rest of the section on the argument. Take a sheet of paper and
let its reading be just BLANK or STAMPED. There is one move: stamp it if blank, and leave it
alone if already stamped. It is finite, with two readings. It is permanent, since STAMPED
stays STAMPED. It has a flip, since BLANK goes to STAMPED. Both possible readings now end at
STAMPED. The paper's fibres, the ink and your memory are outside this two-state description;
the merge is a loss from the reading, not the disappearance of every physical trace.
Everything the argument from fresh states needs is here, and the move merges. Now
set the price of that move to zero. The toll fails, and you can watch it fail: the flag went
up at zero cost.
The premise dropped on this way out is the charge on forgetting. (A price of one on that move
satisfies all three premises, so the premises can hold together; the third way out is about
whether they must.) Nothing in counting stops you from setting that price to zero. Only a
claim about the world does. The nearest such claim is Landauer's, and I have to be exact
about the gap between the two: the premise as written charges \emph{every} forgetting move,
whether or not you knew which state you were in, and Landauer's own heat, as the coin under
the cup below will show, is owed only for what you didn't know. Merge pricing keeps only a
yes-or-no distinction: whether any pair can merge. The one-bit reset is where it comes from,
and it measures neither the full worst-case entropy loss nor the heat of any particular
preparation. The counting needs only that rule.

Here is what Landauer said, in 1961, as exactly as I can put it. I went past the
summaries and read the paper itself. A logical operation with no single-valued inverse (a step that
forgets, in this book's words) must produce heat, ``typically of the order of kT'' per operation, where
k is Boltzmann's constant and T is the temperature; and for the specific case of resetting
one bit whose value you don't know, the minimum is kT times the natural log of 2, about 0.69
kT. I want you to hear two things in that. First, ``of the order of'': he was not handing out a
number to three decimals. Second, and this surprised me, he did not measure anything. The
paper is argument, with models. He writes that he can ``show, or at least very strongly
suggest'' the conclusion, and that his reasoning gives ``no guarantee that this minimum is in
fact achievable.'' That's the founding paper of the whole subject, and it's a careful man
saying ``I think this is right and here's why.'' I like him more for it.

Was it measured, eventually? Yes, and only recently. In 2012 a group at the École Normale
Supérieure in Lyon, Antoine Bérut and Sergio Ciliberto's lab working with Eric Lutz, trapped
a single glass bead, two millionths of a metre across, in a
double well made of laser light, and used the two wells as the two values of a bit. Then they
erased the bit, by lowering the barrier, tilting the trap, and raising it again, many times
over, slower and slower, and measured the heat each time. The average heat came down toward
Landauer's kT ln 2 as the erasure got slower, closer the slower it went, and never under it,
on average. Single runs went under it; the bound is about the average, and any one erasure
can beat it. And if you only succeed in erasing half the time the floor drops to zero, which
the paper's formula shows and which I think is the most honest line in it. Others have done
it since with different devices. So it was predicted in 1961 by argument and seen in a
laboratory fifty-one years later.

And is it settled? No, and I'd be lying by omission if I left that out, because the people
who doubt it are not cranks. John Norton, a philosopher of physics, has argued since 2005
that the usual proofs of the principle quietly assume what they're trying to prove, and that
the kinds of process they assume, combined, could be made to break the very law the
principle is supposed to guard. An earlier objection, made in 1998--99 by Norton and his Pittsburgh colleague John Earman, also a philosopher
of physics, was that the principle can't be independent of the second law. Charles Bennett, who did more
than anyone to build the subject, rated that one ``in my opinion the one of greatest merit,''
and then disagreed with it. Others replied to Norton; Norton replied back. The Stanford Encyclopedia
entry on the topic, written by a philosopher of physics who works on exactly this, ends
without a verdict. I've read what I could of both sides and I'm not qualified to referee them, and I'm
not going to pretend the laboratory settles a question about what the principle means in
general, because measuring one bead doesn't do that.

What I did with it is this, and I think it's the only honest thing to do. The charge on
forgetting is written into this book as a \emph{named premise}. It's a definition the
theorems take as an assumption, and nowhere is it proved as a general fact, because it isn't
provable from counting; for a particular machine with a particular price list you can see it
hold (the stamp at cost one, above), which is a different thing. If Norton turns out to be
right, every theorem in this section still holds; they just have one premise fewer that the
world agrees to. If Landauer's side turns out to be right, it supports a thermal price under
its conditions; the whole-number charge on every merging move is still the ledger rule stated
here. Either way, nothing in this section says a device does anything until someone measures
the device. The counting is mine to prove. The physics is a premise I've named, and what
settles it is a measurement, which a proof can't do.

Naming a premise, though, isn't the same as leaving it unplaced, and a hedge isn't a
position, so I'll give mine.
Earman and Norton's objection is a dilemma. Either an information-theoretic exorcism of the demon
assumes the second law, which they call the \emph{sound} horn, and then it adds nothing the
second law didn't already give; or it rests on a new principle tying information to entropy, the
\emph{profound} horn, and nobody has given that principle independent grounds. A named premise
is the sound horn, on purpose. That's where Bennett ended up in 2003, and Norton's ``Too Good to
Be True'' (written in 2025, published in 2026) says the careful literature almost always accepts
that horn, and argues that whatever succeeds there is ordinary thermodynamics relabelled. I'll
take that. Ordinary thermodynamics, relabelled onto a ledger, is all this section asks of the
physics. And on the counting I'm on Norton's side outright. His 2018 paper ``Maxwell's Demon Does
Not Compute'' exorcises the demon with Liouville's theorem and nothing else, no information and
no computation: dynamics that keeps every patch of states the same size can't crowd a big set
of states into a small one. The counting core of this section, that a step losing nothing can't
carry a no-state into a set that stays up, is that point in finite, discrete form. And if you
want the best case for the premise itself, the one I found is James Ladyman, Stuart Presnell,
Anthony Short and Berry Groisman (2007): from one of the standard statements of the second law, the one named for Kelvin, they derive
that a logically irreversible operation can't be carried out thermodynamically reversibly by any
of their L-machines. That's a physical argument under their stated model of a machine.
It deserves to be argued with on those terms; it does not by itself establish the book's
whole-number ledger charge.

One question a physicist asks before any of that, and it's a good one: the laws underneath
never merge anything. Classical mechanics carries each exact state forward to exactly one next
state and could carry it back again, and Liouville's theorem adds that a patch of states keeps
its size as it moves; quantum mechanics is unitary, which is one-to-one too. So when this
section says a step merged two states, where did the difference go? It went out of the
machine. The merge is in the machine's own description, the states its reading is about. The
machine together with everything around it still runs one-to-one, and the distinction the
machine forgot survives. It gets pushed out into the surroundings. The surroundings are the
endless strip of the first way out, the machine that keeps every history: the column of
states never used before, which the universe as a whole may have to spend and the machine
doesn't, because the machine isn't the universe and its memory fills.
Pushing a distinction out isn't yet heat: another memory could keep it as a readable record.
It's heat when the reset removes real uncertainty into a thermal reservoir, and then Landauer's
premise bounds the mean heat handed over. None of
that heat has to be heat \emph{wasted}. Takahiro Sagawa's 2014 analysis says that erasure
can, in principle, approach a process that produces no entropy overall: the reservoir's
entropy goes up by what the machine's goes down. A positive mean heat transfer can then
be unavoidable without being wasteful. A known input has no uncertainty to remove, and
this entropy-loss premise alone sets no positive heat floor for it. The reset can dissipate under the stated thermal-model assumptions, and a reset device that wasn't built for that one input
keeps a floor that survives going slowly (Section~\ref{sec:bits-zero}).

Ladyman and his coauthors and Sagawa aren't disagreeing. They use ``reversible'' for two
different things. Ladyman's L-machines are devices, and a device counts as reversible only if it
produces no entropy on every input it's fed, each one known (their section~4: ``the L-machine is
thermodynamically reversible if and only if'' every one of its processes, one per input, produces
no entropy). Sagawa's reversible erasure is a
process on one given spread of inputs, with the device tuned to that spread. The standard eraser
is reversible in Sagawa's sense and not in Ladyman's: on an even mix of 0 and 1 it produces no entropy, and on each known input it
produces $k_B\ln2$. One identity holds the two together. For a fixed device that sends every
input to one output, and any spread $q$ of its inputs, the average over inputs of the entropy
produced on each known input equals the entropy produced on the spread $q$, plus $k_B$ times the
Shannon entropy of $q$. The identity holds because the heat is the same average either way, the
device being fixed, and the output is the same either way. The only difference is at the
start: the spread's own entropy includes $k_B H(q)$ for not knowing which input it is, and
each known input's doesn't.
Sagawa makes the first term on the right zero; Ladyman reads the left side, which is then
$k_B H(q)$, and more than zero.

\subsection{How much: the price grows with the squeeze}

The toll charges at least one unit, and that's a floor for raising one flag. The counting
of states says more if you let it. Say there are m states that already read yes and k more
are turned to yes in one move. (That's a different k from the one in Landauer's kT; when
the two meet, below, Boltzmann's constant gets a little B hung under it, $k_B$, so you can
tell it from a count of states.) All m plus k of them end up on the m yes-states. That's a
squeeze by a factor of (m + k) over m, and if you accept a slightly stronger version of the
forgetting price, that each unit of cost pays for at most one \emph{halving} of the number of
distinguishable states, then the move costs at least the number of halvings in that squeeze,
which is the base-two logarithm of (m + k)/m.

Back to the stamp from the third way out, but give the reading four possible values this
time: A, B, C and YES. Write them on four cards. Choose one secretly, then cover its face
with an identical opaque YES label. Read only the new face: all four possibilities now give
YES. Before the move, identifying the original face took two yes-or-no questions (one of the
first two? then which one?); afterward there is only one possible face to report, so that
reading has lost two bits, which is two halvings. Peeling the label off would recover the old
face, so this tabletop version models the loss from the reading; it does not demonstrate
physical erasure. So that move costs at least two units, and two is enough, since a cost of
exactly two satisfies the halving rule. The general statement is m + k at most 2 to the cost
times m, and there is also a logarithm form that rounds both logarithms up and is weaker for
it (three states and one newcomer round to the same two bits on both sides, and the rounded
form says nothing). The halving premise, like the one before it, is a definition used as an
assumption. The units are halvings. To turn a halving into joules of heat you multiply by
$k_B T \ln 2$, and that multiplication is physics; the counting stops before it.

That little $k_B$ deserves a short trip of its own, because it sits exactly where counting
turns into physics, and its name is a small history lesson. Ludwig Boltzmann's grave in
Vienna has $S = k \log W$ carved on it (that $k$ is the same $k_B$, before anyone hung a B
under it): entropy is a constant times the logarithm of the number of ways the parts could be
arranged. The idea is his. The constant, and the equation written that way, came from Max
Planck, in his work on radiation around 1900. In his Nobel lecture in 1920 Planck said the
constant ``is frequently termed Boltzmann's constant, although to the best of my knowledge
Boltzmann himself never introduced it,'' and guessed that Boltzmann never believed anyone could
measure it accurately. I'd assumed Planck named it after Boltzmann. His own words point the other
way: it was other people calling it that, and who first did, I couldn't pin down. So
the most famous constant in this corner of physics wears the name of a man who didn't write it
down. Does that change the heat floor? It doesn't, but look at the job the
constant does in that equation. Take it away and what's left is the logarithm of a count,
which is a number of halvings, which is what the squeeze bound hands you. The constant is the
exchange rate, and whether the world honours that rate for a merge is the premise. No
theorem here settles it.

The premise, stated exactly, needs one new piece of notation: for a list $D$ of states, write
$|D|$ for how many it has, and $\mathrm{img}_i(D)$ for the number of \emph{different} states
the move $i$ sends them to.

\begin{premise}[Halving price]\label{prem:halving}
Each unit of cost pays for at most one halving: for every move $i$ and every list $D$ of states with
no repeats, $|D| \le 2^{\mathrm{cost}(i)} \cdot \mathrm{img}_i(D)$. (It implies merge pricing, since a merge sends two different states to
one and so needs $\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$.)
\end{premise}

There's a plainer way to read that premise, and it's worth having because it says what the
premise is \emph{about}. Look at one landing spot of a move and count how many states land
there; call the biggest such count the move's worst pile-up. The premise holds exactly when
the cost covers the worst pile-up in halvings: a cost of one allows piles of two, a cost of
two allows piles of four, and a pile of three already needs a cost of two. In one direction,
hand the premise one whole pile. It lands on a single spot, so the premise says the pile has
at most that many members. In the other, any list of states splits by where its members land,
each part sits inside one pile, so the list is at most the number of landing spots times the
worst pile-up, which is what the premise says. So the halving price asks a move to pay for the
worst it could ever do, whichever state it's actually handed. The worst case is on purpose,
and it has a home in physics. In the branch of thermodynamics that prices a single run that
has to succeed every time, with no averaging over many runs, Philippe Faist, Frédéric
Dupuis, Jonathan Oppenheim and Renato Renner derived in 2015, in that framework, what they give as
the least work any logical process needs, and when every input might occur and no error is allowed, their bound comes to
$k_B T \ln 2$ times exactly that logarithm. Take an AND gate as the example: three inputs
land on 0, so it needs at least $\log_2 3$, about 1.6, halvings' worth of work (two units,
in whole numbers). The premise asks for that bound of a device that has to work whatever
it's handed, and it counts it in units of cost. Joules don't come into it.

\begin{theorem}[The squeeze bound]\label{thm:squeeze}
On a finite machine with a permanent reading and a cost satisfying the halving price, let
$m$ be the number of states that read yes, and let a move $i$ turn $k$ different no-states
to yes. Three numbers are in play: $m$ counts every yes-state of the machine, reachable or not; $k$
counts a list of distinct no-states that the move turns to yes, and the move may turn others too;
and $\mathrm{cost}(i)$ is the price the cost assigns to the move. Then
\[
m + k \;\le\; 2^{\mathrm{cost}(i)} \cdot m, \qquad\text{and, when } m \ge 1,\qquad
\mathrm{cost}(i) \;\ge\; \log_2 \frac{m+k}{m}.
\]
When $m \ge 1$ the two displayed bounds say the same thing. (When $m = 0$ there is nowhere
for a newcomer to land, so $k = 0$ too.)
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put the $m$ yes-states and the $k$ newcomers in one list; it has $m + k$ different members.
By permanence every yes-state lands on a yes-state, and by hypothesis every newcomer does
too, so all $m + k$ land among the $m$ yes-states: $\mathrm{img}_i \le m$. The halving price
gives $m + k \le 2^{\mathrm{cost}(i)} \cdot \mathrm{img}_i \le 2^{\mathrm{cost}(i)} \cdot m$.
\end{proof}

The four card readings are the case of one yes-state and three newcomers, where the bound is
reached. With one newcomer the bound says the move costs at least one, which is the toll
again. The counting argument also shows that at least as many states collapse as there are
newcomers, without any price premise.

The bound is reached, whatever the numbers. Pick how many states already read yes and pick a
cost. As long as the old yes-states and the newcomers together fit under that cost's pile-up
allowance (a cost of one allows twice the yes-states, a cost of two allows four times), there is
a finite machine with a permanent reading and the halving price that has exactly that many
yes-states and a move of exactly that cost turning those newcomers to yes. The move turns every
other no-state of that machine to yes as well, filling the allowance to the brim. No cost meeting
the halving price on that machine charges the move less. So the least whole-number cost that
meets the bound is exactly the rounded-up logarithm, $\lceil \log_2 \frac{m+k}{m} \rceil$.

Four more facts about the halving price, and the last one is a limit. First, the plainer
reading above is a theorem on a finite machine: the halving price holds exactly when no move has
a landing spot with more than $2^{\mathrm{cost}(i)}$ states landing on it. Second, for the eight-state machine
described later in this section that's a theorem about its own price list: no
move has a larger pile-up than $2^{\mathrm{cost}}$, so the halving price holds, and the toll follows
from it; and the price
list is the least that meets the halving price, since any price list that does charges every move at
least what this one charges. Third, the squeeze bound is met with
equality there: its stamp turns on the four states whose flag is down, beside the four whose flag is already up, and
$4 + 4 = 2^{1} \cdot 4$. Fourth, and this is the limit, the small
machine of Part~III (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}) as a whole does not meet the halving price, whatever procedure you use to decide
whether two of its states are equal, because one of its zero-price moves, the one that takes one off
a number the machine holds, lands two different states of the whole machine on the same
state (the pair is in
Theorem~\ref{thm:frag-merge-split}), and a pile of two at price zero is all it takes to break the
halving price. What does hold there is merge pricing asked of the record's part of the state alone,
and it gives the toll on that machine too (Theorem~\ref{thm:record-merge-toll}, below).

\subsection{The same bound, written in bits, and when it's zero}
\label{sec:bits-zero}

There's one more way to say all this, and I include it because it's the way physicists say
it and because it says exactly when the heat floor is zero: when no two states you might be in land on one. Its two ends are a move that forgets nothing and a move on a state already known, and the second I find more instructive than any case where it isn't.

Claude Shannon, in 1948, gave a number to ``how much you don't know'': if something could be in
any of n states and you have no idea which, your uncertainty is log base two of n bits, and
that's the most it can be for n states. If you push your uncertainty through a step that
forgets nothing, it stays the same; through a step that merges two states you might have
been in, it drops. Now push it through the permanent flip. Before the move, you might be in any of the m + k states
in play. After it, you're in one of m. So your uncertainty afterward is at most log2 of m,
whatever you believed before. If you started with no idea at all, every one of the m + k
states equally likely, your uncertainty was exactly log2 of (m + k), and the move removed at
least log2 of (m + k)/m bits: the same number as the halving count, now in Shannon's units.
Landauer's principle, in the form physicists write it, then says a step that removes that
many bits from the state gives off at least $k_B T \ln 2$ of heat per bit. Put the two
together and the flip gives off heat, and the exact statements below say how much and under
which side conditions, one of which (the temperature has to be taken as zero or above) is
easy to skip and shouldn't be.

Why does Shannon's number share a name with the physicists' entropy at all? There's a story
about it. Shannon wanted to call it uncertainty, and the mathematician John von Neumann
told him to call it entropy instead, for two reasons: the same formula already lived in
statistical mechanics under that name, and nobody really knows what entropy is, so in an
argument he'd always have the upper hand. It's a great story. It comes from Myron Tribus, who spent years tying information theory to
thermodynamics, who
said Shannon told it to him in 1961, and who printed it, with Edward McIrvine, in \emph{Scientific American} in
1971. Then in 1982 an interviewer, Robert Price, asked Shannon about it, and Shannon said he
didn't think von Neumann had told him any such thing. So it's a
legend with one witness, and the person the witness quoted doesn't remember saying it. What
doesn't hang on the story: the two formulas really do have the same shape, and it still
takes Landauer's premise, a named assumption, to turn a count of bits into heat.

Now the exact version, with the notation built first. A \emph{spread} (probabilists say distribution) is a way
of giving each state a chance $p(x) \ge 0$, with the chances adding to 1. Its Shannon
entropy, in bits, is
\[
H(p) \;=\; -\sum_{x:\,p(x) > 0} p(x)\,\log_2 p(x),
\]
where the big sigma means ``add up, over every state $x$ with a chance above zero,'' and each
term is a state's chance times the bits it would take to single that state out. That comes to
$\log_2 n$ when $n$ states share the chance evenly and less when the chance is lopsided. Pushing a spread through a move $i$ gives the spread of where you land:
$q(y) = \sum_{x:\,\mathrm{step}(x,i) = y} p(x)$. The bits the move \emph{removes} are
$H(p) - H(q)$.

Try four equally likely cards, A, B, C and D. Send A and B to a box marked X,
C to Y and D to Z. Beforehand each card has chance $1/4$, so the four terms in
the sum are each $1/2$: two bits. Afterward the box chances are $1/2,1/4,1/4$,
and the three terms are each $1/2$: one and a half bits. Half a bit was lost on
average. You can see where: half the time the box is X and leaves one binary
question unanswered: A or B? The other half of the time Y or Z tells you the
starting card exactly. An actual draw never loses half a card; the half belongs
to the average uncertainty over repeated draws.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[thiele]
\node[cnode] (a) at (0,1.5) {A: one quarter};
\node[cnode] (b) at (0,.5) {B: one quarter};
\node[cnode] (c) at (0,-.5) {C: one quarter};
\node[cnode] (d) at (0,-1.5) {D: one quarter};
\node[pipe,text width=4cm,minimum width=0pt] (x) at (6,1.5) {X: one half\\Origin could be A or B};
\node[pipe,text width=4cm,minimum width=0pt] (y) at (6,-.5) {Y: one quarter\\Origin was C};
\node[pipe,text width=4cm,minimum width=0pt] (z) at (6,-2.5) {Z: one quarter\\Origin was D};
\draw[pipearrow] (a) -- (x);
\draw[pipearrow] (b) -- (x);
\draw[pipearrow] (c) -- (y);
\draw[pipearrow] (d) -- (z);
\end{tikzpicture}

\small Half the time one binary question remains unanswered; half the time
the origin is known. The average loss is half a bit.
\end{center}

Start with the half of the claim that removes no bits, Bennett's half. A move that forgets
nothing sends each state somewhere different, so the chances are carried along to new
places, one for one, and nothing piles up and nothing spreads out. The uncertainty is the same
number before and after.

\begin{theorem}[A move that forgets nothing removes no bits]\label{thm:u04-injective-entropy}
Let the states be finite, listed once each, and let $f$ send states to states with
$f(a) = f(b)$ only when $a = b$. Then for every assignment of chances $p$, the pushed spread
$q$ has $H(q) = H(p)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
An injective map on a finite list of distinct states is a reshuffle of that list: every state
is hit exactly once. So $q(f(x)) = p(x)$ for every $x$, and the sum defining $H(q)$ is the sum
defining $H(p)$ with its terms in a different order.
\end{proof}

That's why a price on removed bits can leave every reversible move costing nothing, which is the shape the
toll needs: the ledger's cost lands only where something was forgotten.

\begin{theorem}[Entropy after a permanent flip]\label{thm:entropy-ceiling}
On a finite machine with a permanent reading, let $m$ be the number of states that read yes,
and let a move $i$ turn $k \ge 1$ different
no-states yes. For any spread $p$ whose chance lies on those $m + k$
states, the spread after the move has $H(q) \le \log_2 m$. For the even spread on the $m + k$ states, the move removes at least $\log_2 \frac{m+k}{m}$ bits and at least $\frac{2k}{m+k}$ bits; the first is reached when $m$ divides $k$, the second when $k \le m$. \end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
All the starting chance lands among the $m$ yes-states: the old ones stay yes and the
newcomers turn yes. There must be at least one landing state, so $m\ge1$.
The first question is how much uncertainty those $m$ places can hold.

Here is the small fact about logarithms that does the work. For $y>0$,
$\ln y\le y-1$. Picture the gap $y-1-\ln y$. Its slope is $1-1/y$:
negative below $1$, zero at $1$, positive above $1$. The gap falls to zero and
then rises, so it never goes below zero.

Call the positive landing probabilities $q_1,\ldots,q_r$. There are at most $m$
of them and they add to one. Compare each with the even share $1/m$. Apply the
logarithm fact to the ratio $1/(m q_j)$ and multiply by the chance $q_j$:
\[
q_j\ln\frac{1}{m q_j}\le\frac1m-q_j.
\]
Now add over the occupied places. On the right the even shares total $r/m\le1$,
while the actual shares total exactly $1$. The sum is therefore at most zero.
On the left, splitting the logarithm gives $-\ln m-\sum_jq_j\ln q_j$.
Move $\ln m$ across and divide by $\ln2$ to count in bits. This says precisely
$H(q)\le\log_2m$: no arrangement of the chance among those places holds more
uncertainty than the even arrangement.

Before the move, the $m+k$ starting states were equally likely. Their uncertainty
was $\log_2(m+k)$. Subtract the greatest possible uncertainty left at the end:
the loss is at least $\log_2((m+k)/m)$. If $k$ is a multiple of $m$, keep each old
yes-state where it is and send an equal number of newcomers to each. The landing
chances are then even too, so this bound is reached.

For the other bound, count one landing pile at a time. A pile of $s$ equally likely
starts receives chance $s/(m+k)$. Once you know that pile was reached, there are still
$s$ equally likely origins to distinguish: $\log_2s$ bits have disappeared there.
Its share of the total loss is therefore $s\log_2s/(m+k)$.

A pile of one contributes zero. A pile of two contributes $2/(m+k)$. For every
larger whole number $s$, $s\log_2s\ge2(s-1)$. To check that inequality, subtract
$2(s-1)$: the difference is zero at $s=2$, and its slope for $s\ge2$ is
$\log_2s+1/\ln2-2>0$. It grows from there.
Thus each pile costs at least $2/(m+k)$ for every origin after its first.
There are $m+k$ origins and at most $m$ piles, leaving at least $k$ such extra
origins. The loss is at least $2k/(m+k)$.
When $k\le m$, send each newcomer to a different old yes-state and leave the old
states fixed. All piles then have size one or two, exactly the sizes where the
inequality is an equality. That construction reaches the second bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{premise}[Landauer's principle, as a premise]\label{prem:landauer}
For the chosen physical memory and its input distribution, assume that a step lowering
its logical-state entropy by $\Delta H$ bits transfers mean heat
$Q \ge k_B T \ln 2 \cdot \Delta H$ to a bath at temperature $T$, where $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant.
Here $Q$ is an average over that preparation, not a bound on each individual trial.
Applying this premise requires a physical model in which the logical entropy loss has
this thermodynamic meaning; a bare state-transition table does not supply one. In particular
the memory is symmetric, its logical states alike in their own entropy, as Landauer assumed;
for a memory whose states differ, the floor changes (Maroney 2009), and erasure work in an
asymmetric double well has been measured below $k_B T \ln 2$ (Gavrilov and Bechhoefer 2016).
\end{premise}

\begin{corollary}[Heat floor of a permanent flip]\label{cor:heat-floor}
Under Premise~\ref{prem:landauer}, with $k_B T \ge 0$, the flip of Theorem~\ref{thm:entropy-ceiling} from the even spread gives off at least $k_B T \ln \frac{m+k}{m}$, and at least $\frac{2k}{m+k}\,k_B T \ln 2$; with $k_B T > 0$ that is strictly positive.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:entropy-ceiling} gives an entropy loss of at least $\log_2((m+k)/m)$ bits, and of at least $2k/(m+k)$ bits. Multiply by the nonnegative factor $k_B T\ln2$ and use
Premise~\ref{prem:landauer}. The identity $\ln2\,\log_2 x=\ln x$ gives the displayed
floor. Here $m>0$ and $k>0$, so $(m+k)/m>1$ and its logarithm is positive; if
$k_B T>0$, the heat floor is strictly positive too.
\end{proof}

How big is that? Take the case where the squeeze is two, one state flipping in beside one that
was already yes, and the floor is $k_B T \ln 2$. At room temperature, about 300
kelvin, that's roughly three zeptojoules: three thousandths of a billionth of a billionth of a
joule. And that's the \emph{biggest} floor a one-state flip gets from this corollary. With one newcomer the floor shrinks as more states already read yes, because the
squeeze gets thinner: with a thousand of them it's $2\ln 2/1001$ of $k_B T$, about a seven-hundred-and-twentieth, some five hundred times less than the case of two. So, for an even spread over the states in play, one
unit of cost is not one halving. It's one halving exactly when the squeeze is two; for any thinner
squeeze and an even spread, the physics asks for less than a halving, and the toll still charges
a whole unit, because the cost comes in whole numbers. The entropy road to the toll, a little further down, doesn't need that rounding: entropy pricing asks about every spread, and the worst one takes a full bit. Read in the worst case over what the machine might be
holding, the way the halving price reads a move, it's at least a full bit every time. A permanent flip
merges two states (Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges}); put half the chance on each, and the move
removes a full bit, however many states already read yes. So the gap
between the unit of cost and the bits is a fact about the even spread, and in the worst case the flip removes
at least the full bit the unit pays for. Whatever the size,
it's heat only if you grant the premise; nothing on this page measured anything. The bead experiments above probe this energy scale. Ordinary CMOS switching is a different comparison: the implementation figures cited next are much larger than this floor. One 2023 tally of the numbers puts
switching a single CMOS gate at a hundred attojoules at the low end, over thirty thousand
times this. The point of the number isn't that
a permanent flip is expensive but that, on the premise, it isn't zero.

A related logarithm appears in a different physical question. Y\^uto Murashita,
Ken Funo and Masahito Ueda (2014) study processes whose reverse histories can include
ones with no forward counterpart. They call this \emph{absolute irreversibility}.
If the reverse histories with no forward partner carry some share of the probability,
their bound on mean entropy production picks up the logarithm of one over what's left. In
their free-expansion example, gas that starts confined to a tenth of a box gives the
logarithm of ten.

Make the confined fraction the old yes-states' share of the pile, the yes-states over the
yes-states plus the newcomers, and out comes the same logarithm as the squeeze bound. That
numerical match does not identify two physical processes. The arrows specify neither a
thermodynamic reverse experiment nor its path probabilities, so they don't determine that
share of reverse histories. The state count alone says nothing about absolute
irreversibility, its absence, or a heat equality. Gonzalo Manzano, G\"ulce Karde\c{s}, \'Edgar Rold\'an and
David Wolpert (2024) study such trajectory-level questions for computations with
one-way transitions and random stopping times. Their physical premises are additional
to the counting done here.

The even spread is the easy case, and it's fair to worry that the heat depends on picking it. It
doesn't. Any spread that gives a real chance to every yes-state and to the state that
flips will do.

\begin{corollary}[Positive heat for any full spread]\label{cor:u04-full-support-heat}
On a finite machine with a permanent reading, let move $i$ turn a no-state $s$ yes. Take any
spread $p$ that gives positive chance to $s$ and to every yes-state. Under
Premise~\ref{prem:landauer} with $k_B T > 0$, the heat the move gives off is strictly positive.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
After the move, $s$ and the yes-states all land among the yes-states, and there is one more
of them than there are yes-states, so two distinct states with positive chance land on the
same state. That merge removes a positive number of bits
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u04-point-sum} below), and a positive temperature times a positive number of
bits is positive heat.
\end{proof}

There's a third road to the toll here too, and it's the same shape as the merge road, with
the bits removed, in place of whole units, as the price of forgetting.

\begin{definition}[Entropy-priced]\label{def:u04-entropy-priced}
On a finite machine, a cost is \emph{entropy-priced} when, for every move $i$ and every spread
$p$, the cost of $i$ is at least the bits the move removes:
$\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge H(p) - H(q)$, where $q$ is $p$ pushed through $i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The toll from entropy pricing]\label{thm:u04-entropy-toll}
On a finite machine with a permanent reading and an entropy-priced cost, every move that
turns the reading from no to yes costs at least one. So the machine with that cost is a
Thiele machine (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}), and every run from a no-state to a
yes-state costs at least one.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let move $i$ turn $s$ yes. By Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges} it lands two different states on one. Put half the chance on each: the move removes one bit, so the cost of $i$ is at least one. The run-level floor is the universal floor
(Observation~\ref{thm:universal-floor}) applied to that system.
\end{proof}

There are three roads to the toll, with two different strengths. Entropy pricing
and the halving price are equivalent: the most bits a deterministic move can remove
is the base-two logarithm of its largest pile of starts sharing a destination.
Merge pricing asks only for a cost of at least one whenever any pair collides. It is
the two-state restriction of the stronger conditions.

Try eight equally likely cards all sent to one box. The loss is three bits. A
charge of one meets merge pricing but fails entropy pricing and the halving price,
which require at least three. All three conditions give the permanent-record toll;
only the stronger two give the full squeeze bound.

\begin{theorem}[Entropy pricing, halving, and pairwise merge pricing]\label{thm:one-premise}
Take a finite machine and a move $i$.
(1) If no state has more than $K \ge 1$ states landing on it under $i$, every spread loses at
most $\log_2 K$ bits through $i$; and if some state has exactly $K$ states landing on it, the even
spread on those $K$ loses exactly $\log_2 K$ bits. (2) A cost is entropy-priced
(Definition~\ref{def:u04-entropy-priced}) exactly when it satisfies the halving price
(Premise~\ref{prem:halving}). (3) A cost satisfies merge pricing
(Premise~\ref{prem:merge-pricing}) exactly when it satisfies the halving price for every list of
at most two different states, and exactly when it satisfies entropy pricing for every spread whose
chance sits on at most two states. The first of those two equivalences uses no finiteness.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Sort the possible starts into piles according to where the move sends them.
Suppose the landing place is $y$ and its total chance is $q(y)>0$.
Knowing that you landed there leaves only the starts in that pile in question.
Their chances, now measured within the pile, are $p(x)/q(y)$.
They add to one, and there are at most $K$ of them.
The logarithm argument in the preceding entropy bound says their uncertainty
is at most $\log_2K$ bits.

Average that remaining question over the landing places, giving each its chance
$q(y)$. This is exactly the information the move discarded. Indeed, a start $x$
contributes
\[
p(x)\log_2\frac{q(y)}{p(x)},\qquad y=\mathrm{step}(x,i),
\]
and summing these terms gives $H(p)-H(q)$ by grouping the output terms by their
landing places. An average of numbers no greater than $\log_2K$ cannot exceed
$\log_2K$. For equality, put equal chance on every member of one pile of size $K$.
There are $\log_2K$ bits at the start and none at the single landing place.

(2) An entropy price must cover that even preparation on every pile. A pile of
size $n$ therefore requires cost $c\ge\log_2n$, or equivalently $n\le2^c$.
That is the halving rule: no landing place accepts more than $2^c$ starts.
Conversely, if the halving rule holds, part (1), with $K=2^c$, says no preparation
loses more than $c$ bits. The same price covers them all.

(3) Now allow at most two starts. If they land separately, the move loses nothing.
If they land together, the halving rule reads $2\le2^c$, which asks for at least
one whole unit. This is exactly merge pricing. Nothing in that two-start argument
needs the rest of the machine to be finite.

The chance calculation makes the same demand. Two possible starts hold at most
one bit, so a charge of one covers every spread over a merging pair. Equal chances
on that pair lose exactly one bit and force that charge. A single possible start,
or two that stay separate, lose zero. So restricting entropy pricing to at most
two possible starts gives merge pricing too.
\end{proof}

So merge pricing is weaker than full entropy pricing, though both force the
one-unit toll under the permanence and finiteness premises. The prices are rules on
moves. Reading one as physics takes Landauer's premise for the actual spread and a
stated exchange rate from bits or units of cost to heat.

Now for the case where the floor is zero. Take the coin under a cup: toss a fair coin under it without looking at how it lands, and let the rule be to set it heads up. You might have
had tails; now you have heads; one bit of what you didn't know is gone, and that's the bit the
principle charges for. Now lift the cup, see heads, put the cup back, and apply the rule
again. Nothing you didn't know changed, and no bit was lost. And the principle, applied to a state
you already knew, demands nothing: the premise holds exactly when the heat is zero or more,
which is to say it sets no positive floor. Setting a coin known to be tails to heads may have a finite-time cost under
the chosen thermal dynamics; setting one you know
is heads changes nothing. What the premise gives up either way is a floor that survives going
slowly. Whether the hand that sets the coin keeps one is a question about the hand, and I come to
it below. If you lift the cup after an uncertain toss, you have also made a record
correlated with the coin. Resetting that record has to be analysed with those
correlations and with the controls available. If instead the coin was supplied
heads with certainty, there was no uncertain toss to record. These are different
preparations. Knowing the result does not by itself locate a heat payment in
the observer.

The entropy-loss bound depends on the preparation and on what the move does to it.
Here ``known'' means a preparation concentrated on one logical state, or a conditional
ensemble whose side information is explicitly included in the account. Merely telling a
spectator which way the coin landed does not change an unchanged device's heat. This is the generalized
form of Landauer's principle, worked out by Owen Maroney in 2009, in a paper he wrote at the
Perimeter Institute in Canada (he has been a philosopher of physics at Oxford since 2011), and by Sagawa in 2014, and Landauer
himself had the seed of it in 1961: for a row of bits all already ONE, he wrote, there's no need
to carry out any operation, so no entropy changes and no heat is given off, and resetting a row
all ZERO to ONE involves no entropy change either, because neither row carries any
information.

\begin{theorem}[A known state gets no heat floor from the premise]\label{thm:known-state}
On a finite machine, if the spread puts all its chance on one state $s$, then any move removes
zero bits, and Premise~\ref{prem:landauer} for that move holds exactly when $Q \ge 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A spread on one state has entropy 0, and so does its image, which is again on one state. So
$\Delta H = 0$ and the premise reads $Q \ge 0$.
\end{proof}

Be careful with that one, because it's easy to overread. ``The premise sets no heat floor for a known
state'' does not mean a stamping machine run on a known-blank sheet dissipates nothing. A model of the stamping apparatus may impose a finite-time cost, but the
logical change alone does not establish it. The restricted thermal results are proved here for Bennett's walker (Theorem~\ref{thm:time-bill}), found for a dragged bead by Schmiedl and Seifert and for the specified classical jump-process models by Shiraishi, Funo and Saito, and how much depends on the device's physical
implementation, its control protocol and how fast it goes. What the
theorem says is only that the \emph{premise} sets no floor there. The floor comes from what you
didn't know. That's a sentence about the premise's floor, and the device is a separate matter. And notice that the
toll still charges the known-state stamp one unit, because the toll is a rule about the
\emph{move}, and the move doesn't know what the observer knows. That's the worst-case gap from
the third way out showing up again, and it's the price of having a rule a machine can follow
without asking who's watching.

The physics of all this has a standard review, the physicists Juan Parrondo, Jordan Horowitz and
Takahiro Sagawa's ``Thermodynamics of information'' (2015), which sets Landauer's bound, its
generalized form and the costs of measurement and feedback side by side. And the gap between a
device and the spread it runs on has a physicist's number on it. Artemy Kolchinsky and David
Wolpert (2017) showed that a fixed process built to dissipate as little as possible for one spread
over its states pays extra when it runs on another, and the extra is how much closer the process
brings the two spreads, measured in relative entropy; the extra was later named mismatch cost.
That's the worst-case gap again, priced for an actual spread, where the toll prices the move.

Fix a thermal protocol with the entropy-balance identity just described,
using the same controls and environment for each input. A floor then comes
from comparing its inputs. Take
$K$ inputs the device sends to the same output, and spread your chances evenly over them. The
identity of Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} that ties Ladyman's reading to Sagawa's says the
average, over the $K$, of the entropy the device produces on each one known equals the entropy it
produces on the even spread, plus $k_B\ln K$. The second law makes the entropy produced on the
spread zero or more. So the average is at least $k_B\ln K$, and the worst of the $K$ is at least
the average: on some one of them the device produces at least $k_B\ln K$ of entropy, and, when dissipated work is temperature times entropy production, at
least $k_B T\ln K$ of dissipated work. Slowing this same protocol does not
remove that worst-input bound. Kolchinsky and Wolpert's formula says,
under their conditions, which input pays: the one the device's own best spread gave the least
