chance. A device can make one input cheap only by making another dear. Choosing different controls for different known inputs changes the protocol
being compared. The bound above concerns one fixed protocol across them. So the floor sits
on the merging move, on its worst input, whatever anyone knows, and that's the shape of the toll.
The bound on a device left to relax from a known start, in the next subsection, is one more floor
of this kind.

There's a second piece of fine print on Theorem~\ref{thm:known-state}, and it's about who works the controls.
The entropy-loss bound supplies no positive floor for a known input. Whether a device
can approach that floor also depends on its controls: lower this barrier, tilt that well,
raise the barrier again. Those operations have a timing and a physical implementation.
The entropy calculation alone does not price either.

Paul Riechers, Alexander Boyd, Gregory Wimsatt and James Crutchfield (2020) analyse
metastable memories under \emph{time-symmetric} control: the prescribed control is the
same played forwards or backwards, with the relevant time-reversal conventions. A
symmetric clock pulse can meet that restriction; an arbitrary clocked pulse need not.
For memory states unchanged by time reversal, their low-error result singles out the
memory states that the desired logical map, applied twice, fails to bring back to where
they started. They call those transitions \emph{nonreciprocal}. With equal local-equilibrium free
energies, the leading minimum-work term as the error allowance $\varepsilon$ tends to
zero is proportional to
\[
k_B T\ln(1/\varepsilon)\,
\Pr\bigl(C(C(m))\ne m\bigr).
\]
The probability is over the initial memory states. This is a low-error scaling with
physical premises, not an exact finite-error heat charge on every execution.

A permanent flip from no to yes is nonreciprocal at that no-state: a second application
cannot return it to no. A known input at that state can then face the extra work
cost in their restricted control setting, even though its initial logical entropy is zero.
Their class also includes a three-state cycle, which merges nothing. The distinction is
about the permitted controls as well as the logical map. It neither changes
Theorem~\ref{thm:known-state}'s entropy calculation nor identifies the book's abstract
merge price with a universal physical heat floor.

A deterministic run from a known start has a known state at every step, so the premise sets
no floor under any of its steps; each that changes something can dissipate under the stated thermal-model assumptions,
and a fixed device keeps the floor above on each step that merges.
One more limit, about which states collide. The counting guarantees a
collision among the already-yes states together with the entering no-state. It does not guarantee that the entering state takes part in the collision. Take four states with only the first reading no, and a move that sends the first state to the second, the second to the third, and leaves the third and fourth where they are: the second and third both land on the third, and the first never shares with anyone. For an input distribution
supported only on no-states, this counting argument alone forces no positive entropy
loss. Whether other states in that support merge depends on the move. The operation-level
ledger toll still follows under merge pricing.

What this section earns comes to this. A finite machine's permanent flag-raising
instruction has two allowed starting states that land on one state. Prepare those two
with equal chances: that instruction removes one bit, and under the adopted physical
premise its mean heat is at least $k_B T\ln2$. That is a worst-case preparation, not a
positive charge on every execution. A known start gives no positive entropy-loss floor. Any finite-time dissipation depends on the device's dynamics, controls and speed; under the fixed-protocol entropy-balance assumptions above, merging $K$ inputs
forces at least $k_B\ln K$ of entropy production on one of them. The
ledger charges the merging move whatever the preparation, because merge pricing says so. The counting proves a collision, the preparation
determines the uncertainty removed, and the physical premises connect that removal to heat.

The general case is the one that shows you where the bits go. Split the bits removed
state by state. Each state $x$ you might be in carries its chance $p(x)$ along to where it
lands, $\mathrm{step}(x, i)$, and finds whatever other chance landed there too. If nobody else
landed there, its term is zero. If others did, its term is the difference between how crowded its
landing spot is and how much of the crowd it brought.

\begin{theorem}[The bits removed, one term per state]\label{thm:u04-point-sum}
On a finite machine, for any move $i$ and any chances $p(x) \ge 0$, with $q$ the pushed
spread,
\[
H(p) - H(q) \;=\; \sum_{x:\,p(x) > 0} p(x)\,\bigl(\log_2 q(\mathrm{step}(x,i)) - \log_2 p(x)\bigr).
\]
Every term is zero or more, so a move never adds bits. If two different states $x \ne x'$,
both with positive chance, land on the same state, the sum is strictly positive.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Group the sum for $H(q)$ by where things land: the chance $q(y)$ at a landing spot is the
sum of the $p(x)$ that land there, so
$H(q) = -\sum_{x:\,p(x) > 0} p(x) \log_2 q(\mathrm{step}(x,i))$. Subtract from $H(p)$ term by
term. Each term is non-negative because the landing spot holds at least what $x$ brought,
$q(\mathrm{step}(x,i)) \ge p(x)$, and the logarithm keeps order. If $x$ and $x'$ share a
landing spot, that spot holds at least $p(x) + p(x') > p(x)$, so the term for $x$ is
strictly positive.
\end{proof}

\subsection{What you're entitled to, and what you're not}

Let me total it: what have you earned the right to conclude, and where is there still a way out?

You've earned this first, and it needs no premise but one next state for every state: on any machine run by one rule, finite or endless, a run that raises a reading and keeps it up either merges two of its own states or never repeats one, and on any machine at all a single move
that raises a kept reading without merging anything has to send the kept states one-to-one into a
part of themselves with a gap left over, which takes endlessly many of them. Either way it is a merge, or an endless supply of states never used before. You've earned this: on any machine with finitely many states, a move that raises a flag
either forgets something or takes a flag down somewhere else. That is pure counting, with no physics and no
premise beyond finiteness, and the half of it where nothing comes down is the pigeonhole on four states.
You've earned this: on a finite machine, if a flag, once up, stays up, then raising it
has a collision somewhere. If it raises several no-states at once, the yes-states together
with those newcomers land on at least that many fewer spots than there are of them. This does
not say that each newcomer shares its destination; this one is counting again. And you've earned this: if forgetting
is charged for, the toll follows, and if forgetting is charged per halving, the size of the
toll follows too; each of those derivations hands back a system with the five parts and the
toll, so Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s floor applies to it as it stands.
This is the rule from Section~\ref{sec:toll}, now derived, with every premise named, for any
finite machine with a flag that stays up. In that section I only declared it.

Now for what you haven't earned, which I list so you don't assume it. You haven't
earned that forgetting costs anything in the world; that's Landauer, it's measured for beads
and argued over for the general case, and in this book it's an assumption with a name.
And even granting it, Landauer's entropy-loss bound demands no positive heat from a run whose state is known (the lifted
cup of the coin example), so what the physics forces is a floor on a device that has to work whatever it's
holding. An individual run can fall below an ensemble average bound. Knowing a state does not by itself prove that another person or memory paid the difference.
You haven't earned that any machine you'd actually want to build is of this kind, either,
and there are two easy ways to miss. A machine that keeps its running total inside its own
state, as a number with no ceiling, has infinitely many states, so the finite premise fails
for it as a whole. And you can't patch that by giving the total a ceiling. A total that only
climbs, held in finite memory, eventually either stops at its top, and then two different
histories leave the same top value, which is a merge, or rolls back over to zero, and then it
doesn't only climb. So any running total a finite machine keeps for itself has a horizon:
it's honest up to its width and no further. And a machine whose price list charges the step that raises the flag, but lets
some other step merge two states at no cost, raises the flag honestly and still doesn't
charge for forgetting in general, so the merge-pricing premise fails for it. Either one puts
a machine outside these theorems as stated, though a finite piece of it can still sit
inside. The example I build later (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}) misses in both ways. It keeps
counters with no ceiling, so it's infinite outright, and some of its ordinary steps, counting a
counter down among them, can land two different states on one at no charge on the ledger. So the counting, as
stated, doesn't reach it: it forces the toll only on machines with finitely many yes-states that price every merge,
and that example is neither. It doesn't need the counting, though: the moves that raise its flag merge states themselves, so the same cost lands on them directly (Theorem~\ref{thm:record-merge-toll}).

A finite piece can still sit inside, and the smallest one I could build where every
premise can be seen to hold is this. None of them is left as a hypothesis. It has four slots times a flag, eight states, and three kinds of move: stamp (set the flag, go to the next slot, cost one), jump to a chosen slot (cost two), next slot (cost zero). It's finite and permanent; the next-slot
move forgets nothing; the stamp and the jump merge; merges are priced, and priced per halving. So this
section's two conclusions hold on it outright. The counting lemma underneath, that a duplicate-free list in which no landing spot is hit by more than a set number of members has at most that many times as many members as landing spots, is the plainer reading of the halving price above. Merge pricing alone
would take any price of at least one for the jump. The jump's price of
two is what the halving price asks, since the jump squeezes four states into one. One more fact
about it: each move's price is exactly the number of halvings in its largest
squeeze. A move that costs one has no spot hit by more than two states, a move that costs two has none hit by more than four, and some spot is hit by exactly that many (stamp squeezes at most two states into one, jump to a slot squeezes four, and next-slot squeezes nothing).

The example Part~III builds runs this eight-state machine. Seen through a window that shows only a line
number, read modulo four as the slot, and a flag, a short program of that machine, once a
two-instruction setup has run, does what the
eight-state machine does, one move at a time, and pays exactly what the eight-state machine charges. The example as a
whole prices its record and not every merge: some of its zero-price steps merge states, and
whatever those merges cost the hardware is off the ledger, so the finite piece is a piece. The toll on
the whole example comes from the record's part of the state (Theorem~\ref{thm:record-merge-toll}).

Finiteness did one job in the counting. It forced the step that raises a permanent flag to merge two
states. On the machine of Part~III no count over the whole machine has to force that, because the
merge is in plain view.
Its record moves are the check, the commitment and the raised flag that the opening's lock puts in
order, and it names them CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY: COMMIT names a
checked claim in a slot called the channel, and CERTIFY raises the flag. CERTIFY takes a state with the flag down and the same state with the flag up to one place,
since a flag that's already up just stays up. Its COMMIT overwrites the channel, so two states that
differ only in what the channel names land on one state. Part (1) of the theorem below shows
both. So any price list that
charges every merge of that machine's own step charges the flag-raising step, with no premise that
the machine is finite. It isn't: its versions and its ledger grow without bound.

Finiteness is still there, in the smallest place it can be. Hold every part of the state but the
flag fixed, and the flag has two readings, down and up. CERTIFY sends both to up, and it does the
same to everything else from either, so the two states land together. That is the counting of
Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges} on a set of two. So the choice I made in the opening's list isn't the merge, and it isn't the shape of CERTIFY. It's that the step never reads the flag: the rest of the state moves by its own rule and the ledger adds the instruction's price, whichever way the flag reads, so no instruction keeps a copy of the old reading, and any that raises the flag lands its two readings together. Make CERTIFY trap instead when the flag is already up, and the merge moves rather than goes away: the state it traps lands with the state that was trapped already, since a trapped machine only pays. That's the halted state stepping to itself again, and it holds of every record move: any of the three that fails lands with the same state already trapped. The one way out of the flag's merge is to write the old reading into a part of the state that grows, a list of every reading so far, say, and that is a state never used before, the other column. A ledger that adds more for a re-raise than for a raise doesn't do it: the state with the flag up and the ledger a little lower lands where the raise lands, and the merge has only moved again.

That leaves the other miss, the unpriced merges. The example's price list, in Part~III, puts
its flat moves at zero, and a flat move merges (DEC, counting a counter down, lands two states on one),
so full merge pricing and that price list can't both hold on that machine. They don't have to. Split a
state into its base part, which is what a two-counter machine would show (the line number and the
two counters), and its record part, which is everything else: the versions (each counter's count
of how many times it has been written), the table of facts, the channel, the trap latch (which goes up when a record move fails, after which only the ledger moves), the ledger and the flag. Then price only the merges the record layer
makes.

\begin{premise}[Record-layer merge pricing]\label{prem:record-merge}
A move that sends two different states with the same base part to one state costs at least one. \end{premise} Part of where that line falls is forced. The line number has to be in the base part, or DEC, which can land two lines with the same counters on one, makes a record-layer merge at no cost; each counter has to be there, or its version, or DEC's own merge gets charged; and the flag or the trap has to be outside it, or nothing charges CERTIFY. Where the versions, the table, the channel and the ledger sit moves nothing below.

The merges among base parts are the flat part's business, the ones any two-counter machine
makes, and whatever heat they cost is the flat part's heat. The premise prices only merges
between states with the same flat part. A step like DEC, which changes that part, can
lose a version number at no cost, and the premise doesn't object. Merge pricing implies this
premise, so it asks less, and on the record distinctions it is still an assumed operation-level price; identifying
it with heat needs a physical model. And it is a price on this machine, not a source of the toll on
any machine. A certifying move whose effect on the base read the flag, say one that moved a
counter up when it raised the flag and left the counter alone when the flag was up already, would raise the flag and send no two states with the same base to one state, and the premise would have nothing to charge at the raise. It would still merge: the state with the flag down and the state with the flag up and that counter one higher land together, across two base parts, where the premise doesn't look. And on this machine its trap would still be charged when it fails. The small
machine's record moves treat the base the same whichever way the flag reads, which is why the
premise does its job there, and the theorem below is stated for that example and no other.

\begin{theorem}[The toll on the example machine]\label{thm:record-merge-toll}
For the small machine of Section~\ref{sec:smallest}, with no finiteness premise: (1) CERTIFY merges, and so do COMMIT and CHECK of every claim, and each joins two different states with the same line and counters. (2) Every cost that satisfies merge pricing for that machine's step charges CERTIFY, every COMMIT and every CHECK at least one, and obeys the toll, so the machine with that cost is a Thiele
machine. (3) No INC, DEC or HALT sends two different states with the same line and counters to one
state. So the machine's own prices, base moves at zero and each record move at one, satisfy Premise~\ref{prem:record-merge}, they're the least prices that do, and merge pricing fails for them. (4) Every cost that satisfies
Premise~\ref{prem:record-merge} obeys the toll, so the machine with that cost is a Thiele
machine.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) For CERTIFY, prepare two states identical except for the flag. Give both a
channel holding a commitment. One flag is down and one is up. CERTIFY raises the
first and leaves the second up. Both advance one line and add the same charge;
every other field agrees. They have become the same full state.

For COMMIT, put the requested fact, at the counter's current edition, in both
tables. Leave one channel empty and put that very commitment in the other.
COMMIT writes the same commitment into both channels and treats every other
field alike. Again the full successors agree.

For any CHECK, fill the fact table to its sixteen-entry limit. CHECK then fails,
whatever claim it was asked to test. Compare that untrapped state with an otherwise
identical state whose trap is already up. The first sets its trap; the second is
already frozen. Neither changes the other core fields, and both pay the same
charge. Their successors agree. In each construction the starting line and
counters agree as well, so these are record-layer merges.

(2) A price on every merge charges each of those instructions at least one.
Only CERTIFY can raise the certificate. Its merge therefore supplies the toll.

(3) Check the free instructions by asking whether two states with the same line
and counters could become one. The table, channel, trap, ledger and certificate
are left alone, so any difference in those fields survives. On a live state the
shared line and counters choose the same instruction branch. A counter write
adds one to its edition; different edition numbers stay different after the same
addition. All unchanged editions stay different too. Hence no remaining field
can hide a difference between those sources.

A trapped state stays exactly where it is under a free instruction. Two different
trapped states therefore stay different. A live state remains live under these
instructions, so it cannot meet a trapped one. That exhausts the cases.
The free instructions make no record-layer merge, and all three kinds of record
instruction do. Charging the former zero and the latter one satisfies the premise
and is the smallest such price list. Full merge pricing still fails: the zero-price
DEC pair in Theorem~\ref{thm:frag-merge-split} starts with different counters and
lands together.

(4) Any record-layer merge price charges the CERTIFY pair from (1).
Since no other instruction raises the flag, this gives the toll for every raise.
\end{proof}

So this section reaches the example machine. On it the toll follows from record-layer merge pricing, and the example's
own price list, flat moves at zero included, satisfies that premise. This is a result about
its ledger, not a heat bound. There's a second way to settle the clash, which I note and didn't take. Morita's reversible two-counter
machine runs every step backwards and is still
universal: with its input encoded, it computes anything a Turing machine can. Put the record over a base like that, with the base's step taken as the program's own step from line to line and the halt left with no next step, and every base step is one-to-one, and full merge pricing permits those base steps to cost zero. That price list
would put the flat moves at zero; the lower-bound premise alone does not require zero charges. It isn't the example's flat part, though. The example has a move for each two-counter instruction, acting from every live state, not a step for each line of one program, and DEC $c$ $j$ sends states on any two lines with the same counters, $c$ above 0, to the same window, so whether it merges turns on the rest of the state and not on the program being reversible. That base
wouldn't be getting anything for nothing: what it doesn't forget it keeps in its counters, which
is the column of states never used before, again. I haven't built that machine.

And you haven't earned anything about \emph{what} the flag means. The pigeonhole on four states doesn't know what it's certifying. The cost is for raising a flag that
stays up. Whether raising that flag ever amounts to standing behind a structural fact, the
``vouching'' I keep promising and keep not delivering, is a question for the certified example in Part~III,
and here it has moved exactly this far: on a finite machine that charges for every merge, if that flag stays up, it was paid for.

One last thing, because it should nag at you. The toll is forced by the
premises, but the premises were chosen, and ``permanent'' in particular was chosen by me. Why
should a flag stay up? Why not let it come down, pay nothing, and be honest about it?
That's a fair question, and merge or revoke is the start of an answer (the three-card machine only showed that
the converse of Corollary~\ref{cor:permanent-forced} fails): on a finite machine that charges for every merge, a flag that
goes
up at zero cost is a flag the same move takes back somewhere, and a record that can be silently
taken back is the thing a hash chain and a write-once disk were built
against. ``Permanent'' here is exactly that: the flag can't be lowered. The toy in Section~\ref{sec:toll}
has it only because none of its three moves happens to lower the flag, and durability is the
one job of a record it has; I chose it. Whether that was the
right job to pick is something you can argue with me about, and I'd want you
to.

And ``permanent'' is an idealization, which I should say before a physicist does. No physical
record lasts forever. A bit held behind an energy barrier leaks over it at some rate, however
slow, and a closed finite system comes back around, which is Zermelo's point from the counting
(Theorem~\ref{thm:reversible-keeps-nothing} is the finite form).
The toll theorems in this section, the ones that start from a flag that stays up, need permanence on every state the machine can reach, including states a given run never visits, forever; on states nothing reaches it never comes into it, and merge or revoke does without it. Weaken that to ``the flag stays up on the states that actually turn up,
for as long as anyone cares,'' and merge-or-revoke tells you what goes wrong: the move could take the flag down somewhere the machine could go and never does, and then it isn't forced to merge at all. A
version of the toll stated in chances is the noisy steps of Section~\ref{sec:what-a-chair-is}:
a step that squeezes nothing on average can't raise a reading that stays, and one that can
strictly bunches the even spread. A version stated in time spans is a different theorem, and
what I have of it is below.

One piece of it I can hand you, and the step law of Section~\ref{sec:what-a-chair-is} is its
general form. Take one move and repeat it from one start, forever. On a finite machine the states that run passes through are
finitely many, so it falls into a loop. If the move forgot nothing on those states, it would
be a reshuffle of them, and a reshuffle brings every one of them back around, the start
included, where the flag was down. So if the flag goes up along that run and stays up from
some point on, the move merges two states \emph{the run itself visits}. The state they share is
one the machine actually passes through. And it doesn't touch the known-state point above: a merge
among states the run visits still receives no positive lower bound from the entropy-loss
premise when its state is known. The argument holds for any map on finitely many states iterated from a start whose flag is down, with the flag up at every step from some point on; no permanence premise is used.

Runs that mix different moves split two ways, and the answer is short enough to give here. If the moves are picked from outside, in any order at
all, the answer is no. Take two states, one reading no and one reading yes. One move swaps them; the other does nothing. Run the swap once and then the do-nothing move forever: the flag goes up at the first step and
stays up for good, and neither move merges anything anywhere. The swap would take the flag down
from the yes-state if it ever ran there; on this run it never does, and that's exactly the
weakened permanence this paragraph is about. But if the machine is closed, picking its next
move from its own state, the run is the orbit of one map, the step with whatever move the state
picks, and the single-move argument applies to that map as it
stands. Now say the moves come in a
pattern that eventually repeats, one phrase of moves played over and over. Suppose the flag is down at some step after the
repeating starts, and goes up and stays up after that. Count the repetitions from a step where the flag was down (start
the phrase at that move if you have to) and run the same argument on the whole phrase treated as one move, at the states where each playing of it begins. It merges two
of those states, both visited; follow the two through the phrase, and the first move
where their paths meet merges two states the run visits at that move's place in the pattern.
So the answer is no for moves picked from outside, and yes for a closed machine, or for a repeating program once the flag is down somewhere after the repeating starts.

Two chapters remain in this part. The next takes the record off its two places and lets it sit
anywhere in an order, to see what the two places were doing. The one after is about a different
way out entirely. Forgetting has had its chapter; the question after that is whether
\emph{finding out} costs, because the demon's whole trick was that it knew which way the molecule
was going, and I owe you a straight answer on what knowing costs.

%===========================================================================
\section{The whole direction}
\label{sec:direction}
%===========================================================================

The record in Definition~\ref{def:thiele} is a place in any order, and the toll charges any move
that climbs. Up to here the proofs were done on two places, blank and written, because that's the
record you can point at. \emph{Established} never felt like a switch to me, though. It feels like
a direction with lines drawn across it, and the switch is just the first line. This section does
the proofs on the whole direction, and finds out that the two-place case was a case: nothing the
switch needed gets left behind, and the one thing a single switch can't do, hold three or more
stages, falls out as a count.

A row of cells that only ever go from blank to written is a direction: you can tell how far
along it a state is, and nothing walks it back. A single cell, a cup turned once, has two
positions. The question for this section is blunt: with the record anywhere in an order, which
of the results so far (the universal floor, the merges, the squeeze) come along as they stand,
and which ones need the order to be more than a preorder?

\subsection{A row of cups}

Get four cups and a pencil. Write five stages of an experiment on a strip of paper,
left to right: \emph{proposed}, \emph{set up}, \emph{run}, \emph{read}, \emph{recorded}.
Agree to do them in that order. Put an upside-down cup between each pair of neighbours.
The first means ``the setup happened,'' the second ``the run happened,'' the third
``the result was read,'' the fourth ``the result was recorded.'' As you complete a
stage, turn over its cup. Cups only ever get turned right side up; none has a reset
wire. These are records of completed acts. A fourth cup up does not make a false
conclusion true, and a different experiment may need a different order.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[thiele]
\node[pipe,text width=3.4cm,minimum width=0pt] (a) {proposed\\\texttt{0000}};
\node[pipe,text width=3.4cm,minimum width=0pt,below=0.55cm of a] (b) {set up\\\texttt{1000}};
\node[pipe,text width=3.4cm,minimum width=0pt,below=0.55cm of b] (c) {run\\\texttt{1100}};
\node[pipe,text width=3.4cm,minimum width=0pt,below=0.55cm of c] (d) {read\\\texttt{1110}};
\node[pipe,text width=3.4cm,minimum width=0pt,below=0.55cm of d] (e) {recorded\\\texttt{1111}};
\draw[pipearrow] (a.south) -- (b.north);
\draw[pipearrow] (b.south) -- (c.north);
\draw[pipearrow] (c.south) -- (d.north);
\draw[pipearrow] (d.south) -- (e.north);
\end{tikzpicture}

\small Read down the drawing. Zero means cup down, one means cup up. Four cups give five stages
along this run because each new stage turns up one unused cup.
\end{center}

Two things to notice with the cups in front of you. Each cup by itself is the two-place record:
it reads yes or no, and once yes it stays yes, which Part~II will call a latch
(Section~\ref{sec:latch}). And four cups were
enough for five stages. Try it with three, and you'll find you can't: three cups that only ever
turn up, in order, give you at most four different arrangements along the way. I'll prove both of
those in a minute, and the proof is about as short as the experiment.

Now a harder strip. Some checks don't line up. One person repeats the experiment;
another independently works through the calculation. Neither act includes the other.
Draw a diamond: \emph{neither} at the bottom, \emph{experiment repeated} on the left,
\emph{calculation checked} on the right, \emph{both} at the top. There are two ways
up, and the middle points don't compare, which is what a \emph{partial} order allows.
Put a cup on each point except the bottom, one for the repeat, one for the calculation,
one for both. Each cup is still a latch. The three cups tell you which acts have
happened. They do not decide whether the experimental model or the calculation's
premises were appropriate.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[thiele]
\node[pipe,text width=3.6cm,minimum width=0pt] (n) at (0,0) {Neither act\\\texttt{000}};
\node[pipe,text width=3.6cm,minimum width=0pt] (r) at (-3.2,2.6) {Experiment repeated\\\texttt{100}};
\node[pipe,text width=3.6cm,minimum width=0pt] (c) at (3.2,2.6) {Calculation checked\\\texttt{010}};
\node[pipe,text width=3.6cm,minimum width=0pt] (b) at (0,5.2) {Both acts\\\texttt{111}};
\draw[pipearrow] (n) -- (r);
\draw[pipearrow] (n) -- (c);
\draw[pipearrow] (r) -- (b);
\draw[pipearrow] (c) -- (b);
\end{tikzpicture}

\small Read the cups as repeat, calculation, both. Neither middle point
includes the other. The third cup repeats information already supplied by
the first two; it is useful for showing thresholds, not needed for storage.
\end{center}

Whatever the shape of the strip, a straight line of stages or a diamond or something with a
hundred points, I'll call the set of places the record can be the \emph{direction}, and each
question ``has the record reached at least this place?'' a \emph{line} across it. One line is
one cup.

\subsection{The order, said exactly}

The strip and the diamond each come with an order you can see by looking: whether one place is at
or below another. Said exactly, the order is a test. For any two places $x$ and $y$ it answers ``is
$x$ at or below $y$?'' with yes or no, and I write a yes as $x \le y$. The test has to obey two
rules: every place is at or below itself, and if $x \le y$ and $y \le z$ then $x \le z$. An order
that obeys just those two is called a \emph{preorder}. If it also obeys a third rule, that $x \le y$
and $y \le x$ together force $x = y$, it's a \emph{partial order}, and that third rule is called
antisymmetry. The two-point order, no below yes, is the cup. The whole numbers in their usual order
are a straight strip that never ends.

The cups say the same thing in their own terms. For a place $a$, the cup for $a$ asks ``has the
record reached at least $a$?'', so with the record at $x$ it's up exactly when $a \le x$, and I
write its answer as $[a \le x]$. In the row of cups I said the cups together tell you which place
the record is at. On the strip and the diamond you can check that with your eyes, and Part~II
proves it again from the latch side whenever the order is partial (Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-growing}),
though the first time through I hadn't asked what in that proof was doing the work. My first guess
was that it held for every order.

Why bother with the bare preorder at all, when every strip on the table is a partial order? I bothered because
I wanted to see what the third rule was doing, and the way to see what a rule does is to take it
away. Take a preorder with two places, call them \emph{left} and \emph{right}, where each is at or
below the other. There are two cups, one asking ``at least left?'' and one asking ``at least
right?'', and both are up at left and both are up at right. Look at the table and you can't say
where the record is. Now build a record that swaps between left and right on every single step and
charges nothing. Every rule I'm about to state is satisfied. The record never drops below anywhere
it was, because each place is at or below the other. No cup ever moves, so the toll in the next
subsection has nothing to charge. The record moved on every step and nothing on the table noticed.

\begin{theorem}[The cups fix the place, and only with antisymmetry]\label{thm:dir-lines}
(1) In a partial order, if two places $x$ and $y$ leave the same cups up, $[a \le x] = [a \le y]$
for every $a$, then $x = y$. (2) In a preorder that isn't a partial order this can fail: there's a
preorder with two different places that leave the same cups up, and a record over it, driven by
the computation and growing in that preorder, that changes on every step while no cup moves.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Look at the cup for $x$. It's up when the record is at $x$, since $x$ is at or below itself,
so it's up at $y$ too, and that says $x \le y$. The cup for $y$ gives $y \le x$ the same way.
Antisymmetry gives $x = y$. (2) Left and right above, with the record swapping every step.
\end{proof}

So in a partial order the cups are the place, and in the preorder I built they aren't. That second
half holds in every preorder that isn't partial, by one line: if
$x \le y$ and $y \le x$ with $x \ne y$, then a cup that's up at either one is up at the other, by
transitivity. So the cups fix the place if and only if the order is partial. My first guess was right on every
strip I could draw, and it was right because of a rule I hadn't noticed I was leaning on. On a
bare preorder, putting two places on the same rung tells the toll not to care about moves between
them, and it doesn't. I don't think that's a defect; it's the order telling you what you agreed to
count.

\subsection{The toll, over the whole direction}

One cup had one rule: the step that turns it right side up pays. Now there's a row of cups, or a
diamond of them, and a single step can turn over several at once. The rule I'd guess first
turns out to be the right one: \emph{a step that turns over any cup pays at least one.} A step
that turns over three cups at once still only has to pay one. The rule asks whether a step turned
something over. It doesn't ask how many.

That rule buys the same thing one cup bought. Take any run, and suppose some cup is up at
the end that was down at the start. Somewhere along the run a step turned that cup over, and that
step paid. So the run paid at least one. Count the same way and you get more: the run paid at least
once for every step that turned anything over.

Now look at what that argument didn't use. It didn't care whether the cups sat in a row or a
diamond or something with a hundred points. It didn't care how many there were. It didn't even use
the fact that cups never get turned back down. If something could knock a cup back over, the
argument still works, because all it needs is the one step where that cup went up.

To say it exactly I want to translate it into places. The cup at a place
$a$ is up exactly when the record is at or above $a$. Say a step takes the record from $x$ to $y$.
The cup at $y$ is up afterwards, since $y$ is at or above itself, and it was down before exactly
when $y$ isn't at or below $x$. And if $y$ is at or below $x$, any cup that's up at $y$ was already
up at $x$. So a step turns over some cup exactly when it lands somewhere that isn't at or below
where it started. The same reasoning says a run ends with some cup up that was down at the start
exactly when it ends somewhere that isn't at or below where it started.

\begin{theorem}[The toll over any direction]\label{thm:dir-toll}
Take a machine whose record is a place in any preorder, and say a step \emph{turns a cup over} when
it takes the record from $x$ to a place that isn't at or below $x$. (1) Every step that turns a cup
over costs at least one exactly when every run, from whatever state it starts, that ends somewhere not
at or below its start costs at least one. (2) When that holds, a run costs at least the number of its
steps that turn a cup over. (3) It holds exactly when every cup, on its own, obeys the two-place
toll: for every place $a$, a step that turns the cup at $a$ from down to up costs
at least one. (1) is the floor over any order (Observation~\ref{thm:general-floor}) said in cups, and the universal floor (Observation~\ref{thm:universal-floor}) is (1) with one cup.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) and (2) are the walk above. For the other half of (1), a run of one step that turns a cup over
ends somewhere not at or below its start. (3) is the translation above.
\end{proof}

When the cups only ever go up, as on the strip and the diamond, a step that turns a cup over is
just a step up.

That surprised me a little, because I'd filed the floor away as a fact about one bit, and nothing in it was
about one bit. It was about one cup going up, and anything you build out of cups has that.

\subsection{One line isn't enough}

Now comes the payoff I promised at the start of this section. Could a cleverer single cup do the job of all four, with one latch and some decoding that reads the record's place off the
latch and whatever the machine shows? Section~\ref{sec:latch} rules that out in the
smallest case: over a machine with one visible state, a record that climbs through three places can't be
produced by one latch and a decoding, because one latch and one visible state make two outcomes and
the record has three.

So try a second guess, closer to the cup's own rule. The cup's rule was ``new value is old value
\emph{or} the event.'' The obvious rule for a whole row is ``new place is old place \emph{joined
with} the event's place,'' where joining two places means going to the lowest place at or above
both. On the row, the event names a place, and you turn up every cup as far as that place. To see
it break, take the strip $0 < 1 < 2$, a cup at $1$ and a cup at $2$, over a machine with one
visible state, so the event has to be one fixed place. Let the record jump from $0$ straight to $2$,
turning up both cups in one step, and stay put at $1$ and at $2$. From $0$ the event has to turn up
both cups, so the fixed place is $2$. From $1$ the same event would turn up the second cup as well,
and the record stays at $1$.

What works is giving every cup its own event, and letting the event for a cup look at where the
record already is. Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-growing}, in Part~II, says exactly that, and this is why it has
to. That leaves the question of how many cups. In the row of cups I asked you to try five stages with three
and said you couldn't. Here is the count, with the matching example added, and with an arrangement of
$k$ cups read as a $k$-bit word, a one for every cup that's up.

\begin{theorem}[Lines a direction needs]\label{thm:dir-bits}
(1) A list of different arrangements of $k$ cups, each keeping up every cup the one before had up
(a chain of different $k$-bit words in which each word's set bits are among the next word's), has
at most $k + 1$ members, and for every $k$ there's such a chain with exactly $k + 1$. So a straight
strip of $n + 1$ stages needs exactly $n$ cups. (2) Over a machine with one visible state, take the
record on the strip $0 < 1 < 2$ that jumps from $0$ to $2$ and stays put at $1$ and at $2$. It
grows and is driven by the computation, and no rule of the form ``join the record with a fixed
place'' reproduces its steps.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Going from one arrangement to the next, which is a different one, turns up at least one more
cup, and there are $k$ cups, so there are at most $k$ steps and $k + 1$ arrangements. For the
matching chain, take no cups up, then the first, then the first two, and so on, packed to the
left: that's the row of cups. (2) Joining $0$ with a fixed place $g$ gives $g$, and from $0$ the
step has to give $2$, so $g$ is $2$. Joining $1$ with $2$ gives $2$, and from $1$ the step has to
stay at $1$.
\end{proof}

So five stages need four cups, and neither one nor three will do it, as long as the cups only turn
up. An ordinary binary counter holds a thousand stages in ten bits, because its bits go
down as well as up, and the theorem says nothing against that. The switch isn't wrong:
it's the first line, and a straight strip with more than two places needs more of them, exactly one
fewer than it has stages. A direction that branches needs at least as many cups as the steps in its longest strict climb, and at least as many as it takes to tell its places apart, the rounded-up logarithm of how many there are. Put three places above a bottom, none of them above another: the longest climb is one step, and one cup can't tell four places apart, so it takes two, and two do it, though not two lines: one cup that goes up at the first and the third, and one that goes up at the second and the third. It can need more than both. Take two places each below two others: one step of climb, four places, and two cups still won't do, because both upper places would have to keep up every cup either lower one has up, and two cups allow at most one arrangement like that besides the lower places' own.

\subsection{Why crossing a line has to cost}

The last chapter showed that the cup's toll isn't an arbitrary rule. It's forced by three premises, and the
argument that ties them together was the
pigeonhole: on a machine with finitely many states, the move that raises a record that goes up and stays up has to land two
possible states on one state (Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges}), and a step that
lands two states on one is a step that forgets which one it came from. Does that survive the whole
row of cups? Mostly, and the parts that don't survive are the interesting ones.

The counting needs a flag, because what it counts is the collection of states with that flag up, and now there are many cups, each one a yes-or-no reading that could serve as the flag, so the first job is to pick one. My first guess
was the cup for the place where the record starts. That goes nowhere: the starting state
already has that cup up, so it's already in the collection, and there's no state coming in from outside. The cup
that works is the one the step turns over, the cup for the place where the record lands. It's up
after the step, since a place is at or above itself, and it was down before, which is what turning a cup
over means. So the collection is every state with that landing cup up, and the state the step
starts from is the one coming in from outside.
If the move keeps every state in the collection inside it and never lands two states on one, the states already inside use up every state in the collection between them, and there's none left for the newcomer. So one of two things
happened. Either two states landed on one, or some state that was in the collection got moved out, which
means its landing cup went back down. I'll call that second thing a \emph{revocation}.

\begin{theorem}[Turning a cup over merges]\label{thm:dir-merge}
On a machine with a record in any preorder, where each place has finitely many states with its cup up: (1) if a move turns a cup over
at some state and lands the record at a place $a$, then either the move merges two states, or
there's a state with the cup at $a$ up that the same move takes to a state with the cup at $a$
down, which is a revocation; (2) if the record only grows, so that no cup ever goes back down, the
move merges; (3) if the record only grows, the toll holds exactly when every move that turns a cup
over at some state, and merges, costs at least one, so merge pricing gives the toll.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Gather every state with the cup at $a$ up. There are finitely many. If the move keeps each of
them there and is injective, it maps that collection into itself without two landing on one, so it
hits all of them, including the state it sends the starting state to; injectivity then says the
starting state was in the collection already, and it wasn't, because its cup at $a$ was down. So
either some state in the collection has its cup at $a$ knocked down, or the move isn't injective. (2) Growth rules out the
knocking down. (3) If the toll holds, every move that turns a cup over somewhere pays, merging or
not. The other way, a move that turns a cup over merges by (2), so the hypothesis charges it.
\end{proof}

It's the old counting argument again, run once for every cup.

Each premise there can be knocked out, and I wanted to see each one go, because a premise you've
never seen fail is one you don't understand yet.

Knock out finiteness. Take the whole numbers as the states, which gives a row of cups that never
ends, and let the record be the state itself, one more on every step, at no charge. Every step turns
up one more cup. The step never merges anything: different numbers go to different numbers. Merge
pricing holds, because there are no merges to price, and the toll fails on every single step. The
counting broke at the one place it needed the collection to be finite. Every state moved one along, and there was
always another state to move to. That's Charles Bennett's 1973 construction in miniature: a machine that
keeps its whole history never has to forget, so it never has to merge. It hasn't got out of paying.
Every step lands it on a state it has never used, and that's the fresh-state column. The toll fails here
because merge pricing only charges merges and this machine pays by taking a state it has never used, which that price list
doesn't charge. Take the infinity away and the supply of fresh states goes with it.

Knock out growth. Take a two-state machine whose record flips back and forth between two places, so
a cup goes up on one step and gets knocked back down on the next. The two states just swap with each other,
so nothing merges, and the price list is honest about merges. The step that turns the cup up
pays nothing. It takes the other branch of (1) and revokes: the state that had the cup up gets moved to where it's down.

Knock out the price on merges. A two-state machine that stamps every state with yes turns the cup
up wherever it was down, merges at the stamp, and charges nothing. Of course the toll fails; nobody
asked the merge to pay.

\begin{theorem}[Each premise does work]\label{thm:dir-escapes}
(1) There's a machine with infinitely many states, a growing record and an honest merge price on
which every step turns a cup over and the toll fails. (2) There's a two-state machine with an
honest merge price whose record doesn't grow, which turns a cup over and fails the toll. (3)
There's a two-state machine with a growing record whose merges aren't priced, which fails the toll.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The three machines above, in order.
\end{proof}

So
the toll over a whole direction rests on exactly the three things the cup's toll rested on:
finitely many states with each cup up, a record that doesn't come down, and merges that pay. Nothing extra got
smuggled in when one cup became a row, and nothing the one cup needed got left behind.

I'd half expected the diamond to need something new, some extra rule for the two middle cups that
don't compare. It didn't. Every cup gets its own collection of states, and the argument on each is the old one.


%===========================================================================

\section{Learning borrows, committing pays}
\label{sec:narrowing}
%===========================================================================

I ended the chapter on the toll's reason owing you an answer about knowing. What keeping takes
so far sits on forgetting: under merge pricing, a finite machine's permanent flag-raising
instruction was paid for because it merges two states somewhere. But there's a thing that looks
like the opposite of forgetting and feels like it ought to cost at least as much, probably more,
and that is finding out. Every time a machine rules out a possibility, it knows more than it did. If
forgetting a bit costs, does learning one cost too? I had a strong feeling about this, and you
probably have it too, so I'll say it first: learning is the expensive part. Most physicists had
that feeling as well, for a long time. It's why the demon took a hundred and fifteen years to
exorcise, or didn't. ``Exorcise'' is the word the people who think it worked like to
use. John Earman and John Norton, the doubters from the last chapter, called their two-part
paper on it ``Exorcist XIV: The Wrath of Maxwell's Demon,'' and I read that Roman numeral as a
joke about how many times the demon has been declared gone. So hold the word loosely. This
section is me finding out where the feeling goes wrong, and where it's right. I'll give the answer
up front. Looking can have a physical cost; its value needs a model of the measurement. But it doesn't have to
merge anything, so it owes no floor, and a ledger that charges merges can charge it nothing. What
it does use up is a blank page to write on. Learning borrows that page. Wiping the page to use
it again is a merge, and that's where the floor gets paid. Committing, making a record nobody can
hand back, is paying for good. I'm going to tell you the version where the exorcism worked,
Charles Bennett's,
because it's the version that says where the heat goes, and the third way out in the last chapter, the one Landauer's premise is there to close, stays open behind it.

\subsection{Bennett moves where the heat is paid}

In 1982 Charles Bennett, who'd already shown in 1973 that computation can be done without
forgetting if it keeps its whole history and pays by taking states it has never used instead, took the demon apart one step at a time. The being looks at a molecule and writes
down which side it's on. Is writing that down a merge? Picture the being's notepad, which
starts blank. After looking, the notepad says ``left'' or ``right.'' There are two possible worlds before
the look (molecule left, pad blank; molecule right, pad blank) and two possible worlds after it (left,
``left''; right, ``right''), so nothing merged: two went in, two came out, and you can read the before off the
after. Copying what you see onto a blank page forgets nothing, and a step that forgets nothing
owes no floor under Landauer's premise. Any finite-time physical cost additionally depends on the chosen dynamics and protocol. But it did use
something up: the blank page. Before the look, the pad was blank and
ready; after it, the pad is full. Brillouin had priced one particular way of looking (bouncing
light) and took it as the price of getting information at all. Bennett gave a way of looking
that, on his account, doesn't pay that price. It borrows a page instead.

So where is the heat floor? The being has one notepad and a lot of molecules. After the first
molecule the page is full, and to do the next one it has to wipe the page. \emph{Wiping} takes two
possible worlds (pad says ``left''; pad says ``right'') to one (pad blank), and that's the merge,
the step with no way back. For a complete reusable engine under the stated thermal assumptions, the
memory reset and the feedback process must be accounted for together. The
cycle cannot turn information about the molecule into net work from a single
bath while restoring every other resource for free. It's the rule from his 2003 notes that I quoted in Section~\ref{sec:toll}: erasing
and merging carry the unavoidable charge, and copying onto a blank place to write doesn't. The
look borrows the page. Resetting an uncertain page without using its
correlation with the molecule has the corresponding entropy-loss floor under
the thermal assumptions. While the molecule is still available, the joint
operation can instead undo the copy; the four-state example below does that.
A blank supplied at the start is an initial condition. To charge its
preparation, specify what uncertain state was reset and how.

Section~\ref{sec:toll} separated making a record from resetting it. Now you can see
exactly which step pays, and why the other one was tempting, because looking \emph{feels} like the active part,
the thing the being does, while wiping feels like housekeeping.
In that reset protocol, the housekeeping is where the entropy-loss floor applies. If there's one sentence in this section I'd want you to carry out of it, it's that one, and the idea in it is Bennett's.

\subsection{Two different things called ``narrowing''}

Here is what I had to get straight in my own head before any of this made sense, and I'll give
it to you as a picture because that's how I eventually got it.

Draw the machine's possible states as a row of dots. Now draw a second row above it: the
dots that \emph{you}, standing outside, still think it might be in. Those are two different rows:
the first is a fact about the machine, and the second is a fact about you, about what you've
seen and what you've ruled out. Both rows can shrink, but they shrink for different reasons, and
only one of them costs.

The machine's row shrinks when two of its states land on the same state, which is a merge, and
a merge is what the price charges. Under the halving rule from Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, a run can't shrink the
machine's own row by more halvings than it paid for. That's the theorem just below, and
it's that section's halving price run forward along a whole program, where that section took it one step at a time. There is no new idea in it,
only the same counting of states.

To state it exactly, write $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ for the index-bit count of $n$: the smallest whole number
$k$ with $2^k \ge n$, the fewest yes-or-no questions that can guarantee identification among $n$ things
when arbitrary binary splits are allowed. It is $0$ at $n = 1$, and $0$ at $n = 0$ too, since $2^0 \ge 0$; the definition covers empty lists, where the logarithm of zero isn't a number. Wherever I write an ordinary logarithm without the rounding, its argument
is positive. For a run $t$ and a list $D$ of
starting states, let $\mathrm{img}_t(D)$ be the set of states the run can end in, starting
from somewhere in $D$, and write $|\mathrm{img}_t(D)|$ for how many there are (in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} the
symbol for one move already meant the count; here I need the set and its size both). Let
$\mathrm{cost}(t)$ be the run's total cost.

\begin{theorem}[The machine's own narrowing is priced]\label{thm:machine-narrowing}
If the cost satisfies the halving price (Premise~\ref{prem:halving}), then for every run $t$
and every list $D$ of starting states with no repeats,
\[
|D| \;\le\; 2^{\mathrm{cost}(t)} \cdot |\mathrm{img}_t(D)|, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \lceil \log_2 |D| \rceil \;\le\; \mathrm{cost}(t) + \lceil \log_2 |\mathrm{img}_t(D)| \rceil. \] \end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
After each move, gather the states still possible and count each different state once.
If the first move costs $c_1$, the halving rule says the original count is at most
$2^{c_1}$ times this new count. If the next move costs $c_2$, the new count is at most
$2^{c_2}$ times the count after that. Put the inequalities together: the original
count is at most $2^{c_1}2^{c_2}$ times the count after two moves.

Carry on to the end. The factors multiply, their exponents add, and the added prices
are exactly $\mathrm{cost}(t)$. The last collection is $\mathrm{img}_t(D)$, giving
the first inequality. An empty run contributes no factor and leaves the collection
unchanged, so it fits too.

For the rounded count, let $k$ bits suffice to number all the endpoints.
There are then at most $2^k$ endpoints, and the first inequality gives at most
$2^{\mathrm{cost}(t)+k}$ starts. That many bits therefore suffice for the starts.
This also covers an empty starting collection, whose stipulated index-bit count
is zero, without taking a logarithm of zero.

Rounding throws some information away. Four starts and three endpoints both need
two index bits, so the rounded comparison alone permits zero cost. The unrounded
comparison still sees that four is more than three and forces a positive charge.
\end{proof}

The run itself is the witness;
nothing else is handed in. That will matter in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}, and I'll say why at the end of this
section.

Your row shrinks when you see something that some of your candidates couldn't have shown you,
and you cross those candidates off. Nothing happened to the machine. It didn't merge anything; it
didn't know you were watching; it would have done the same thing with nobody there. The
physicist Edwin Jaynes had a name for mixing these up, and I think it's one of the most useful
names in all of science: the mind projection fallacy, treating what you know about a thing as
if it were a property of the thing. Your list of candidates is in your head, and the machine's
row is in the machine. The halving price is about the machine's row, and crossing a candidate
off yours doesn't move it.

And here I have to be fair to Jaynes, because he'd argue with where I just took his phrase. In
a 1965 paper on Gibbs's and Boltzmann's entropies he wrote that entropy is ``an anthropomorphic
concept'' (a phrase he credited to the physicist Eugene Wigner), and by that he meant a property
of the particular experiments you or I choose to do on a physical system. On his account the
system alone doesn't carry it. So for Jaynes the second law is
about what's known too, and the line I'd have liked to draw, that the second law has opinions
about the machine and none about you, is exactly the line he'd refuse. Who's right is one of
the oldest fights in statistical physics, Jaynes's reading against Boltzmann's, and I can't
settle it and don't have to. The spreads in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s entropy
theorems are spreads over the states the device might be in when the step runs, and every
theorem there holds whether you read those chances as ignorance or as physics; ``the floor
comes from what you didn't know'' is the same sentence in either reading, with ``you'' being
whoever built the spread. What I need from the fallacy is only this: the two
rows are different rows, and only one of them is the machine's.

\subsection{The demon on a sheet of paper}

Build it, because the whole claim is four dots and two arrows and you should see it merge or
not merge with your own eyes.

The machine has a hidden bit (think of it as the molecule's side) and a display (the
notepad). It has four states, written as pairs, hidden bit then display: 00, 01, 10, 11. It has two moves.

MEASURE copies the hidden bit onto the display, by adding it in the way that a light switch
adds: if the hidden bit is 1, flip the display; if it's 0, leave it. Draw the arrows: 00 goes
to 00, 01 goes to 01, 10 goes to 11, and 11 goes to 10. Look at the arrowheads: every state has
exactly one arrow landing on it, so nothing merged and MEASURE forgets nothing. Look at the two
states where the display starts blank: 00 goes to 00 and 10 goes to 11, which is the copy onto a blank page, (hidden, blank) to (hidden, hidden), and it's the use that matters here. And the light switch isn't one way of copying among several. A MEASURE that merges nothing, copies onto a blank display and leaves the hidden bit where it was has nowhere else to send 01 and 11: each has one landing left on its own side.

WIPE sets the display to 0 whatever it held. 00 goes to 00; 01 goes to 00 as well. 10 goes to
10; 11 goes to 10 as well. Two arrows land on 00 and two on 10, which is a merge, twice over.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}ccc@{}}
Hidden bit, display before & After MEASURE & After WIPE \\ \hline
00 & 00 & 00 \\
01 & 01 & 00 \\
10 & 11 & 10 \\
11 & 10 & 10 \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Now follow only the prepared cases: $00,10$ become $00,11$ after the
copy. WIPE sends those two to $00,10$, still two different full states.
The hidden bit retains the distinction. The instruction price nevertheless
charges WIPE because its rule merges other possible pairs, as the full
column shows. That worst-case charge is not a one-bit entropy loss on
this particular correlated preparation.
Under any price that charges per halving, WIPE costs at least one, while MEASURE is allowed to cost
zero. Zero on the price list isn't zero spent: a physical MEASURE can dissipate under its specified dynamics, and it uses up the blank display. What it doesn't do is merge, so it owes
no floor.

Now be the observer. You can see the display and not the hidden bit. What you're shown, the
display here, is what I'll call a \emph{window}: the part of the state an outside observer gets
to see. Section~\ref{sec:windows} is about windows in general; here the window is just the display. The display starts
blank, so your list of candidates is \{00, 10\}: two possibilities, one bit you don't know. The
machine runs MEASURE and you look at the display. If it shows 1, the only candidate that could
have produced it is 10, and if it shows 0, only 00, so your list went from two to one and you learned
the hidden bit. The machine's price for that move, on a list that charges merges, is zero, and
what it spent was the blank display. Its own row of possible states went
from \{00, 10\} to \{00, 11\}, still two; nothing it could have been got merged with anything
else. You narrowed and it didn't. That's the measuring half of Bennett's argument on four dots,
and WIPE's charge is the wiping half. So the demon just broke something: one bit gained, nothing
charged. The thing it broke, written out so you can see exactly where the
crack runs, is this: for every list of starting candidates, every run, and every actual start in the
list, the index bits the observer gains (log2 of the candidates before minus log2
of the candidates after, both rounded up) are at most what the run was charged. On four dots that
sentence is false.

\begin{definition}[What an observer knows]\label{def:knowledge}
Fix a window $w$ from states to what can be seen. Given a list $\Omega$ of candidate starting
states, a run $t$, and the actual start $s_0 \in \Omega$, the observer's \emph{knowledge}
$K(\Omega, t, s_0)$ is the list of candidates $s \in \Omega$ whose run shows the same thing
through the window at every step as the actual run does.
\end{definition}

If that definition looks familiar, it should. It's the standard way logicians of knowledge set
it up: what you know is whatever holds of every case you can't tell apart from the actual one,
given everything you've seen (Fagin, Halpern, Moses and Vardi's \emph{Reasoning About
Knowledge}, 1995, builds a whole subject on it, runs and observations included). And it's the
logically omniscient kind, the kind where knowing some facts means
knowing everything that follows from them, at no extra cost (Section~\ref{sec:established} comes
back to that flaw). I'm using it on purpose, flaw and
all. This section is about learning, and learning in that sense is exactly the thing that
doesn't have to merge. Settling, making a result stay so it can't be handed back, is the separate
act with a price, and nothing in this definition settles anything.

\begin{theorem}[An observer can learn with no merge]\label{thm:observer-free}
There is a four-state machine (the demon), a window (the display), a cost satisfying the halving price, a run of cost
0, and candidates with $|\Omega| = 2$, for which $|K(\Omega, t, s_0)| = 1$. So the claim
``for every $\Omega$ with no repeats, every $t$, and every $s_0$ in $\Omega$: $\lceil\log_2|\Omega|\rceil - \lceil\log_2|K(\Omega,t,s_0)|
\rceil \le \mathrm{cost}(t)$'' is false for that machine and that cost. In the same machine,
every cost satisfying the halving price charges WIPE at least one.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The machine and run are the four dots above: MEASURE is a bijection, so cost 0 satisfies
the halving price; the observer's two candidates show different displays after MEASURE; WIPE
sends two pairs of states to one each, so the halving price needs its cost $\ge 1$.
\end{proof}

The demon is the picture, and the smallest case is smaller than it. The claim as written already fails on
a machine with two states that the window tells apart and every move priced at zero, because the
observer's very first look tells the two apart, and it never fails on a machine with one state. That's why the interesting version is
learning \emph{after} the first look, which is where the three states of
Theorem~\ref{thm:three-states} come in. And WIPE's price needs less than the halving rule: merge pricing
alone charges it at least one.

There is one thing to be exact about. The halving rule is a floor: it says merges cost at least this
much, and it doesn't say anything costs zero. So the theorem exhibits \emph{one} price schedule
that meets the halving rule and charges MEASURE nothing. A different schedule could meet the rule
and still charge MEASURE; nothing in counting forbids overcharging. The claim is that learning
is not \emph{forced} to cost a unit. That's what ``borrows'' in the section's title means: the
look takes a page and pays nothing, and the unit, like the floor, comes due at the wipe.

The physicists had this freedom on the books long before me. Paul Fahn (1996), doing the entropy
accounting of Szilard's one-molecule engine step by step, argued for a symmetry between the measuring step and the erasing step: on his account,
which of the two you charge is partly a choice of bookkeeping, and the
total is what's fixed. Sagawa and Ueda (2009) derived a bound on that total, with the split
depending on the memory. So, on their accounts, ``a schedule could charge MEASURE instead'' is a known freedom in how the books are kept,
and I didn't find a loophole. The other reading is very
much alive too. Ruth Kastner (2025) argues that Brillouin was essentially right after all: once the
physics of a real measurement is put back in, it's measurement that pays and
foils the demon, erasure drops out of the dissipation, and Bennett's floorless copy fails as physics.
The theorem above is about price lists, so it stands either way. What hangs on her is whether a
real demon can look without a floor, which is the same question the next paragraph's doubter presses
on.

And the doubter from the last chapter cuts this side too, so I owe it to you, since I leaned
on him there. In 2013 John Norton argued for a no-go result: at the scale of molecules, thermal
jiggling keeps any process that's supposed to be thermodynamically reversible from ever
actually finishing, and finishing it takes more entropy than Landauer's amount. If he's right,
Bennett's measurement has a floor in practice after all, because it's one of those processes.
The theorem above survives that, because it's about price lists: a schedule that meets the
halving rule isn't forced to charge the copy, whatever a real device spends. What wouldn't
survive is the physics I've been hanging on it, that a real demon's look owes no floor, only the
dissipation of happening that going slowly shrinks. If Norton is right, the line between learning and committing keeps its counting and
loses its physics. I can't referee that one either.

\subsection{Who holds the pen changes who pays}

Now comes the part that I think is the most beautiful fact in here, and you find it by playing
with the four dots rather than by thinking about them. Run MEASURE \emph{twice}. The first copies the
hidden bit onto the display. The second adds the hidden bit in again, and adding a bit twice
with a light-switch add gets you back where you were: the display is blank again. Check the
arrows: 10 to 11 to 10. The display went full and then blank, and nothing merged, and the
price on the ledger was zero both times. So a display that was blank before the first
MEASURE \emph{can} be put back to blank with no merge and no floor, by a second MEASURE, though not
by WIPE. This is the borrowed page being handed back: while the original is still there to check
against, the copy can be un-copied. Each MEASURE still dissipates by happening, and going
slowly shrinks it.

What's the difference? MEASURE \emph{consults the hidden bit} when it clears the display. It knows
what's written there, because it has access to the thing it was copied from, and so it can undo the
copy. Nothing gets erased. WIPE doesn't look. It sets the display to 0 regardless,
and ``regardless'' is exactly the many-to-one. Bennett has the general form of this in the 2003
notes: he lists the ``erasure of one of two copies of data known to be identical'' among the
logically reversible operations, because you're removing a duplicate, and no information is
destroyed. And it goes further than Bennett in
work that came after him: the quantum physicist Lídia del Rio and colleagues argued in 2011
that the floor on erasing a system depends on how much the eraser already knows about it,
dropping to zero, and in the quantum case below zero. The heat of clearing a record falls on
whoever clears it, and its floor is lower the more they know. Try it with a red or blue card
under a cup and a note that is blank or marked.
Start with the note blank. Lift the cup: for red, toggle the note (blank to marked,
marked to blank); for blue, leave it alone. The note now reports the colour. Repeat
that same rule while the card is still available, and the note returns to blank.
Check all four card-and-note combinations: the rule undoes itself, so no two land
together. Erase the note regardless of the card instead, and for either card both
note values land on blank. That rule merges on the full set of combinations. On
the matched pairs you actually prepared, the card still has the information, so nothing is
lost there; the merge is in what the rule has to do to every combination it might be handed,
which is what a rule that doesn't look has to answer for. Cards and paper don't measure heat.
What they show is which information each rule gets to use.

\subsection{The smallest machine that teaches with no merge, and the one that can't}

There are two more small facts, and then the point. The demon measures what you learn by comparing the
start to the end, but an observer's very first look already rules things out before any step
runs, so the fairer question is: after that first look, can a \emph{step} teach you more, at
zero cost? Yes, and the demon still does it. And the smallest machine
that can is three states in a ring: U goes to V, V goes to W, W goes to U, and the window
shows ``true'' only at W. Start with candidates \{U, V\}; both show false. Take one step. From U
you now see false; from V you now see true. One step told them apart, and a ring forgets
nothing, so a zero price meets the halving rule and is the price chosen here.

Two states can't do it, ever, with any arrows, and this is the one that needs no price
premise at all. If a machine has only two states and you can't tell them apart at the first
look, then the window shows the same thing on both, and those two are \emph{all the states there
are}, so the window shows the same thing everywhere, forever, and you never learn anything.
Try to draw a counterexample. You'll draw the
same two dots a few times and give up, and the giving up is the proof. Three is the smallest
number of states on which two states that look alike at the first look can come apart at a
later look, and that's what teaching is.

\begin{theorem}[Three states are the minimum for teaching at zero cost]\label{thm:three-states}
Call a machine a \emph{zero-cost teacher} when it has a cost satisfying the halving price, a list of
candidates with no repeats containing the actual start, and a run of cost 0 after which the
observer knows strictly more than after the first look, $|K(\Omega, t, s_0)| <
|K(\Omega, [\,], s_0)|$. There is a zero-cost teacher with exactly three states, and there is
none with two or fewer.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Three: the ring $U \to V \to W \to U$ with the window true only at $W$, candidates
$\{U, V\}$, one step, cost 0 (a ring is a bijection, so cost 0 satisfies the halving price).
Two or fewer: the actual start is always in the observer's knowledge, so knowing strictly more
after the run needs at least two candidates still left after the first look, which agree there.
On a machine with two or fewer states those two are all
the states there are, so the window takes one value everywhere and no later look can
separate them. This half never uses the price at all.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection*{Finish together, for the first time}

Run the machine from $N$ different starts and photograph its full configuration at
every tick. Put the photographs in rows, one row per start, one column per tick.
Every run finishes for the first time at tick $T$. Through that finish, two different
states in the same column must have different successors.

The sheet has $N(T+1)$ photographs, including the starts and finishes. Could two of
them show the same full configuration? In the same column, cancel backwards and the
starts would have to agree. In different columns, give both configurations the same
remaining steps. One run would finish before its promised first finish. Every photograph
has to show a different configuration.

\begin{theorem}[Room for synchronized first completion]\label{thm:synchronized-room}
Let $F$ be a total rule, $A$ a set of $N$ distinct starts, and $H$ a completion reading.
For every $a\in A$, suppose $F^T(a)\in H$ and $F^t(a)\notin H$ for $t<T$.
Suppose $F$ is injective on $\{F^t(a):a\in A\}$ for each $t<T$.
Then all states $F^t(a)$, with $a\in A$ and $0\le t\le T$, are distinct.
Any carrier containing these runs therefore has at least $N(T+1)$ configurations.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First compare photographs in the same column. If two showed the same state,
look one column back. The rule keeps different sources in that column apart,
so their predecessors must already have been the same. Repeat until the first
column: the starts agree. Thus different starts cannot give the same photograph
at the same time.

Now compare different columns. Suppose run $a$ at time $i$ shows what run $b$
shows later, at time $j$, with $i<j\le T$. Run $b$ has $T-j$ ticks left before
its first finish. Starting from the identical state, run $a$ must follow those
same remaining steps and finish too. Its time would then be $i+(T-j)$, earlier
than $T$ because $i<j$. That contradicts the first-finish promise for run $a$.

No two places on the sheet can therefore show the same full configuration.
There are $N$ rows and $T+1$ columns, counting time zero, so the machine needs
at least $N(T+1)$ different configurations to hold the sheet.
\end{proof}

That is the room required by the whole sheet of possible runs. The photographs can come
from separate executions of one machine. What keeps different columns apart is the
common first finish: a cycle with no such finish can put the same state in several columns.
\footnote{The count is of full configurations, rather than simultaneously running
machines or newly allocated memory cells.}

\subsection{The certainty bound}

Now I can put the whole path from not knowing to knowing on one page, with what it costs.
 You don't know which state the machine started in. There are a few it
could have been, each with its chance; that's your uncertainty. Run the machine. Every one
of those possible starting states goes somewhere, and only two things can happen to a pair of them.
Either they land on one state, and the difference between them is gone from the machine: a
merge, and the halving price charges for it, at most one bit a unit. Or they land on two
states, and the difference is still in the machine, sitting in its state, kept as two states held apart.
There's no third thing a pair of possibilities can do. So the uncertainty about where it
started splits exactly in two: the part the merges destroyed, paid for in cost, and the part
the end state still holds, paid for by the states it keeps apart.

Now put an observer at the window. Whatever they see is fixed by where the machine
started, so whatever they learn is a fact about the start. And the same split holds for it:
what they learned is either still held in the machine's end state, or it's gone from the
machine and a merge paid for losing it. A run that costs nothing leaves every bit the
observer learned still held in the machine. This is the precise sense of ``learning
borrows'': the observer's copy is a copy, and the machine still holds the original. When
the machine lets go of the original, a merge happens, and the cost comes due.

Said exactly, then: take a spread $p$ over starting states and a run $t$, and write $q$ for the
spread of where the run ends. For an end state $z$ with $q(z) > 0$, the starts that end at
$z$ have chances $p(x)/q(z)$ between them; call that the spread of the start given $z$, and
average its entropy over the ends:
\[
H(\text{start} \mid \text{end}) \;=\; \sum_{z:\,q(z) > 0} q(z)\, H\bigl(\text{start given } z\bigr).
\]
This is how many bits you'd still be missing about the start if someone told you the end. Do
the same for anything $v$ that's fixed by the start, like the whole film of what the window
showed: $H(v \mid \text{end})$ is what you'd still be missing about $v$ once you knew the end.

\begin{theorem}[The certainty bound]\label{thm:certainty-bill}
On a finite deterministic machine with an entropy-priced cost (Definition~\ref{def:u04-entropy-priced}),
take any spread $p$ over starting states, any run $t$, and anything $v$ that the start fixes.
Then
(1) $H(p) = H(\text{start} \mid \text{end}) + H(q)$: the uncertainty about the start is the
