possibilities you started with, rounded up: that's log2 of 6, which is a bit under 3, rounded
to 3. Donald Knuth, a computer scientist at Stanford, gives this, in the volume on sorting of his
\emph{The Art of Computer Programming},
as the lower bound for all comparison sorting, and the shape of
the argument is just: a tree $f$ questions deep has at most $2^f$ leaves, so it can't tell
apart more than $2^f$ cases.

And then the obvious next question: is the floor always the price? Try five cards. There are 120
orders, log2 of 120 is a bit under 7, so you need at least seven questions, and seven is enough,
though not by the obvious method. Finding the way is a good evening with a deck of cards (Knuth
has it, under the name merge insertion, from the mathematicians Lester Ford and Selmer Johnson in
1959). Now take twelve
cards. They can be in 479,001,600 orders, log2 of that is about 28.8, so the count says at least
29. Ford and Johnson's method takes 30, and in 1965 Mark Wells, a mathematician at Los Alamos who
built a programming language for exactly this kind of combinatorial search, showed by a computer
search that nothing does better:
twelve cards need 30. The floor was 29 and the price is 30, so the count is a floor and only a floor;
it never promises the floor can be reached, and the bound later in this section has to be read
exactly the same way.

Ralph Hartley, an electronics researcher at Bell Labs, writing in the Bell
System Technical Journal in 1928, before
Shannon, measured information exactly this way: the logarithm
of the number of possibilities, no probabilities, just a count. I use that measure here, and
I'll say plainly it's Hartley's. Shannon's would need a distribution over the list,
and there isn't one; there's just the list's length.

The same count works with something you can hold. Put three coins under three cups. Each coin
is heads or tails, so there are eight possible rows under the cups. Someone hands you two
answers: heads under the first cup, tails under the second. Lift the first cup and compare, and a
matching answer leaves four possible rows. Lift the second and compare, and a match leaves two. The
last coin can still be either way. The list really shrank: eight, four, two. Nothing in that
count needed a claim about which way the last coin faces.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[thiele]
\node[pipe,text width=4.4cm,minimum width=0pt] (a)
  {Three coins under cups\\8 possible rows};
\node[pipe,text width=4.4cm,minimum width=0pt,below=1.3cm of a] (b)
  {First is heads\\4 possible rows};
\node[pipe,text width=4.4cm,minimum width=0pt,below=1.3cm of b] (c)
  {First heads, second tails\\2 possible rows};
\draw[pipearrow] (a.south) -- node[right=8pt,align=left]
  {Lift first cup:\\find heads.} (b.north);
\draw[pipearrow] (b.south) -- node[right=8pt,align=left]
  {Lift second cup:\\find tails.} (c.north);
\node[align=center,below=0.5cm of c]
  {The third coin could be either:\\heads or tails.};
\end{tikzpicture}

\small These observations halve the candidate list. A price on those
observations is a separate rule; the shrinking list alone supplies none.
\end{center}

This is a parlour game, and an old one. In \emph{A Christmas Carol}, in 1843, Scrooge's nephew
Fred plays a game called Yes and No at his Christmas party: he thinks of something, and
everybody else asks questions he may only answer yes or no. He's thinking of an animal, a
disagreeable, savage one that growls and grunts and lives in London, and the answer is Uncle
Scrooge. Most people know the game as twenty questions, and twenty is a good number for it:
a balanced question splits the remaining field in half, and twenty such questions can
guarantee identification among $2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$ possibilities. A lucky answer to
``is it this one?'' can finish immediately; the count is about handling every possible answer. Push on that, though. The halving only
happens because Fred answers truthfully about what's actually in his head. Lie once and the
count still shrinks; it shrinks around the wrong animal. The cups showed the same thing: the four and
the two are real because you lifted the cup and compared. Being told what was under it wouldn't
have made them real.

Now put it on a run. Say a run comes with a list of states that are ``still on the table,''
the candidates, and a shorter list, with some ruled out. Call the first the prior and the
second the posterior, and I want you to hear those as \emph{a list you could print}. They aren't
``the space of possible worlds.'' Picture the ruling-out as observations, each observation that
ruled something out being one branch point in a tree like the card tree. The bound says that if that tree is no
deeper than the number of paid steps the run took, and the tree has enough leaves to cover
the narrowing in a way I'll spell out in a moment, then the counter rose by at least log2 of
the prior's length, rounded up, minus log2 of the posterior's length, rounded up. Put another way,
the counter rose by at least one unit for each of the \emph{index
bits} the list lost, where the index bits of a list are the yes/no questions it takes to point
at one entry of it, the card count again.

``Paid step'' needs its own sentence. It means a step the price list charges at least one for.
In a Thiele machine the toll guarantees that every crossing of the reading is one; a
price list may put a floor under more steps than that (a look, a send, a check), and
the count takes every paid step there is. The tree is a bare shape, branches and leaves with
nothing written on them, and ``no deeper than the number of paid steps'' is a count along the
run that happened, not a walk down the tree. A paid step doesn't have to have asked any
question at all.

Notice, too, what the bound does and doesn't say about the run. It takes the two lists, the
tree and the covering as given. It doesn't say the run produced the posterior from the prior;
nothing in it reads the lists off the run. What it says is that, given lists, a tree and a
covering that someone supplies, the paid steps of the run cover the rounded drop in list
length. Here Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}'s warning comes due: watching can narrow without costing anything, so the payment can't be
dug out of the narrowing. It goes in as a premise, the tree's depth against the paid steps,
and I'll keep calling it one. There is a version where the run makes the posterior itself, from
a prior and the tests it passed, and there the premise is a share each test keeps.

\subsection{What ``narrower'' buys: a stronger test}

Before the count, one link that's pure logic, and Plato's third account is the whole of it.
Take a list of candidates and an observation, a function that says what each candidate looks
like from outside. The list's \emph{membership test} accepts an observation when some candidate on
the list shows it. Shrink the list, and the test can only get pickier: anything the short
list's test accepts, the long list's accepts too. The word for that, and it runs backward
from English, is \emph{stronger}: the stronger test is the one that lets \emph{fewer} things through.

Pickier, though, isn't the same as strictly pickier, and the cards show the gap. Take all six
orders as the prior, and as the posterior the three where card 1 sits left of card 2:
1-2-3, 1-3-2 and 3-1-2. First observation: ``is 1 left of 2?'' Every survivor says yes, and
the removed 2-1-3 says no, so the prior's test accepts yes and no, the posterior's only yes,
and the posterior's test is strictly stronger. Second observation, same two lists: ``is the first card a 3?'' Now 3-1-2
says yes and the other two survivors say no, and among the removed orders 3-2-1 says yes and
2-1-3 says no. Both tests accept yes and no, so they have the same strength, even though three orders are gone.
What made the difference is a removed candidate whose observation \emph{no survivor shares}. Such a candidate is
Plato's mark, the thing that sets this case apart from everything it could be confused with,
turned into a function. Narrow the list and keep one distinguishing removed candidate, and
the test is strictly stronger; narrow it without one, and the test may not have moved at all.

\subsection{What you've got}

A paid flag is not a true claim; Section~\ref{sec:windows} left it at ``a paid flag is a paid flag,'' and Section~\ref{sec:insight} will say
it flatly. What a paid flag with an object and a checked relation behind it gives you is
\emph{entitlement}: anyone auditing the run may treat the claim as established, and can point at
the event where that became legitimate. (Nothing in the five parts makes the system itself
read the flag; I said that above and I'm saying it again because it's the sentence most likely
to get lost.) Entitlement costs at least the index bits of narrowing it commits to, given
lists, a tree and a covering somebody supplies, and given a run that paid for the tree's
depth. The cups say why entitlement and truth are different. Plato says what the checked
relation has to do, which is to distinguish. Necula says how to build it. Hartley says what to count.

Put the three pieces on one hypothesis list (narrow the list with a test that separates, find
the paid event, count the charges against a tree the run paid for) and you get a single statement, structural entitlement, once
over any Thiele machine and once more on the small machine of Part~III, where the run
starts clean and the paid steps are its own record moves, CHECK,
COMMIT and CERTIFY, at a cost of exactly one each. The first one reads
as follows.

\begin{theorem}[Structural entitlement, over any Thiele machine]\label{thm:ent-cs}
Take a Thiele machine (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}), a state $s$ that reads no, and a run
$t$ from $s$ that ends in a state that reads yes. Take a type of candidates, a type of
observations with an exact equality test, an observation $\mathrm{obs}$ of each candidate, and a
\emph{decoder} $d$ that turns a run into an observation (what its record shows). Take lists
$\Omega$ and $\Omega'$ of candidates and a decision tree $T$ such that:
(H1) $\Omega'$ strictly narrows $\Omega$: every member of $\Omega'$ is in $\Omega$, and some member of
$\Omega$ isn't in $\Omega'$;
(H2) some dropped candidate $w$, in $\Omega$ and not in $\Omega'$, shows an observation different
from every survivor's;
(H3) the decoded run $d(t)$ is shown by some survivor;
(H4) $|\Omega'| > 0$ and $|\Omega| \le L(T) \cdot |\Omega'|$;
(H5) at least $\mathrm{depth}(T)$ steps of the run are charged at least one each.
Then (1) the membership test of $\Omega'$ is strictly stronger than the membership test of
$\Omega$; (2) some step of the run took the reading from no to yes, and that step was charged at
least one; and (3) the sum of the charges of the run's steps is at least
$\lceil \log_2 |\Omega| \rceil \mathbin{\dot{-}} \lceil \log_2 |\Omega'| \rceil$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) is the cards' argument: the dropped $w$ shows something no survivor shows, so the posterior
test says no where the prior test says yes, and every survivor was in the prior, so nothing the
posterior accepts is refused by the prior. (2) The run starts at no and ends at yes, so at some
step the reading goes from no to yes, and the toll charges that step at least one. (3) is a
count: the covering puts every survivor at a leaf of $T$, a tree of depth $\mathrm{depth}(T)$
has at most $2^{\mathrm{depth}(T)}$ leaves, so the index bits are at most $\mathrm{depth}(T)$, and the
sum of the charges is at least the number of steps charged at least one. On a system that obeys
conservation the sum of the charges is the counter's rise.
\end{proof}

With the counter's rise in place of the sum of the charges it's the same count, so for a
system that obeys conservation it's the special case. Three things in the hypotheses
feed nothing, and I'm naming them here so you don't have to find them: (H3) isn't used
by any of the three
conclusions; from (H1) only the inclusion is used, and the gap goes unused; and in (H2)
the words ``not in $\Omega'$'' go unused, since a candidate whose observation differs from every survivor's can't be a survivor itself. And (H4)'s $|\Omega'| > 0$ is used in that proof but can be dropped too: the covering forces it once the prior has a member.

A statement like that is true by packaging: it takes the hypotheses in and hands the
conclusions back, and the right word for it is a checklist, a checklist for leaning on a claim.
It discovers nothing about leaning.

And a checklist isn't nothing. On 30 October 1935, at Wright Field, northeast of Dayton, Ohio,
the Army was evaluating Boeing's new four-engine bomber, the Model 299. Shortly after take-off it
plunged back onto the field and caught fire; that's how the wire report of that day has it, and the
later histories add that it pitched up and stalled first, which is what elevators locked in a raised position
would do. Two men died of their injuries, the Army's pilot, Major Ployer Hill, and
Boeing's chief test pilot, Leslie Tower. The airplane was fine. The crew had left the gust locks
on, a locking mechanism worked from inside the cockpit that holds the control surfaces still while
the plane sits on the ground. There's a
famous line that a newspaper called it too much airplane for one man to fly. I couldn't find that
line in any paper from 1935; the earliest place I could find it is a New Yorker article from December 2007 by Atul Gawande, a
surgeon who writes about how people get complicated work right, and he names no newspaper, so take
it as a lead. What I can find is what came after. The answer was a card: a list of
things to check, in order, every time, and the crews of the airplane worked through written
checklists for each phase of flight. The most careful history of it I found is by Walter Boyne, a
retired Air Force colonel and a former director of the National Air and Space Museum. By his
account it wasn't the first written routine for a pilot; those go back
before the First World War. And it's this crash, he says, that made the checklist the way a crew flew. The airplane went
on to be the B-17. Nothing on that card was a discovery. Every item on it was something the pilots
already knew. What the card did was make sure none of it got left out when it mattered. Putting
entitlement's hypotheses on one list does the same: it finds nothing new about leaning on a
claim, and it makes the hypotheses impossible to drop quietly.

\subsection{A grouping, checked and committed}

Section~\ref{sec:structure} ended on buckets, and the toll of Part~I never needed them: it prices any yes-or-no
reading. In this subsection the word in this section's title gets attached to a partition in a
theorem. Take a pile, a finite list of items, and a \emph{grouping}, a bucket label for each item.
Its partition is ``same label,'' and the classes of that relation are a partition in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:equiv-partition}. The data is a \emph{key} for each item, drawn from any type with at least two values (a grouping's own labels can serve as a key), and a grouping is
\emph{sound} for a key when any two items it puts in one bucket have the same key. The grouping
says ``these belong together,'' and the key says whether they do. One grouping \emph{refines}
another when every bucket of the first sits inside a bucket of the second.

Put two red buttons and two blue buttons on the table, numbered 1 through 4,
with 1 and 2 red. Let the key be colour. Circles round $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$
give a sound grouping: every pair inside a circle has the same colour. Split the
red circle into two singletons and it stays sound; splitting cannot introduce a
mismatched pair. Join 1 and 3 instead and it fails. Changing the circles' names
from A and B to North and South changes none of these checks. That is why the
reading below uses the partition, not the spelling of its labels.

Now comes the rule for the record. Put a tick beside a grouping only after comparing the
colours within each circle. Copy that ticked grouping onto a separate commitment
card, then place the card in a record envelope; charge one tally for each of those
three acts. Change a button's colour between the check and the copy, and the old
tick must no longer authorize the copy. The machine's SET rule below does that by
clearing the current table and channel. A record already kept remains about the
old colours, which it keeps with the grouping.

Here is one example machine that meets the model, the smallest I know that makes a record from a checked claim. It is an illustration; the theorem above holds of any Thiele machine. The \emph{bucket machine} holds a key, a table of checked groupings, a channel, a record, a trap
latch and a ledger. SET costs nothing; it replaces the key and throws away the table and the channel,
which were checked against the old key. CHECK $g$ costs one and passes when $g$ is sound for the
current key, and, when it passes, writes $g$ in the table. COMMIT $g$ costs one and passes when the table holds a
grouping with the same partition as $g$, and puts $g$ in the channel. CERTIFY costs one and passes
when the channel holds a grouping; if the record is still down it then keeps that grouping with the
current key, the key a grouping with its partition was checked against, and a record already kept
is left as it is. A CHECK, COMMIT or CERTIFY that fails traps, and a trapped machine only pays. The
\emph{reading for a grouping $g$} is: the record holds a grouping with $g$'s partition. In words, that reading says ``this grouping has been checked and committed.''

\begin{theorem}[A committed grouping entitles exactly its refinements]\label{thm:partition-reading}
(1) The classes of ``same label'' under any grouping form a partition. (2) Two groupings with the
same partition of the pile have the same reading at every state of the bucket machine. (3) For
groupings $g$ and $h$ of the pile, soundness of $g$ for a key gives soundness of $h$ for that key,
for every key, exactly when $h$ refines $g$. (4) On every run from a clean state (table and channel empty, record down), if the reading for $g$ is up, the record holds a grouping and a key
for which $g$ is sound, and so is every grouping that refines $g$; and for every grouping $h$ that
doesn't refine $g$ there is a key for which $g$ is sound and $h$ isn't. (5) The bucket machine
obeys the toll, and a run from a clean state that ends with the record up has raised the ledger
by at least three.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Every item has its own label, exchanging two items does not change whether
their labels agree, and two agreements through a third label give agreement
with each other. Thus ``same label'' has the three sameness rules, and its
classes form the partition already constructed in Theorem~\ref{thm:equiv-partition}.

(2) The reading asks which items were put together, not what the buckets were
called. Replacing one grouping by another with exactly the same buckets
therefore changes no answer to that reading.

(3) If $h$ only cuts $g$'s buckets smaller, every pair $h$ keeps together was
already together under $g$. Soundness of $g$ gives that pair equal keys,
so $h$ is sound too. If $h$ does anything else, it puts some two items together
that $g$ kept in separate buckets. Give every item in the first item's
$g$-bucket one key value and every other item a second key value. Each
$g$-bucket has a single key, so $g$ is sound. The chosen $h$-bucket contains
both key values, so $h$ is not. This is why the key type needs two values.

(4) Follow the table, channel and record through the commands. They begin
empty. CHECK inserts only a grouping it has found sound for the current key.
COMMIT takes the partition of a grouping already in that table, so the
selected grouping is sound for the same key. CERTIFY keeps that grouping
and that key together; later commands do not replace an existing record.
SET changes the key but empties both the table and the channel, so no old
unchecked carry-over remains there. A failed command traps instead of
inserting an unsound grouping, and trapped commands leave those fields alone.
These are all the ways those fields change. Their promised soundness
therefore survives every command of any run from the clean start.
Apply (3) to the grouping and key in the record: every refinement is sound,
and every non-refinement has the counterexample key just constructed.

(5) Only CERTIFY raises the record, and its price is one, giving the toll.
A successful CERTIFY needs a grouping in the channel. From an empty channel
only a successful COMMIT could have supplied it. From an empty table that
COMMIT in turn needs a successful CHECK. These are three distinct earlier
acts in order, each charged one. The run's nonnegative bill is at least three.
\end{proof}

So ``structural'' has a theorem under it. The reading sees a grouping only through its partition,
which is item (2). If the recorded circles are sound, so is any way of cutting them smaller, whatever the key
is. A grouping that isn't a cutting-smaller can still happen to be sound for this key (paint all
four buttons red and every grouping is sound), but nothing in the record promises it: for some
key it fails. Item (3) and item (4) say exactly that much, and that's all the record buys. It's
the three parts of entitlement from the start of this section in their smallest case: the object
is the grouping, the checked relation is soundness for the key, and the paid event is the CERTIFY,
on top of a CHECK and a COMMIT at a cost of one each. What it doesn't do is make a later move act on the record. The only move that reads it is CERTIFY, and only to leave a kept grouping alone. Like everything in this section, it says what someone auditing the run may conclude.

Before the machine of Part III, I owe you the word the toll is named after, the ``insight'' in ``No Free
Insight'' (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}), because I've been using it as if it meant one thing.

%===========================================================================
\section{What insight is}
\label{sec:insight}
%===========================================================================

I named the rule in this book ``No Free Insight,'' and the name ran ahead of any careful account
of what insight is. The book has been narrowing it ever since: not learning (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}), not
looking, not copying. Part~I already says where to look: learning borrows and committing pays, so the part of insight
a toll can price is the part that stays. It's time to say what that is, and to say it in a way that someone who
studies actual insight, in actual heads, wouldn't laugh at. So who are those people, and what
did they find? I'll go through what I ran into and push on each piece as I go. Where a story reached me
secondhand, I treat it as a lead to check.

\subsection{Sultan and the sticks}

In 1913 the psychologist Wolfgang Köhler went to Tenerife to run a research station with a
colony of chimpanzees, and the First World War then kept him there until 1920, five years longer
than planned, with the chimpanzees to watch.
The famous one is Sultan. Food is outside the cage, out of reach; two sticks are inside, each
too short, but one fits into the end of the other. Sultan tries each stick, fails, sulks,
plays with the sticks, and then, by Köhler's account, at a moment you can see, joins them and
reaches the food. Köhler's words were \emph{Einsicht} and \emph{einsichtig}, which came into English as ``insight,'' and
the whole school of psychology he belonged to, the Gestalt school, said that's what thinking
is: a \emph{restructuring}, the moment two sticks stop
being two sticks and become one tool. Stacking up tries until one works was, for them, something
else. Karl Duncker gave the human version, in German in 1935
and in English in 1945, five years after he died at thirty-seven; he'd spent his last years
working with Köhler at Swarthmore. You can set it up yourself: a candle, a box of tacks, matches,
and the task of fixing the
candle to the wall. The obstacle is seeing the \emph{box} as a possible shelf while it is presented as the container for the tacks. And then he found that if you hand people the box \emph{empty}, with the tacks poured out beside it, they
solve it far more readily. The objects were the same; what changed was which relation among them was on the table.

I like both of these for the same reason: the insight didn't add an object. Sultan had both
sticks the whole time. The box was there the whole time. What arrived was a \emph{relation}, which
is to say a piece of structure in Section~\ref{sec:structure}'s sense, and the arrival was sudden. Hold that, because the thing the toll prices also arrives in one step, and at its
best it's also a relation.

\subsection{It isn't a feeling}

A feeling of getting closer is a different thing to measure from solving the problem. Janet Metcalfe's experiments help separate them. In the 1980s the psychologist Janet Metcalfe asked people to solve
problems while rating, every fifteen seconds, how ``warm'' they felt, how close to the answer.
On ordinary problems, algebra for instance, the warmth climbs steadily and peaks at the
answer, which is what you'd expect. On \emph{insight} problems, riddles of the candle-box kind, the
warmth stays flat, flat, flat, and then the answer arrives, and if anything the people who
felt warmest beforehand were \emph{more} likely to be wrong. She put that last finding in the
title of a 1986 paper: premonitions of insight predict impending error. Those results concern the predictive value of warmth ratings in those tasks. They do not show that a solution has no accompanying feeling, or that every person follows the same curve. Try it yourself: write a number from one to seven every fifteen seconds
while doing a long sum, then while doing a riddle, and compare the curves.

And the most famous insight story there is fits Metcalfe uncomfortably well. Archimedes, a mathematician who died in 212 BC, asked by Hiero, the king of
Syracuse,
whether a goldsmith had cheated him on a crown, gets into a bath, sees the water rise, and
runs home naked shouting ``eureka,'' I've found it. That comes from Vitruvius, a Roman writer
on architecture, writing about two centuries later. Is it true? Galileo Galilei, then a young Italian mathematician, at twenty-two,
in 1586, took it as known that Archimedes caught the goldsmith. What he didn't buy was the method.
Water spilling over the side, as Vitruvius tells it, was to him ``a crude thing, far from
scientific precision,'' and he guessed some writer had set down a rumour. So he wrote a little
tract, \emph{La Bilancetta}, proposing a balance weighed in air and in water instead, which he
thought was probably what Archimedes actually did, since it rests on Archimedes's own results.
Whether there was ever a bath, or a shout, nobody can check now. What survives is a story two
centuries late, wrapped around a real man and probably a real problem. Notice what the legend kept:
the bath, the shout, the running home naked, which is to say the feeling. What it left shaky is the part that
would count as the check, the test that could have caught the goldsmith. The bit everybody
remembers is the bit that tells you least.

So any account of insight that keys on the sensation, the ``aha,'' is keyed to something that
the data says is unreliable. Whatever insight is, it isn't the feeling of having it. That's a
relief, because a system of states and moves doesn't have feelings, and a word that only
meant a feeling would be cheating if I hung it on one. The version this book can price has to be keyed to an \emph{event}, and the
question is which.

\subsection{What happens when a computation learns}

I'll lay out the split first, then say what the toll does with each part, and then say who
decided the split. Keep Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s sheet of paper in front of you: the NO box,
the YES box, the tally line, and the three moves STAY, WORK and VOUCH.

The first thing: \emph{raw observation}. Something comes in and gets written down. A counter
ticks. Nothing is claimed about what it means, nothing is marked as resting on it, and the
reading doesn't move because of it. Later moves can read what it wrote, but that reading is a
move of its own. The demon's pad in Section~\ref{sec:narrowing} was raw observation, and raw observation is what the statistician Dennis Lindley
measured in 1956 as the information provided by an experiment, the words of his title, and
defined as the expected drop in your uncertainty: a real quantity,
and a quantity about what was \emph{seen}. It can cost nothing on the ledger. The toll says nothing at all about a
move that doesn't cross from NO to YES, so a price list may charge it zero: on the paper,
STAY and WORK cost nothing, and Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}'s watcher narrowed a whole row of candidates without paying
anything. ``Can'' is the word that matters. A price list is allowed to charge for looking anyway. And in
the physical world a look takes something too: copied onto a blank page it merges nothing and owes
no floor under Landauer's premise, but it can dissipate under the stated thermal-model assumptions,
and it uses up the page, which means taking states the machine hasn't used, borrowed until the
page is wiped (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}).

Lindley's measure has a back story, and it runs through Bletchley Park. I. J. Good, who was Alan Turing's main
statistical assistant at Bletchley Park in 1941, wrote in 1979 that Turing had worked out the
expected weight of evidence an experiment would give, to judge one of the codebreaking
procedures before running it, and so partly anticipated Lindley by about fifteen years, in work
that stayed secret. Turing measured evidence in \emph{bans}, logarithms to base ten, with a tenth
of one called a deciban, and the name came from the town of Banbury, where tens of thousands of
the sheets used in that procedure were printed. It's the same base-ten unit other people call the
hartley, after the Hartley from the last section. And Good adds that Turing didn't know the
logarithm he was using had already appeared in 1878, in a paper by Charles Sanders Peirce, the
same Peirce from Section~\ref{sec:structure}, who'd called it the weight of evidence. Peirce is as far
back as Good takes it. It changes nothing in the argument, but it shows how well trodden this
first kind of thing is. For a century and a half careful people have measured what an
observation tells you, and every one of those measures is about what was seen. The toll leaves
that side of the line alone.

The second thing: \emph{the raise}. Some move turns the reading from NO to YES, and that move
is where the toll applies. In any system with the five parts that obeys the toll, that move costs
at least one, and every run that starts at NO and ends at YES pays at least one somewhere
along the way, which is Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s universal floor. What's being charged for, at its best, is
exactly the Gestalt thing, a relation committed to: one tool, claimed, out of two sticks. I say ``at
its best'' because Section~\ref{sec:toll} was careful about what YES means: the flag is up, and nothing more. A
crossing that writes down which relation it's committing to carries Sultan's tool with it. A
bare crossing, VOUCH on the paper, commits to no relation at all, and it pays exactly the
same.

The third thing isn't a kind of event. It's an observation about the floor: it's \emph{the same},
whatever is certified. Say the YES state also shows something striking, a deep relation, a
result nobody could have guessed, Sultan's two sticks become one tool. The toll charges the
crossing at least one. It doesn't charge the striking crossing more, because the floor's proof
never looks at anything but the reading before and after. On the paper, VOUCH from NO makes
one mark whether you were thinking of Duncker's box or of lunch. This toy charges one either way. The general toll supplies the same lower
bound for both; an actual price schedule can charge them differently.

The candle box has a footnote that says the same thing from the other side. In 1962 the
psychologist Sam
Glucksberg ran Duncker's problem with money on it: some people were told they could win five or
twenty dollars depending on how fast they solved it. With the tacks in the box, the people
chasing the money did worse than the people who weren't. With the box empty the problem was easier
for everybody, and the accounts I've read don't agree on what the money did there, so I'll leave
that half alone. Paying more didn't buy the insight, and on the hard version it got in the way.
That's a fact about heads. It says nothing about records, and I won't push it further than that. But it makes a
nice parallel to the paper. On the paper a deeper crossing isn't charged more, and in Glucksberg's
room a bigger prize didn't bring the crossing sooner. In neither place does the price measure the
depth.

I'll state them exactly now, for any Thiele machine (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}).
A run is still just a list of moves, carried out in the order written. The
question is which of those moves crosses from no to yes, and what that crossing
lets you conclude about the total charge.

\begin{definition}[Raise, non-raising move]\label{def:u09-events}
In a Thiele machine, a step from state $s$ by move $i$ is a \emph{raise}
when it turns the reading on: $\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{no}$ and
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(s, i)) = \mathrm{yes}$. A move $i$ is a \emph{non-raising move} when no
step by it, from any state, is a raise. Raw observation, the first thing above, is one kind.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[What the toll prices, and what it doesn't]\label{rem:u09-three}
All three read straight off Definition~\ref{def:certsys} and Observation~\ref{thm:universal-floor},
with Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s board as the example. (1) The toll puts no bound on the cost of a non-raising
move; on Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s board STAY and WORK are non-raising moves and cost $0$. (2) Every
raise is charged at least $1$, by the toll, and every run from a state reading no to
one reading yes has total cost at least $1$, by the universal floor. (3) The floor is the same:
the floor's proof uses nothing about the end state but its reading, so it gives the same floor of $1$ whatever else the end state
shows. A higher floor needs more hypotheses than the toll, and those hypotheses do the work. A system that
wants to charge more for a deeper certification has to write that into its price list, move
by move; the toll doesn't do it for anyone.
\end{remark}

So the account comes down to two facts and a warning: looking can stay off the ledger, turning the reading
on can't, and the toll alone does not charge more for a remarkable claim, though another pricing rule
or an additional requirement could.

Who decided the split? The costs alone didn't. The toll prices exactly one thing, the crossing.
A price list is allowed to put a floor under more moves than that (a look, a send, a check) and
allowed to leave other moves at zero, so the sorting into non-raising moves and raises
is by whether the reading moves, and that sorting is this book's. The part that's \emph{forced} is
the floor under the crossing, once you grant a reading that stays up, finitely many states
that read yes, and a price on every merge; Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} is the argument; anything a price list charges
beyond that is a choice, and any concrete machine owes you its whole table so you can see
which choices it made.

\subsection{Test, then commit, and nothing forces the second to follow the first}

The philosopher Karl Popper said a theory earns its standing by being \emph{exposed}: you make a
conjecture, you try to kill it, and what survives a real attempt counts for something, where
``real'' means the test could have failed. His word for that earned credit is \emph{corroboration}. I lean on that idea all through this book (Section~\ref{sec:established} gives it its full due), and this
subsection shows where a Thiele machine has a version of it and where that version is weaker
than Popper, which I have to say plainly.

Add a fourth move to the paper: CHECK. It looks at something (a sum, a coin under a cup, a
formula against a row of values), and it can come out pass or fail, and it doesn't move the
box. Charge it whatever you like; charging it on the attempt, pass or fail, fits Popper,
because what made his test count was that it was really run and could have failed. CHECK is
the test, and it's a non-raising move in the sense above,
because it never turns the reading on. VOUCH is the commit. So the honest protocol is two
moves: test, then commit, and the costs are separate, one for the checking work and one for
the crossing.

But nothing in the five parts makes the second move wait for the first. The step is handed
the current state and a move name; the toll looks only at whether the reading crossed. Play
VOUCH from NO with no CHECK anywhere before it, and you land in YES and make one mark, the
same box and the same mark as the player who checked first. The two tally lines differ by
exactly what the CHECK was charged, and if you charged it nothing they don't differ at all.
The mark for the crossing is the same mark either way. The receipt says a commitment was paid
for; it does not say the commitment was earned. Popper's corroboration needs the test; the toll doesn't.

You can build a system that makes the commit wait. Let CHECK leave a mark in the state when it
passes, and write the step so VOUCH only crosses when that mark is there. Making VOUCH wait like that is a design,
written into the step function, and it's a perfectly good one. Nothing in the five parts or
the toll asks for it. The gap between the word and the bare system is real, and I'm leaving
it in plain sight: the toll prices the commit, and whether the commit was
preceded by a test is a fact about the run, or about a design somebody chose. The five parts don't
guarantee it.

\begin{remark}[Nothing makes the crossing wait]\label{rem:u09-no-wait}
Read off Definition~\ref{def:certsys}. The toll constrains
$\mathrm{cost}(i)$ for moves that cross, and nothing else; the step function is any function
of the current state and the move. So a Thiele machine may have a move that crosses
from a state no check has touched, and the toll still holds. On Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s board extended with
CHECK, the run $[\mathrm{VOUCH}]$ from NO crosses with one mark, and
$[\mathrm{CHECK}, \mathrm{VOUCH}]$ crosses with one mark for the crossing plus whatever CHECK was charged, one mark in all if CHECK is priced at zero. Making a crossing depend on an earlier check is a
condition on the step function, which a particular system can impose and the definition does
not.
\end{remark}

\subsection{What the word means}

Insight, in the sense this book prices, is a distinction made to stay: a move that flips a
reading from off to on, for good, and that move costs at least one, in any system with the
toll, whatever the reading is about and whatever its depth. At its best the reading is a relation
committed to, a claim checked and closed; a bare crossing that commits to nothing pays the same,
and the toll doesn't tell the two apart. Part~III's certified machine is one way to make
sure a crossing is the first kind. There are three boundaries, each from a different place.
From Metcalfe: it isn't a feeling, and a system's version has to be an event. From the proof:
the floor is the same; a shallow commit and a deep one both cost at least one, and cost is not
depth. A system can pay heavily to check a trivial claim, and Duncker's box, a real insight, is
still one small commit. And from the two-move protocol: a paid flag proves nothing on its own.
Price and correctness are separate books.

Which leaves a suspicion I'd have in your place. Everything so far has been one reading on one
sheet of paper, with a rule I chose and a count I bolted on. Is the shape of that record
something I picked, or is it what any base-driven record has to look like, on any machine at all?
The next section answers it: take \emph{any} machine that steps, bolt a record onto it, and see what
shape it's forced into. How a concrete machine hangs actual claims on its parts, a checked
property of one counter at one edition, and where those sit in the state, comes in Part~III (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}).

%===========================================================================
\section{Records over any base: the latch}
\label{sec:latch}
%===========================================================================

The blank cell comes back here, over any machine: a reading that goes from no to yes because the
machine did something, and stays. For the whole book so far I've been building up a thing with a
flag and a counter, and you'd be right to suspect that the whole apparatus is special pleading for one machine, the
one I keep promising to build. So this section answers the suspicion
with no particular machine in it at all, and sees what's left. Take \emph{any} machine that steps deterministically, anything at all with states and one next state for each. Call it the base: the part of the state the record watches. Now put a record over it, under rules I'll state,
and ask: what can the record be?

The answer is one shape, and I'll show you the shape first because it's a thing you can
build from a cup and a die.

\subsection{A cup and a die}

Put a cup upside down on the table. The rule is that the first time a coin lands in front of it,
you turn it right side up. There is no rule for turning it back over. Now roll a die, and put a
coin down on every six. Roll twenty times. If a six appears, the cup turns over on the first one and stays
turned over. Write down which roll did it. That number is where the record happened,
and the cup afterward is the record. If no six appears, the cup stays down; a reachable
event need not occur on every trial.

For the deterministic base in the theorem, write the rolls down first and replay them.
The base state is the fixed list and a finger pointing to its next entry; a step moves
the finger one place, regardless of the cup. The event asks whether that entry is six.
Nothing about the cup changes which entry comes next.

The cup is a \emph{latch}. Electrical engineers have had the circuit since 1918, when two British
physicists teaching engineering in London, William Eccles, a radio pioneer, and Frank Jordan,
applied for a patent on a two-valve arrangement that holds whichever state you last put it
in; it became the flip-flop, and the registers and caches in the device you're reading this on
descend from it. Cut its reset wire and what's left has one input, ``set,'' and the rule \emph{new state = old state or set}: once set, it stays set. The cup is that circuit:
a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off.

(Eccles and Jordan didn't call it a flip-flop. Their 1919 paper calls it a \emph{trigger relay}.
Where the newer, sillier name came from I can't source, so I'll leave it at that.)

Is a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off only a picture, or did anybody ever build one on
purpose? Somebody did, and for a reason that's very close to this book's. In the mid-1950s Wen
Tsing Chow, an engineer at the Arma division of the American Bosch Arma Corporation in Garden City,
New York, was asked by the United States Air Force, in the accounts of his career I could find, for
a more flexible and secure way to hold
the fixed numbers, the targeting constants, inside the guidance computer of the Atlas missile.
What he and his Arma colleague William Henrich patented (filed in 1957, granted in 1962, under the
plain title ``Storage matrix'') was a grid with a connection at every crossing, where you set the numbers by
taking out the connections you didn't want, physically or by burning them out with too much
current. The word \emph{burn} is right there in the patent, and people still say they burn a
chip. The descendants are called programmable read-only memories, PROMs, and a fuse blown in
one stays blown: there's no current you can send to grow it back. The grid was a whole memory built out of
cups with no reset wire, made because somebody wanted numbers nobody could quietly change later. That
doesn't prove anything here, because the theorem below doesn't care what a cup is made of. But it's
good to know the shape wasn't invented for a sheet of paper. Somebody needed it, for stakes a
good deal higher than a die.

Now the claim, stated loosely and then exactly: \emph{every base-driven record, over any base, is a cup with no reset wire, turned by some event the base passes through.}

\subsection{What ``base-driven'' has to mean}

The content is in the definition, and I'll give you all five rules, because the theorem is only as
strong as they are.

A machine \emph{extends} a base when there's a map from the bigger machine's states down to the
base's, and that map starts in the base's start states, reaches every one of them, moves in
step with the base (one step up top is one step down below, through the map), and agrees
about halting. The bigger machine may carry as much hidden state as it likes beyond the base,
and that's what the words ``any base'' are about: the base doesn't get to see the extension, and the extension
doesn't get to change what the base does.

The extension carries a \emph{record}, a yes/no reading, and a \emph{ledger}, a counter. It's a
\emph{base-driven record} when five things hold. One: the record's next value depends only on the
base's current state and the record's current value. (I'll call this \emph{driven by the computation}. It says the record answers to what the machine is doing. A clock on the
wall or someone's hand doesn't get a say.) Two: the ledger never goes down (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). Three: the step that turns the
record on costs at least one; that's the toll (Section~\ref{sec:toll}). Four: once on, the record stays on;
that's permanence (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}). Distributed-systems people have a name for a predicate like that. The
computer scientists K. Mani Chandy and Leslie Lamport, in their 1985 paper on taking a consistent
snapshot of a distributed system, called a property \emph{stable} when once it holds it holds
forever after, and stable properties are the ones a snapshot can be trusted to detect. Five: some run from a start state actually reaches a step that
turns the record on; otherwise the record is decoration.

I'll write the rules out exactly. On/off is true/false, $\lor$ is ``or'' (on when either side is
on), and $\mathrm{next}^k$ is $k$ steps.

\begin{definition}[Base, record-carrying machine, cover]\label{def:u11-base}
A \emph{base} $B$ is a set of states with a step function $\mathrm{next}_B$, a set of starting
states, and a halting predicate. A \emph{record-carrying machine} $M$ is a set of states with a step
function $\mathrm{next}_M$, a set of starting states, a \emph{record} $\mathrm{rec}$ from states to
Booleans, a \emph{ledger} $\mu$ from states to whole numbers, and a halting predicate. The cost of a
step is $\mathrm{cost}(m) = \mu(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) \mathbin{\dot{-}} \mu(m)$. A \emph{cover} of $B$
by $M$ is a map $\pi$ from states of $M$ to states of $B$ that sends starting states to starting
states, has every starting state of $B$ as the image of some starting state of $M$, commutes
with the steps, $\pi(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = \mathrm{next}_B(\pi(m))$, and agrees about halting:
$m$ halts exactly when $\pi(m)$ does.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Base-driven record, latch]\label{def:u11-honest}
$M$ with cover $\pi$ is a \emph{base-driven record} over $B$ when
(R1, driven
by the computation) there is one function $f$ such that, for
every state $m$,
$\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = f(\pi(m), \mathrm{rec}(m))$; for every state $m$, (R2, ledger)
$\mu(m) \le \mu(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$; (R3, toll) if $\mathrm{rec}(m)$ is off and
$\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$ is on, then $\mathrm{cost}(m) \ge 1$; (R4, permanence) if
$\mathrm{rec}(m)$ is on, so is $\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$; and (R5, a reachable write)
some starting state $m_0$ and some $k$ have $\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M^k(m_0))$ off and
$\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M^{k+1}(m_0))$ on. An \emph{event} is a function $h$ from base states to
Booleans, and its \emph{latch} is the step $(b, r) \mapsto (\mathrm{next}_B(b),\, r \lor h(b))$. $M$
\emph{factors as the latch of} $h$ when, for every state $m$ (reachable or not),
\[
(\pi(\mathrm{next}_M(m)),\ \mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m))) = (\mathrm{next}_B(\pi(m)),\ \mathrm{rec}(m) \lor h(\pi(m))).
\]
\end{definition}

The theorem says that under those rules the base state and the record move \emph{exactly} as a latch:
the record switches on at the first base state where some event holds, if it started off, and never goes off, and
the event is read off the extension's own rule by asking it what it does when the record is
off (stated exactly below). The theorem is about what the base and the record do together.
The hidden state the extension carries can't push the record anywhere (R1) doesn't allow, since
the record's next value is a function of the base state and the record's own value. The theorem
doesn't say the whole extension is a bare latch machine, and it doesn't make hidden state show up
anywhere in particular: an extension can carry a field that touches neither the record nor the
ledger. And the event is pinned down only on base states that some state with the record off
covers; on a base state with no such state above it, $f(b, \mathrm{off})$ is whatever (R1)'s
function says, and nothing in a run ever consults it.

I promised the content was in the definition, and the proof bears that out: it is a
short case split on whether the record is already on, and it uses only \emph{two} of the five
rules, ``driven by the computation'' and ``permanent.'' The ledger, the toll, and the reachable-write clauses play no part in it. A
latch is what you get from ``answers only to the base'' plus ``never comes back down'' alone. The other three rules matter for the \emph{converse}: for any base and any event the base can reach, the latch of that event, priced at one unit per write, \emph{is} a base-driven record.
The event can be one that holds everywhere, and then its latch is up after one step from every start
and tells no two starts apart. It's still a latch and still base-driven: the converse doesn't ask
the record to distinguish anything. A record that starts off and tells two starts apart at some step has to latch an event that has held along one run by then and not yet along the other, and the latch tells them
apart for as long as that stays so.
Put the two together and base-driven records are exactly
latches: one shape, and no others, over any base.

\begin{observation}[The record is a latch]\label{thm:u11-latch}
Let $B$ be any base, $\pi$ a cover of $B$ by $M$, and suppose $M$'s record is driven by the
computation (R1), through a function $f$, and permanent (R4). Then $M$ factors as the latch of the
event $h(b) = f(b, \mathrm{off})$. In particular every base-driven record factors that way; (R2),
(R3) and (R5) are not hypotheses.
\end{observation}

\begin{proof}
Ask the extension what it would do with the record off above each base state $b$.
Call its answer $h(b)$. Rule (R1) lets you ask that as one function of $b$:
no other hidden field is allowed to change the answer.

Now take an actual state. If its record is off, (R1) gives exactly that answer
$h(b)$ for the next record. If its record is already on, permanence keeps it on,
whatever $h(b)$ says. Together those two cases say ``keep an existing on,
otherwise use $h(b)$,'' which is $r\lor h(b)$.

The cover already says that the base part takes its own next step.
Put that base step beside the record rule just obtained and I have the stated
latch equation. No charge or starting condition entered the argument.
\end{proof}

The latch's nearest neighbours are in verification, and they're old. The computer scientists
Mart\'in Abadi and Leslie Lamport, then at Digital's research lab in Palo Alto, added
\emph{history variables} to specifications in 1991: extra state that records what has happened and
never steers the system, used to prove that one specification implements another. A history
variable that only ever turns on is the cup. Temporal logic has the same record as an operator.
In the past-time temporal logic that Orna Lichtenstein, Amir Pnueli and Lenore Zuck set out in
1985, ``once $h$'' holds now exactly when $h$ has held at some point so far, and a runtime monitor
keeps it in one bit with the update $r' = r \lor h$. Klaus Havelund and Grigore Ro\c{s}u, two
computer scientists working on runtime verification, synthesized monitors of exactly that kind for
safety properties written in that logic in 2002. That update is the latch of
Definition~\ref{def:u11-honest}, word for word. The observation adds the other direction:
a record driven by the computation that never comes down can't be anything else.

One thing about that proof deserves a second look, because it cuts both ways: it never asks what
the base is. The cover decides that: whatever the map sends down is base, and the record's rule is
allowed to read all of it; whatever stays up top is extension, and (R1) keeps the record's rule
from reading it. Draw the line low, so the base is only the computation's own working state, and
(R1) is a real demand. Draw it high, put every table and every refusal bit into the base, and (R1)
is easy to meet, and the latch shape comes out exactly the same. So the theorem holds wherever
you draw the line, and that's exactly why it can't tell you where a record's meaning lives. The
meaning lives in what the event $h$ reads, and that's in the base by construction. On the small machine
of Part~III (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}), the checks that give the flag its meaning sit in the base its
cover picks out. So when that machine arrives, ask it first which parts it puts above the line.

\begin{theorem}[Every reachable latch is a base-driven record]\label{thm:u11-converse}
Let $B$ be any base and $h$ any event. Let $\mathrm{Latch}_h$ have states $(b, r, x)$, starting
states $(b, \mathrm{off}, 0)$ with $b$ starting in $B$, step
$(b, r, x) \mapsto (\mathrm{next}_B(b),\ r \lor h(b),\ x + \delta)$ with $\delta = 1$ when $r$
is off and $h(b)$ is on and $\delta = 0$ otherwise, record $r$, ledger $x$, halting as $b$
halts, and cover $(b, r, x) \mapsto b$. Suppose some starting $b_0$ and some $k$ bring
$\mathrm{Latch}_h$ from $(b_0, \mathrm{off}, 0)$, in $k$ steps, to a state whose record is
still off and whose base state satisfies $h$. Then $\mathrm{Latch}_h$ is a base-driven record
over $B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The construction keeps a base state, a flag and a tally. Looking only at the
base state gives the promised cover: a start lies over the chosen base start,
every base start has such a flag-down, tally-zero start above it, and each
step advances the base exactly once. Halting is read from that same base state.

The next flag consults only the present flag and the base event, giving (R1).
The tally adds either zero or one and never falls, giving (R2).
If the flag rises, it was off and the event held, exactly the case that adds
one, giving (R3). An on flag stays on under the displayed rule, giving (R4).
Finally the supplied run reaches a state with the flag still off and the event
true. Its next step raises the flag, giving the reachable write (R5).

Whenever a base run reaches the event at all, use its first such visit.
Before that visit the flag remains off, so this is the supplied kind of run.
\end{proof}

What about a base that never merges, a reversible one? It can carry a record, and the next
theorem says exactly what it pays. Keep every earlier record value in a history beside the latch,
one more entry on every step, and the whole step merges nothing either. But that history needs a
fresh slot at every step, forever, so the machine never comes back to a state it has been in,
which puts it in the fresh-state column. On a finite state space there aren't fresh states to go on taking forever, and a permanent record
can't be written by a step that merges nothing at all. A step that merges nothing is
called \emph{injective}: no two states go to the same next state. Keep the old readings on a strip, newest first. If the strip reads
$[\mathrm{off},\mathrm{off}]$ and the current reading is on, the next strip
reads $[\mathrm{on},\mathrm{off},\mathrm{off}]$. The notation $r::H$ below
means exactly that: put the old reading $r$ at the front of the old strip $H$.

\begin{theorem}[Records on reversible machines]\label{thm:u11-reversible}
(1) Let $B$ be a base whose step is injective. The machine with states $(b, r, H, x)$, step
$(b, r, H, x) \mapsto (\mathrm{next}_B(b),\ r \lor h(b),\ r:: H,\ x + \delta)$ ($\delta$ as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse}), starting states with $r$ off, $H$ empty and $x = 0$, has an
injective step, never visits the same state twice on a run (the history gets one entry longer on
every step), and under the supposition of Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse} it is a base-driven
record over $B$. (2) With finitely many states reading on, a single injective step with a permanent reading never turns that reading from off to on.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Suppose two full states have the same successor. Can you recover what they
were? Their successor base states agree. The base keeps different sources
apart, so their earlier base states agreed too. Their new history strips
also agree. The first entry of each strip is the old record, so the old
records agree; removing that first entry leaves the old histories, which
therefore agree as well.

Those equal old base states and records determine the same charge $\delta$.
Subtract it from the equal new tallies and the old tallies agree. Every part
of the two earlier full states agrees, so they were the same state. The step
is one-to-one.

On a run the strip grows by one entry every tick. A full state cannot recur,
because its strip would have to have two different lengths. Carrying that
strip changes neither the base nor the flag nor the tally rules checked in
the preceding construction, so all five base-driven record conditions still
hold under the supplied reachable-event premise.

(2) Suppose instead there are only $K$ on-states and an off-state enters them.
Permanence sends all $K$ on-states into that same collection, and the entrant
lands there too. A one-to-one step would have to put $K+1$ different sources
into $K$ places. It cannot. Hence a permanent reading with finitely many
on-states cannot rise under a one-to-one step.
\end{proof}

So a base that never merges can carry a record without merging anywhere only by paying in fresh states: once the record is up, the run never comes back to a state it has been in (Proposition~\ref{prop:heat-or-room}). A history that grows by one entry every step is one way to supply them, and a base that never repeats a state, a counter, supplies them already. A machine with finitely many states hasn't got fresh states to go on taking, so it
can't carry one without merging: on a finite machine an instruction that first raises a permanent reading must
merge some possible states. The entering state need not belong to the colliding
pair; Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} prices the instruction under merge pricing.

Process-calculus people ran into the same thing from the other side. Vincent Danos and Jean
Krivine, two theoretical computer scientists in Paris, wanted to pin down what a transaction is. In
2004 they had built a reversible version of CCS, Robin Milner's calculus of processes that talk to each
other, where every step can be rolled back, and in 2005 they modelled a transaction in it as a process that wanders
freely through everything that can be undone until it performs an action declared irreversible,
which is the commit. The way I read it, they start from steps that all come undone and ask what has
to be added before anything sticks, and the theorem above starts from a record and asks what the
step under it must be. In their calculus, as in the theorem, a permanent effect needs a step with no
way back, and the calculus has to say which steps those are. The word I tripped on was
\emph{declared}. Theirs are labelled. Mine, I thought, are picked out by counting, since on a finite
machine the first write merges whatever anyone calls it. Push on that and it gives. I choose the
event $h$, and on a base that grows its history forever the write merges nothing, because it pays in fresh states instead (Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-reversible}), so there my permanence is declared too.

There's an arrow of time in that theorem, and I should say where it came from, because I put it
there by hand. Every starting state has the record off. That's the only reason a raised record
means the event happened: it was down at the start, and only $h$ lifts it. Turn the cup up before
the first roll and it tells you nothing about the die. So the clean start is an assumed ready
state, a past hypothesis in miniature. The past hypothesis is David Albert's name for an assumed
low-entropy beginning of the universe, which several of the accounts below lean records on.
Whether every trusted record leans on it is their argument, and I'm not settling it. Nothing in this book derives one; every theorem here that reads a raised record as news that the event happened assumes its small version and starts from there. The latch observation doesn't need it, and that's why on its own it can't say the event happened.

When I went looking for who else had found the arrow hiding in the start, I got five papers that
read like five unrelated answers. They lined up once I asked each one the same thing: what does
the cup being down at the start rest on? There are two places to put it. You can put it at the
beginning, as a fact about how things started. Or you can put it in the structure of what causes
what. David Wolpert, then a physicist at Los Alamos and the same Wolpert as the free-lunch theorem,
sorted memory systems in 1992, and one of his kinds works only because it begins in a prepared
state set up by a process that runs one way, which is how it leans on the second law. That's the
cup put down by somebody before the game, at the first place. Wolpert and Jens Kipper, a
philosopher at Rochester, put in 2024 that sorting on a formal footing, and they say plainly that
they have no formal proof this kind can only remember the past. I trust them more for that
sentence. What I think they're saying is that a prepared start buys you a memory, and getting its
direction too takes something they can't yet prove.

Aram Ebtekar, an independent researcher in Vancouver, and Marcus Hutter, who works on the theory of
general artificial intelligence at Google DeepMind and the Australian National University, built in
2024 a reversible toy world, imposed a past hypothesis on it, coarse-grained it, and got records of
the past and none of the future. As I read their route, the clean start doesn't go straight to the
records. It goes through a causal structure first, and the arrows come out of that. Thomas
Blanchard, a philosopher of science at Cologne, got in 2024 the same lopsidedness of knowledge out
of the causal Markov condition, a condition on causal structure. So Blanchard starts at the second
place, which is the middle of Ebtekar and Hutter's road. That took me a while to see, because one
is a toy world and the other is philosophy of causation. They go from the start to causes to
records; he goes from causes to records. The fit is my reading, and it's mine to defend. And Carlo
Rovelli, two years before his paper on the cost of choosing from Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}, studied traces in ``Memory and entropy'' (2022)
and concluded that a memory turns low entropy into available information. He's at the first
place, and he says what the beginning gets spent on. Read against the latch, that's the blank the
record uses up: the flag can say yes once because it started at no.

So does the latch explain why records point backwards? It doesn't,
and I'll say that plainly so it doesn't look
like it does. The step runs forwards and the runs start clean, and a theorem built on those two can
only hand the arrow back. Push further and it gives in a second place. The history that grows
forever looked like a way around the clean start. It starts empty, so it leans on the same blank.
Under a step that forgets nothing, on a finite set, no permanent record can ever be written, past or
future, which is Zermelo again. On the map the book sits at the first place, with Wolpert and
Rovelli, and it sits there by assumption. Ebtekar and Hutter at least imposed their start on a
world with its own dynamics and watched what came out. I wrote mine into the definition.

Constructor theory, which Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} brings in as a neighbour of the
counting argument, has a paper on time (Deutsch and Marletto, 2025) saying that laws stated as which transformations
a device can and can't bring about can't mention time at all, so duration has to come from
relations between physical systems, clocks, that have their own dynamics. What I think they're
saying is that whenever you want a duration you point at a second system and count what it did.
This book is in that position by construction. The step count is the only time in it, and it
comes from the machine's own steps. The next subsection has a record turned at the fifth tick of a
hidden clock, and (R1) throws it out, which read beside them is a rule about which system may be
the clock: the one being recorded. Push on it, though. Their laws have no step in them, and the
paper's work is getting duration and dynamics out of clocks and timers. I put a step,
$\mathrm{next}_B$, into the definition of a base. So I'm in their position only at the far end of
their argument, where a clock already exists. The base is my clock, and I assumed it.

Physicists have built this latch on paper too, in quantum mechanics, and it behaves the way the
last theorem says. The question that sorted them for me is where the cup puts what it forgets,
since a closed quantum system with separate energy levels comes back (Bocchieri and Loinger,
Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}) and the theorem left only
two ways to pay for a record that stays: fresh states, which here mean a history that never ends, or a
merge. Klaus Hepp, a mathematical physicist at ETH
Zurich, wanted a measuring device inside quantum mechanics itself, and studied in 1972 a particle
that flips spins in a long chain as it passes, now called the Coleman-Hepp model (I know Hepp's
paper only from accounts of it), and John Bell (1975) took it apart: the record is exactly definite
only for an infinitely long chain, which is the fresh-state column above, a history that never
ends, in quantum clothes. Jonathan Halliwell, a theoretical physicist at Imperial College London,
used in 1999 a two-state detector that flips once when a particle crosses a point and is kept from
flipping back by a large environment, which is a latch with the environment holding the history.
His abstract calls it \emph{effectively} irreversible, and I like that he puts the word
\emph{effectively} right there where you can see it. And Murray Gell-Mann, the
physicist who named the quark, and James Hartle, of the University of California at Santa Barbara,
gave in 1995 the property a name inside their framework of decoherent histories: the permanence of
the past, past alternatives that stay settled as the story is extended into the future. They name
(R4) for whole histories and leave the cup to others. So Hepp's chain, as Bell read it, is exact and infinite, and
Halliwell's detector is finite and only effectively permanent. Mine is finite, exact and permanent at once, and it
gets there by letting the first write merge. Push on that and it gives: I never say where the
merged state goes. Hepp's chain had to be infinite. Halliwell had to put his in an environment.
Mine just goes, and the toll writes a unit in a counter. That's fine in a model of computation,
and it's exactly where this stops being physics.

\subsection{Both rules do work: the toggle and the timestamp}

A theorem with two hypotheses should have two counterexamples, one for each hypothesis
dropped, and it does, and they're the two ways a record goes wrong in the world.

Drop permanence. Take a base that just counts, and a record that flips at every step: on,
off, on, off. It's driven by the computation; it's not permanent; and it's not a latch of
any event. Such a record is a \emph{toggle}, a piece of working state. A record you
can revoke is working state wearing a record's clothes, and if a revocation has to stick,
that's a \emph{second} latch (``revoked''), which is how certificate revocation lists actually work:
you add an entry; you never delete the certificate. Alin Tomescu, a computer scientist then at
MIT, and his coauthors (2019) built
append-only authenticated sets and dictionaries for transparency logs, and revocation fits that
shape exactly: a revocation goes in once and stays. The pair lemma (stated below) covers two
latches that can each read the other; do it with two cups where the
second only turns over on an even roll \emph{if the first is already up}, and you'll see the
second can never turn before the first.

Dialogue theorists built a version of that two-latch rule for arguments. Give each speaker a row of
cups, one for every claim they've made. Everybody I read in this field is answering two questions
about those cups: whose hand turns them, and can they come back down. C.\ L.\ Hamblin, an Australian
philosopher and logician who also came up with reverse Polish notation for early computers, wrote
\emph{Fallacies} (1970), and it has a chapter on formal dialectic where each speaker has a
\emph{commitment store}, a list of what they're on the hook for, and the rules of the dialogue
update it, while the speaker doesn't. I know that chapter from other people's accounts of it. Hamblin's
store is an answer to the first question, and it's (R1) for arguments: the cup answers to what happened in
the dialogue, and the speaker's hand is kept off it. Henry Prakken, who works on AI and law at
Utrecht, built in 2005 dialogue games for argumentation on stores like that and made commitments
sticky: a claim can be retracted only when it has been challenged, and claims and backtracking
carry a price. He also floats a convention that once a player has retracted a proposition, that
player can't take it on again, which is a revocation that stays revoked, the way an entry on a
revocation list does. Prakken's rules are an answer to the second question, and it took me a second pass to see
that they're two answers: a cup can come down, and coming down costs, and once it
has, the taking-back is itself a cup that stays up. Erik Krabbe, an argumentation theorist at
Groningen, names in 2001 the awkward part of that: retraction is frowned on, and yet resolving a
dispute takes somebody retracting a doubt or a point of view, so the rules have to say when taking a
commitment back is allowed. As I read him, he's standing between the two ends of the second
question. A store that never gives can't settle a dispute, and a store that gives whenever it's asked isn't a store.
The part of all that I'd keep is Hamblin's, that the store belongs to the rules and doesn't belong to the speaker. Take the pen away from the program. And this book answers Krabbe with a price: a
take-back is a second cup, ``revoked,'' and turning it costs at least one like any other write, so a
retraction is allowed, permanent and paid for, which is Prakken's convention with the toll attached.
Where mine gives is his first condition. He lets a claim come down only when it's been challenged,
and nothing in my latch asks why the second cup turned. The pair lemma lets the second cup's event read the
base and the first cup, and nothing in it requires a challenge to be there.

The same field has a notion that looks a lot like earning. In the abstract argumentation of Phan
Minh Dung, a computer scientist at the Asian Institute of Technology in Bangkok (1995), arguments
attack one another, and the \emph{grounded} semantics starts from the arguments nobody attacks and
keeps adding the ones they defend. Look at how it's built: things go in and never come out, which
is a row of cups turned one at a time. Pietro Baroni and Massimiliano Giacomin, at Brescia,
introduced in 2007, and Martin Caminada, then at Aberdeen, revisited in 2014, \emph{strong
admissibility}: a set is strongly admissible when every argument in it is defended by others in the
set that don't lean back on it, so the support bottoms out. Strong admissibility is the argumentation form of an
earned claim. Above the bottom, nothing in it is in by default, which puts it at the far end
from Burge's default on the testimony map in Section~\ref{sec:windows}. Caminada argues it plays a vital part in the dialogue games that decide
grounded acceptance. I've read Caminada's paper; Dung's and Baroni and Giacomin's I know through
what later papers say about them. Notice the bottom, though. An argument nobody attacks gets in
on a check that can't fail, and this book says a check that can't fail establishes nothing
(Section~\ref{sec:established}). Now
turn that on my own cups, because it lands. My first write needs only that $h$ holds, and what $h$
reads sits in the base, where the latch theorem doesn't look. I charge a unit for it, and a unit is a
price, not a check. So my earned records bottom out the way Dung's do, in something let in
without an argument, and the one difference is that mine pays to get in. Whether a machine's
earned record certifies exactly the strongly admissible sets is the kind of statement I'd have to
prove before I said it, and I haven't.

A record that's allowed to change its mind isn't lawless, though; it's somebody else's subject.
Count how many times the cup may be turned. Once, from down to up, is the latch. More than once and
you're somewhere else, and the people who went there sort it two ways: by how many turns are
allowed, and by how long the game runs. The philosopher Hilary Putnam, then at MIT, and E. Mark
Gold, a computer scientist at a research lab in Santa Monica, in back-to-back papers in 1965, looked
at questions a machine answers by guessing and revising, where the answer is whatever the guesses
finally settle on. Putnam's paper says outright that you're never sure you have the correct answer.
That stopped me the first time. What kind of answer can't you ever be sure you have? The way I came
to read it: the cup's position at any moment is the current guess, the answer is where it ends up,
and nobody watching can tell when it's done moving. Yuri Ershov, a logician in Novosibirsk, sorted
those in 1968 by how many revisions they're allowed (that's how his hierarchy is described; I
haven't read his paper). Allow one, from no to yes, and you get exactly the sets a program can list.
That level is in a modern account of the hierarchy by Rod Downey, Carl Jockusch, Timothy
McNicholl and Paul Schupp, four computability theorists, and you don't need their word for it. If a
program lists the set, guess no for every number and flip the guess to yes when the number shows up
on the list. Going back, if every guess flips at most once, from no to yes, run all the guessing
side by side and write a number down the moment its guess says yes. Those listable sets are what a permanent record raised by a search catches. Allow two, three, and so on, and every
extra change buys new sets: the rungs of the ladder are all different. A record that can come back
down lives on that ladder. Now put Putnam's worry on my cup, because it lands. On the bottom rung a
yes is final the moment it appears, and a no never is, since down means not yet. A single cup of mine can
certify that something happened and can never certify that it didn't; a final no would take a second
cup, turned by finding a reason, and that's the pair of latches again. That's what the bottom rung
costs, and I'd rather name it. This book stays on the bottom rung; I'm pointing at the ladder, and I'm
not climbing it.

The ladder doesn't stop at finite time, and the people who followed it past infinity have
names for the two kinds of record I just described. A definition that only ever adds, stage
after stage, and keeps everything it has at each limit, is an \emph{inductive definition}
(the long treatment is a 1974 chapter by Wayne Richter and Peter Aczel, two recursion theorists).
It's the latch run through the infinite, a cup that goes up at some stage and is still up at
every stage after. Let it take things back, and keep what stays put from some stage on, and you
have what John Burgess, a philosopher and logician at Princeton, called in 1986
\emph{quasi-inductive} definitions, which he met in the revision theories of truth that grew up
beside the logician Saul Kripke's 1975 theory of truth, which builds up the true sentences in
stages. Burgess's paper measures how complicated the truths of those theories get. I've read its
abstract, but not the place where he names them. What took me a few reads is that Burgess's rule at a
limit is Putnam and Gold's rule, keep whatever the guesses settled on, applied at every limit stage
along the way. That's my reading of how the two fit. If it's right, the split between a
cup that only goes up and a cup that settles is the same split at finite time and past it: a
permanent record is the first kind, and a toggle that's allowed to settle is the second. Joel Hamkins
and Andy Lewis, two set theorists, let a Turing machine keep running through the ordinals in 2000.
At a limit a cell keeps its value if it settled, and reads 1 if it kept flipping back and forth
forever, and the trick they use again and again is the toggle: flash a flag on and off every time a
guess changes, and at the limit the flag is on exactly when the guess changed infinitely often. A
flag that can come back down is how that machine learns what no finite run could tell it. A
permanent one can't do that trick, because at a limit a cell that only ever goes up just stays up.
So past infinity the toggle is the clever one: a latch tells you a thing happened at least once,
and their flashing flag tells you it happened infinitely often. I threw the toggle out a few
paragraphs back anyway, and I'd do it again, because before the limit its reading can't be relied
on, and nobody using a machine of mine gets to wait for a limit. One finite-time fact belongs beside it, so nobody concludes too much
from permanence. Hao Wang, a logician then at Oxford, described in 1957 a machine whose only write
is to mark a square and which can never erase one, and it computes everything a Turing machine
does. Permanence of a machine's own memory costs it no computing power, given an endless tape: each
mark goes on a square nobody marked before, which is the fresh-state column again. What the book prices is a
permanent reading raised by a step that has to work whether or not the reading is already up, which
is a different thing. So the cost I named a paragraph ago is a cost in what a reading can claim,
and computing power doesn't pay it.

Drop ``driven by the computation.'' Take a base that counts, and a record that switches on at
