the fifth tick of a \emph{hidden clock}, whatever the base is doing. It's permanent, and the computation doesn't drive it; such a record is a \emph{timestamp}. A timestamp is not evidence: it says \emph{when} and doesn't say \emph{what happened}, and a record
switched by an outside party or a clock records that party or that clock and leaves the computation
out. Try it with the recorded die list. Keep a second tally hidden beside it, and turn
the cup when that tally reads five before a move; then advance both the tally and
the finger on the list. Run two trials from the same list entry with the cup down,
but start the hidden tally at five in one trial and zero in the other. The next
cup values disagree although everything the base shows agrees, which is the failure
of being driven by the base. If the tally always starts synchronized with the
list position, the position can predict the cup; the distinction matters below.

The two examples do exactly what I said they do: the toggle is driven, isn't
permanent and isn't a latch; the timestamp is permanent and isn't driven. That each also keeps the other rules (the
ledger is the step count, the first switch-on costs one, a run reaches it) is true by
inspection.

Permanent but undriven is a timestamp, driven but impermanent is a toggle, and a record is
the thing that's both. Undriven, for the timestamp, means that along the runs that actually happen the
base state doesn't fix when the record turns; Lemma~\ref{lem:u11-clock-sync} below says why that's
the condition, and what (R1) as written adds to it. That's the whole discrimination, and I think it's the most useful
single sentence in this book for looking at systems other than the one I build, which is
why it's here.

I'll now state the pair lemma and the two counterexamples exactly. The base for both counterexamples is the
counter: states are whole numbers, the step adds one, every state is a starting state, and
nothing halts. Two more bits of shorthand: $\lnot r$ is $r$ flipped, and a statement in
square brackets, like $[k = 5]$, reads on when it's true and off when it isn't.

\begin{lemma}[Two records are two latches]\label{lem:u11-pair}
Let $c_1, c_2$ be two records on $M$, with cover $\pi$ onto a base $B$, such that: there is one
function $F$ with $(c_1(\mathrm{next}_M(m)), c_2(\mathrm{next}_M(m))) = F(\pi(m), c_1(m), c_2(m))$;
the ledger never goes down; a step that turns either record on costs at least one; and each
record is permanent. Then there are $h_1, h_2$ with
$c_1(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = c_1(m) \lor h_1(\pi(m), c_2(m))$ and
$c_2(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = c_2(m) \lor h_2(\pi(m), c_1(m))$ for every $m$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Hold the second record fixed and ask what the joint rule does to the first
when the first is off. Call that answer $h_1(b,r_2)$; it is the first
component of $F(b,\mathrm{off},r_2)$. At any actual state whose first record
is off, that is its next value. At any state whose first record is on,
permanence keeps it on. Thus its rule is $r_1\lor h_1(b,r_2)$.

Now hold the first record fixed and ask the corresponding question with the
second off. The answer is $h_2(b,r_1)$, the second component of
$F(b,r_1,\mathrm{off})$. The same off/on argument gives
$r_2\lor h_2(b,r_1)$. The records may affect each other's raising condition,
but neither can undo an on once it is there.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The toggle]\label{lem:u11-toggle}
Let the toggle have states $(n, r)$, step $(n, r) \mapsto (n + 1, \lnot r)$, every state
starting, record $r$, ledger $n$, cover $(n, r) \mapsto n$ onto the counter. It is driven by
the computation, with $f(b, r) = \lnot r$; it is not permanent; and it factors as the latch of
no event.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
At $(0, \mathrm{on})$ the next record is off, which breaks permanence; and any latch gives
$\mathrm{on} \lor h(0) = \mathrm{on}$ there.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The timestamp]\label{lem:u11-clock}
Let the timestamp have states $(b, k, r)$, step $(b, k, r) \mapsto (b + 1, k + 1, r \lor [k = 5])$,
every state starting, record $r$, ledger $b$, cover $(b, k, r) \mapsto b$ onto the counter. It
is permanent and not driven by the computation.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Permanence: $\mathrm{on} \lor x$ is on. Not driven: the states $(0, 5, \mathrm{off})$ and
$(0, 0, \mathrm{off})$ have the same base state and the same record, and their next records are
on and off, so no $f$ of the base state and the record can give both.
\end{proof}

``Driven'' is a condition on every
state. The timestamp makes every state a starting state, so the two states the proof compares are
both ones a run can begin at, even though a timestamp started at $(0, 0, \mathrm{off})$ would never reach $(0, 5, \mathrm{off})$.

That last sentence does more work than it looks, so I'll state it as a lemma. Start the same timestamp
in sync, at $(b, b, \mathrm{off})$ only. On every state its runs reach, the hidden count equals
the base, and the timestamp is exactly the latch of $[b = 5]$. (R1) still rejects it, because (R1)
asks about every state, and $(0, 5, \mathrm{off})$ is a state, though no run from a synchronised
start reaches it. So (R1) as written separates the timestamp from a latch partly by how the cover is
drawn and through states nobody visits. The separation I mean is the one on reachable states:
the timestamp with every state a start fails (R1) even when only states some run reaches are
counted, since two starting states sit over the same base state with the same record and
disagree about the next one. And the latch theorem holds in that reachable form too.

\begin{lemma}[The timestamp, on the states runs reach]\label{lem:u11-clock-sync}
Say $M$'s record is \emph{driven on reachable states} when (R1) holds for every state reached
from a starting state in some number of steps. (1) If $M$'s record is driven on reachable states
and permanent, then on every reachable state $M$ steps as the latch of some event. (2) The timestamp
of Lemma~\ref{lem:u11-clock} isn't driven on reachable states. (3) The timestamp started in sync, with
starting states $(b, b, \mathrm{off})$ and the same step, record, ledger and cover, is permanent,
isn't driven by the computation, is driven on reachable states, and on every reachable state
steps as the latch of $[b = 5]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(1) is the proof of Observation~\ref{thm:u11-latch}, run on reachable states only. (2) The states
$(0, 5, \mathrm{off})$ and $(0, 0, \mathrm{off})$ are starting states, reached in no steps, and the
proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:u11-clock} applies to them. (3) From $(b, b, \mathrm{off})$ every step adds
one to both counts, so a reachable state has $k = b$ and its next record is $r \lor [b = 5]$. Over
every state, (R1) fails at the same pair as in Lemma~\ref{lem:u11-clock}.
\end{proof}

So ``permanent but undriven is a timestamp'' is a sentence about the timestamp with every state a start,
over the cover that hides its count, and it holds there in the strong form: undriven on the very
states its runs pass through. A timestamp started in step with its base is a latch on the runs it
has, and (R1) throws it out only because (R1) also looks at states those runs never reach.

\subsection{Is there only one such machine? No: one structure, two unforced choices.}

I have to take apart the sentence ``there's only one way to carry a record,'' because three
different things get squeezed into it.

The first claim asks: given the toll and a fixed price list, is there one way to keep the books,
starting at zero and adding each move's price? Yes, on every state reachable from the start;
that's Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s initiality, and it assumes the price list.

The second claim asks: is every base-driven record over a base \emph{the same machine}, charges and all? No,
and the counterexample is embarrassing in its simplicity. Take any base-driven record, give it a new ledger that adds each step's old cost and one unit more,
whatever the step is, and then walk the five rules. The
record still answers only to the base and its own value (R1); the cost never touches it. The
ledger still never goes down (R2); it climbs faster, if anything. The step that turns the
record on still costs at least one (R3), because the toll is a \emph{floor} and a surcharge only
raises the price. Once on, the record stays on (R4), and the same run still reaches the write
(R5). So the surcharged machine is base-driven, and it isn't the machine you started with: wherever
the original sat still at no charge, the surcharged one pays one unit a step for sitting still. Do it
with the cup and the die, and charge one unit for every roll, six or not. The cup turns over on the
same roll as before, so you've changed the cost and nothing about the record. A machine that
charges for CPU time is base-driven and isn't the one that doesn't. The new ledger has to sit beside the old
state and not be read off it. A step's cost is the ledger after less the ledger before, so a ledger read off the
state charges nothing for a step that leaves the state where it was, such as a halted machine stepping to itself,
or for any step on a loop (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). The surcharge is paid in fresh ledger values, the way every
counter that climbs is paid for.

The same base computation and latch are visible after forgetting the new
ledger. The full transition graph can be different: a free self-loop becomes
an endless line of increasing ledger values. So the comparison preserves
base, reading and the stipulated stopping convention, not every full-state
distinction. If the ledger is also observed, these are different contracts.
The construction allows a nonnegative surcharge depending on the current
state in this broader accounting interface. Such a charge is not in general
a price on instruction names alone. The price schedule remains an unforced
choice after the base and event have been fixed.

And then there's the second unforced choice, and this one still surprises me: \emph{which event} is the record?
Nothing in the five rules picks it, beyond (R5)'s demand that it hold somewhere a run reaches; on a base whose runs pass through only one state that leaves one record, and the choice opens as soon as a run passes two states an event can tell apart. The converse above already says so, if you read it
twice: for any event the base can reach, the latch of that event, priced at one unit per
write, is a base-driven record. Do it with the die. One cup turns over on the first six, and another
turns over on the first one. Both are cups with no reset wire; both are base-driven. Roll a one
first, and until a six turns up the two cups disagree about whether anything has been
recorded. So \emph{which permanent reading counts as the record} is a second thing nobody forces
on you. The price list is one unforced choice and the event is the other, and that second choice is the
question Section~\ref{sec:pointer} is about: what, if anything, makes certification the event worth
recording. ``The ledger passed one'' is an event only if the chosen base includes enough
information to decide it. An extension-only ledger is hidden from a base event,
just as the hidden clock was. The unforced choice is among functions of the chosen base.

\begin{corollary}[The event is an unforced choice]\label{cor:u11-event-free}
Let $B$ be any base and $h_1, h_2$ two events, each meeting the supposition of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse}. Then $\mathrm{Latch}_{h_1}$ and $\mathrm{Latch}_{h_2}$ are both
base-driven records over $B$. If some run from a start of $B$ reaches a base state $b$ with $h_1(b)$ on and $h_2(b)$ off, and $h_2$ holds nowhere earlier on that run, then after the step from $b$ the same run has the first record on and the second off.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
That both are base-driven is Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse} applied twice. Along that run the second record is still off when it reaches $b$, since $h_2$ hasn't held, and the latch's own rule keeps it off, $\mathrm{off} \lor h_2(b)$; the first is on after that step, whatever it was before, since $h_1(b)$ is on.
\end{proof}

Now let the cup wobble. Say whatever turns it over sometimes does and sometimes doesn't, with
odds you could write on a card. Does fixing the price list fix the odds? No, and the
counterexample is two cups with the same price tag and differently loaded coins. I'll set it up
carefully. Let a record be a single bit that moves at random: from each value, a list of weighted next values, every weight positive,
never empty, never leaving on once on, and with the write from off to on charged at least one.
Call such a record a \emph{permanent probabilistic record}.
Call two such records \emph{the same schedule} when the same moves are possible and every move is charged the same, and \emph{the same in probability} when the weighted lists give every move the same odds.

\begin{theorem}[The schedule doesn't fix the probabilities]\label{thm:u11-probabilistic}
(1) There are two permanent probabilistic records with the same schedule that are not the same in
probability. (2) There is a permanent probabilistic record that no deterministic latch on its
current value describes.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) From off, one record moves to off or on with weights $1$ and $1$, the other with weights $1$
and $2$; from on, both stay on with weight $1$; both charge $1$ for the write. Same possible
moves, same charges, different weights. (2) The first record moves from off both to off and to
on, while a latch $r \lor h(r)$ gives one value.
\end{proof}

These are finite-weight models on one bit with no base underneath;
they say nothing about any particular machine.

The third claim asks: is there one state space, up to renaming, that every base-driven record-carrier has
to have? No, because the extension may carry any hidden field it likes, so two carriers over one base can
have state spaces of different sizes, and nothing needs them to match.

\subsection{Records with more than two values}

A cup has two positions, and some records have more: a counter of how many checks passed, or a level
that only rises. The same reasoning goes through one threshold at a time. For each value $a$,
``the record has reached $a$'' is a yes/no reading, and each of those readings is a latch. What
doesn't go through is squeezing the whole record into one cup. ``Rises'' needs one word of explanation: the
values come with an order $\le$, ``is at or below,'' which needn't compare every pair (that's
what makes it a \emph{partial} order), and $[a \le x]$ is the yes/no reading ``$x$ has reached $a$.

For example, keep separate records that an experiment was repeated and that its
calculation was checked. ``Repeated only'' and ``calculation checked only'' are
different places; neither includes the other. ``Both'' is above each. In this
order, moving up means retaining what was already done and possibly adding
another act. The order also has three rules: a place includes itself, inclusion
carries through an intermediate place, and two places including each other
are the same place. Those are the rules the proof below uses.''

\begin{definition}[A growing record]\label{def:u11-growing}
Let the record take values in a set $A$ with a partial order $\le$ decided by a Boolean test. A
record $\rho$ on $M$, with cover $\pi$ onto a base $B$, is a \emph{base-driven growing record} when: there
is one function $f$ with $\rho(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = f(\pi(m), \rho(m))$; it grows,
$\rho(m) \le \rho(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$; the ledger never goes down and every step that changes
$\rho$ costs at least one; and some run from a starting state reaches a step that changes it.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Growing records are families of latches]\label{thm:u11-growing}
(1) For every base-driven growing record there is an $h$ with
\[
[a \le \rho(\mathrm{next}_M(m))] = [a \le \rho(m)] \lor h(a, \pi(m), \rho(m))
\]
for every value $a$ and state $m$: each threshold is a latch, whose event may read the current
value. (2) The thresholds determine the value: if $[a \le x] = [a \le y]$ for every $a$, then
$x = y$. (3) For a growing record, charging every change is the same as charging every threshold
that switches on. (4) One latch is not enough: a three-valued record that climbs
$0 \to 1 \to 2$ over a one-state base, each climb charged one, is base-driven, and no single Boolean
latch with a decoding from the base state and the latch reproduces it. (5) A chain of distinct
$k$-bit words, each word's set bits contained in the next one's, has at most $k + 1$ members.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Fix a threshold $a$. If the old record has already reached it, growth
keeps it reached. If it has not, the cup rises exactly when the next record
$f(b,x)$ reaches it. Define the event to say both things: ``not reached at
$x$, reached at $f(b,x)$,'' or
$h(a,b,x)=[a\not\le x]\wedge[a\le f(b,x)]$.
Keeping an existing yes and otherwise using that event gives the stated
latch equation.

(2) Suppose $x$ and $y$ give the same answer at every threshold. Ask the
threshold named $x$ itself. The record $x$ has reached it, so $y$ must have
reached it too: $x\le y$. Ask the threshold named $y$ and get $y\le x$.
The order's third rule says those two records are the same.

(3) If the value stays put, every threshold gives the same answer before
and after. If it grows from $x$ to a different $y$, look at the threshold
$y$. It is reached afterwards. It was not reached before: $y\le x$,
together with growth $x\le y$, would force $x=y$. Thus some threshold
switches on exactly when the record changes. Charging those steps is the
same requirement in either wording.

(4) Keep the base at its sole state and let the record move from zero to
one, then two, then stay at two. Add one to the tally at each climb.
The record rule consults only its present value, keeps it growing and pays
for both changes, so it meets the requirements. A single flag over that
unchanging base offers a decoder only two inputs, flag down and flag up.
It cannot reproduce the three different record values just visited.

(5) Lay the distinct bit words out in their increasing order. At each move
to the next word, at least one bit that was zero must become one; no one
may become zero. Across the whole chain there are only $k$ bits available
for those changes. There are therefore at most $k$ moves between distinct
words, or $k+1$ words including the first.
\end{proof}

I have two cautions about that. In (1) each threshold's event may read the record's current value, so
the events aren't all functions of the base alone. And (3) charges a step when it switches some
threshold on: a step that switches on three thresholds at once owes at least one, and nothing
here makes the charges add up per threshold.

The order need not be finite;
(5) is the finite-memory bound.

\subsection{What leaving the base open buys you}

The reason this section exists is to answer the suspicion I started with. The record isn't
special pleading for one machine. Over any base that steps deterministically, under rules you can read, a record that
answers to the computation and never comes down is a latch on an event, and the proof
doesn't care what the base is. What a particular machine adds on top of the latch is a
\emph{choice of price list} and a \emph{choice of event}, and both are choices. That is why the permanent-flip theorem in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} never needed the word certify: it forces a
merge in whatever stays. The surcharged cup
shows the first: the cost can change and the record not notice. The two cups on one die show
the second: the rules are happy with either event. Any machine that meets the model will have to make both
choices, and whether its choice of event is the right one is a question I'll get to
(Section~\ref{sec:pointer}), and won't claim to have settled. Before that, a record can have
more than two positions. Earlier in this section a record that rises got cut into one cup
per threshold; Part~I's chapter on the whole direction (Section~\ref{sec:direction}) asked how much of the
rest survives once a record has more places to be than up and down, and the answer was all of it.

%===========================================================================
\section{The shadow, exactly}
\label{sec:shadow-exact}
%===========================================================================

Section~\ref{sec:windows} put the machine behind a window and asked what an outsider could tell.
It found that two states can look the same through the window and differ in what matters, and that
a price computed from the window can't be exact if the window has a collision
(Observation~\ref{thm:shadow-price}). That was for one cup. With a whole row of cups in hand I can ask
the sharper version of the same question, which is also the one I actually care about. Take the
ordinary machine, the one with no cups and no ledger, and let it look at itself. What's the shape
of everything it can't see, and what does the toll cost in terms of that shape?

\subsection{The ordinary machine is a shadow}

Take any machine with a record and a ledger, and sweep both off the table, the cups and the
counter. What's left is a machine that steps the same way and knows nothing about either, provided
the step's effect on everything else never depends on the cups or the counter: sweeping them off
has to commute with the step. A system whose control reads its record or its ledger has no shadow
in this sense. Where the premise holds, call what's left the \emph{shadow}. Over any one state of the shadow there's a pile of full states, all casting that same shadow and
differing only in their record and their ledger. Section~\ref{sec:windows} already called the pile over a point the
\emph{fibre} over it. The shadow is one particular window, the one that shows everything except the
cups and the ledger.

The shadow has its own fibres, and every move has piles of its own too: the states a move sends to
one landing spot. I'll call those the move's \emph{landing piles}. A fibre is everything that looks
the same before anybody moves. A landing pile is everything that ends up in the same spot after one
move. Keep the two kinds apart, because the whole section turns on how they meet.

\subsection{Pricing from the shadow}

First the window question, over a whole row. A \emph{window price} charges each step from what the
window shows before and after it. It meets the floor if it charges at least one for every step that
turns a cup over, and it's \emph{exact} if it also charges nothing for any step that turns no cup
over. A \emph{collision} is two steps that look the same through the window, where one turns a cup
over and the other doesn't.

With one cup, the fix in Section~\ref{sec:windows} was to put the cup in the window. So my first
guess for a row was that the window has to show some of the cups. Try the smallest version: a
record in the whole numbers, and a window that shows only the first cup, the one that asks ``at
least one?'' Let the record rise on some steps and hold still on others. Once it's past one, that
cup is up before and after both kinds of step, so a step that turned over a cup further along looks
exactly like a step that turned over nothing, and the two make a collision. So then, I thought, the window
has to show every cup. That's wrong too, from the other side. Take a record in the whole numbers
with two moves, one that adds one and one that leaves it alone, and a window that shows only
whether the record is even, which on the row is whether an even number of cups are up. You can't
read the record off that window, and no flat charge is exact, since some steps turn a cup over and
some don't. But the evenness changes on exactly the steps that turn a cup over, so charging one
exactly when the evenness changed is exact.

\begin{theorem}[Window prices over a direction]\label{thm:dir-window}
(1) If the window has a collision, every window price that meets the floor charges at least one for
some step that turns no cup over, so no window price is exact. (2) An exact window price exists exactly when the window has no collision; on a machine with finitely many states and moves, whose views can be told apart by a yes-or-no test, it can also be computed. (3) Along
any run, a window price that meets the floor charges at least the number of steps that turn no cup
over but look, through the window, like a step that does. Some window price meets the floor and, among the steps that turn no cup over, charges one on exactly those, so that number is the least overcharge; when it can be decided, for each pair of views, whether some step showing them turns a cup over, that price can be computed. (4) A window can
price exactly without showing where the record is: there's a record in the whole numbers with a move
that raises it and a move that leaves it alone, and a window that shows only whether the record is
even; the evenness changes exactly on the rises, no charge that is the same for every step is exact,
and charging one exactly when the evenness changes is exact, although no rule reads the record off
the window. (5) There's a record in the whole numbers and a window
that shows only the one cup ``at least one,'' and that window has a collision.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) The two colliding steps get the same charge. The floor makes it at least one because of the step
that turns a cup over, and the other step pays it too. (2) Without a collision, ``does some step
that looks like this turn a cup over?'' is a question about what the window shows; charge one exactly when the answer is yes. On a finite machine you can answer it for every pair of views. (3)
A step that turns no cup over but looks like one that does gets that step's charge, which is at
least one by (1)'s argument; add along the run. For the other half, charge one exactly when the
answer to (2)'s question is yes, which needs that question to be decidable, and count the
overcharge. (4) A rise changes the evenness and the other move doesn't, so the window sees exactly
the steps that turn a cup over; a flat charge either charges nothing for a rise or charges something
for a step that turns nothing over; and 0 and 2 look the same through the window. (5) The first cup, as above.
\end{proof}

Item (4) changed how I think about this. I'd assumed a window had to see the cups to price them. It
doesn't; it has to see them \emph{move}. A window that cannot tell you your exact place, but detects every rise and every pause,
can charge the right amount every time.

\subsection{What a priced move destroys}

Now the fibres. Part~I showed that the move raising a permanent flag on a finite machine lands two
possible states on one state, and Theorem~\ref{thm:dir-merge} showed the same for a step that turns any cup
over, once the cups only go up. Which two? It matters a great deal. If they're in different shadow
fibres, then the ordinary machine lost a distinction too; the record may also differ between them. If they're in the same
fibre, the ordinary machine lost nothing, and what got destroyed was only ever off the table: two
states that cast one shadow, told apart by their cups or their ledger, crushed into one.

My first guess was that it's always the second kind, because the cups are where everything
happens. It isn't always. It depends on whether the ordinary machine forgets anything on its own.

\begin{theorem}[The toll prices a collapse inside a fibre]\label{thm:dir-fibre}
On a machine with finitely many states and a growing record: (1) a move that turns a cup over
somewhere sends two different states to one landing spot; (2) if the shadow exists, so that sweeping commutes with the step, and the shadow's step for that move
forgets nothing, sending different shadow states to different shadow states, then those two states
are in the same shadow fibre, and every landing pile of the move lies inside one fibre; (3) without
that premise it can fail: there's a two-state machine whose two states sit in different fibres and
whose shadow step forgets, so the merge at the step that turns the cup over lands two states from different fibres
and no fibre loses a point. (4) The halving price, which says a move of cost $c$ shrinks any finite
collection of states by at most a factor of $2^c$, holds exactly when every landing pile has at most
$2^c$ states, on a machine of any size.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) is the counting argument of Theorem~\ref{thm:dir-merge}, with growth. (2) If two states land on one spot,
their shadows land on one shadow spot, and the shadow's step tells shadows apart, so the two states
cast the same shadow to begin with. (3) The stamp of Theorem~\ref{thm:dir-escapes}, with the record's value also shown in the
visible part, so each state is its own shadow: both states land on yes, and so do their shadows. (4) is the worst pile-up of
Premise~\ref{prem:halving}. Any $2^c+1$ states of one landing pile would be a collection that lands
on a single spot, which the premise caps at $2^c$, so no pile has more; and any finite
collection is at most the number of spots it lands on times the biggest pile. Neither half needs the
machine to be finite.
\end{proof}

So on a machine with finitely many states and a record that only grows, when the ordinary machine forgets nothing,
the toll is a price on crushing a fibre: on taking
two states that cast one shadow, which only what's off
the table told apart, and making them one.
The last of those premises is the one I just showed you failing.

\subsection{What the shadow is}

Put the two sections together and you get the shape I've been circling since the Flatland night (the night a video about
\emph{Flatland} gave me the hunch behind this book; Section~\ref{sec:origin} tells it).
The ordinary machine is the shadow of a machine with a row of cups beside it. Over every shadow
state there's a whole fibre, a pile of states that differ only in their cups and their ledger, and
the ordinary machine can't tell them apart, on a machine whose step never looks at the cups. On a machine that obeys the toll, a
step that
turns a cup over costs, whichever cup it is and however many it turns, and on a machine with finitely many states whose record
only grows, when the
ordinary machine forgets nothing, what that cost pays
for is exactly crushing two states of one
fibre into one. A window can charge the right cost without seeing the cups, if it sees them move.
And on a machine with the halving price, where each unit of cost pays for at most one halving, the
cost in bits, times the weight of the spread,
is never less than what got crushed on average.

What I haven't shown is that any of this is out there in the world, that nature keeps a direction
like this over its own shadows. That's a belief of mine, and nothing in this book proves it. What
I've shown, and you can check, comes with its premises showing. A machine whose record is driven by
the computation and climbs a partial order is a row of cups, one latch for every line. If it also
has finitely many states, never lets the record come down, and prices its merges, it has to pay this
way. And when its ordinary machine forgets nothing, what it pays for is exactly this. It's less than the
Flatland night promised me. It's also the part of it that held when I pushed.

\subsection{Shortcuts}

There's a question every machine with a record runs into once its programs can be handed their own code. A cup is worth turning over because something later glances at it
and doesn't have to work the thing out again, the way Section~\ref{sec:structure}'s glance reads
a block's bucket off the table without applying the rule from scratch. Call any move like that a \emph{shortcut}, and
call it \emph{sound} when it gives the answer the long way would have given. (That gloss is about cost, leaning on what
was done so nothing is redone, and the wall I'm about to show you doesn't look at cost at all;
the next section says exactly what it does look at.) So can a machine like that \emph{decide}, from inside, whether its own shortcuts are sound? That question runs into a wall, the same wall Kurt Gödel and Alan Turing hit, and
I have to show you that it's there before I show you anything that pretends to be on the other side
of it.

%===========================================================================
\section{The diagonal}
\label{sec:diagonal}
%===========================================================================

In Section~\ref{sec:structure} I said you'd watch the same move get made again and again as the book went on:
somebody says ``everything is X,'' it's true enough to do real work with, and then somebody
draws the diagonal. I owe you the diagonal itself now, because Sections~\ref{sec:latch} to~\ref{sec:shadow-exact} just handed a record, and a whole
direction of them, to \emph{any} system that steps, and the next thing anyone wants from a system with a record is for
it to tell sound shortcuts from unsound ones by itself. Before I let anything claim that, I
have to show you the wall every such claim runs into, and then show you exactly where a
system with a record stands relative to the wall. It doesn't stand on the far side, because nobody's on the far
side. A record keeps a distinction and pays for it. What it can't do is the judging: no machine
that can hand a program its own code, and can run the flip of a verdict as one of its own
programs, can sort all its programs, from inside, by a question about what they do that some
pass and some fail. So the record carries a commitment, and somebody still
has to make it.

\subsection{Now point it at the record}

The question Section~\ref{sec:shadow-exact} left open can be asked with nothing in it but what Parts~I and~II have built. A
system steps; a record rides along and latches on an event (Section~\ref{sec:latch}); when the event is a
certification, Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} said the reading, with its object and its paid event behind it, is what lets an
auditor treat a claim as established, and for a claim that a shortcut is sound, that's what
makes the shortcut \emph{admissible}. Can a system like that have, as one of its own programs, a procedure that
correctly decides, for every program, ``does this program admit a sound shortcut''? A procedure like that
would be autopilot: hand it any program and it says yes or no, and it's always right.

The exact statement is narrower than the question in plain words, so I'll give it
before the proof. In the theorem, ``admits a shortcut'' is any property of programs with two
features: two programs that behave alike agree on it, and there's one program that has it
and one that doesn't. Those two features are all the argument gets to look at. The diagonal doesn't see
soundness. Each system that wants the wall picks its own property, and whether that
property lines up with being entitled to soundness in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s sense is a separate fact about that system,
checked one system at a time if it's checked at all. A procedure that returns soundness
records for some programs, or only for restricted inputs, or with outside evidence, is not
what the wall rules out.

So in the theorem ``shortcut'' is a label. The plain-words gloss at the end of
Section~\ref{sec:shadow-exact}, leaning on a record so the thing isn't worked out again, is about
\emph{how} a program gets its answer, and how is exactly what extensionality throws away: the
theorem only gets to see what programs do, and it treats any two that do the same as one. A
question like ``is there a cheaper program that gives the same answers?'' isn't the theorem's
question, and a wall for it would need a different theorem. The nearest thing I know of is Manuel
Blum's speedup theorem, from 1967, and it goes somewhere stranger: there are computable functions
with no fastest program at all, where every program for the function has another that's faster on
all but finitely many inputs. Blum's theorem is a fact about cost, not a wall about deciding, and nothing
in this book proves anything in that territory. Each use of the wall also names its sameness. In
the substrate theorem it's the substrate's own $\simeq$; on L it's what a term computes; on the
host of the small machine Part~III builds, it's the partial function a program
computes. A particular notion of shortcut gets the wall only after someone proves it
behaves alike on programs that are the same in the sense in use, and holds of one program and
fails of another.

The answer is no, under premises. The proof is the two index cards, and I'll give you the
premises because they're the whole content. Suppose there were such a decider, one that says yes
exactly when a program admits a shortcut. Build the
flip: ``if the decider says yes about me, behave like a program that admits no shortcut; if
it says no, behave like one that does.'' If the system has a recursion theorem (a program
can be handed its own code), and if that flip is one of the transformations the system can
carry out, and if ``admits a shortcut'' depends only on behaviour (two programs that behave
the same agree on it), and if there's at least one program each way, then there's a program
that behaves exactly like its own flip, and whatever the decider says about it is wrong.
Both cases close in a line each. This rules out a decider that says yes if and only if a program admits a shortcut,
for any substrate with those parts. (A substrate here is the mathematical structure just described: programs, a run that may fail
to give back a state, a counter with a step relation it never goes down along, an
encoding of programs as data, a notion of ``representable'' transformation, and the recursion
theorem for those. It says nothing about what the states are made of.) It's Rice's trick one floor over, and I should be careful
with that. Rice stated his theorem for classes of recursively enumerable sets, the sets a program
can list, and it's usually taught now for the functions Turing machines compute. This wall is
the same diagonal with different premises: it carries its own recursion theorem and its own
list of representable transformations, and it picks the property. So it isn't a corollary
of Rice as Rice stated it, and it doesn't show that any property is harder or easier to decide
than classical halting. And
I want you to have one thing about its proof: it never touches the counter,
the toll, or the step relation. It uses the recursion theorem, representability of the flip,
the two witnesses, and extensionality, and nothing else.

I'll set out the setting and the wall now, with every word pinned down so you can poke at it.

\begin{definition}[Substrate]\label{def:u12-substrate}
A \emph{substrate} has a type of states, a type $\mathrm{Prog}$ of programs, and a run map that
takes a program and a state and either gives back a state or gives nothing. It has a counter
$\mu$ on states and a step relation along which $\mu$ never decreases; an encoding
$\mathrm{enc}$ of programs as states with a decoder $\mathrm{dec}$ such that
$\mathrm{dec}(\mathrm{enc}(p)) = p$; and a predicate $\mathrm{Rep}$ on maps
$f: \mathrm{Prog} \to \mathrm{Prog}$, the transformations the substrate counts as its own.
Two programs are \emph{equivalent}, $p \simeq q$, when $\mathrm{run}(p, s) = \mathrm{run}(q, s)$
for every state $s$. The last condition is the \emph{recursion theorem}: for every $f$ with
$\mathrm{Rep}(f)$ there is a program $p$ with $p \simeq f(p)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Shortcut predicate]\label{def:u12-shortcut-predicate}
A \emph{shortcut predicate} on a substrate is a property $A$ of programs with two programs $y$ and
$n$ such that $A(y)$ holds, $A(n)$ fails, and $A$ is extensional: $p \simeq q$ implies
$A(p) \iff A(q)$. For a Boolean function $d$ on programs, its \emph{flip} is
$f_d(p) = n$ if $d(p)$ is true and $f_d(p) = y$ if $d(p)$ is false.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[No inside decider]\label{thm:u12-no-inside-decider}
Let a substrate carry a shortcut predicate $A$ with witnesses $y$ and $n$. Then for every Boolean function $d$ on programs with $\mathrm{Rep}(f_d)$ there is a program $p$ with $p \simeq f_d(p)$, and $d(p) = \mathrm{true} \iff A(p)$ fails at that $p$. So no such $d$ is right about $A$ on every program. \end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Hand the proposed judge $d$ to the flip construction. The flip is an allowed
program transformation, so the recursion theorem supplies a program $p$
that behaves exactly as its own flip tells it to behave. Now ask the judge
about that particular program.

If the judge says yes, the flip sends $p$ to the no-example $n$. Thus $p$
and $n$ behave alike. The question depends only on behaviour, and $n$ fails
it, so $p$ fails it too. The judge's yes is wrong.

If the judge says no, the flip sends $p$ to the yes-example $y$. Now $p$
and $y$ behave alike. Since $y$ passes, $p$ passes too. The judge's no is
wrong. Those are its only answers.

I used the recursion theorem to obtain this one self-matching program,
the two examples to give the flip somewhere to go, and the rule that alike
behaviour gets the same verdict. The counter, the step relation and the
encoding played no part. Any setting supplying that same fixed point for
the flip gives the same contradiction.
\end{proof}

So what's ruled out is a $d$ that says true exactly when $A$ holds, and whose flip the substrate can represent. Every part I named is a premise, and the theorem covers every substrate that supplies them all.

So the wall is there. The part I have to be honest about is \emph{who counts as a decider}. The theorem rules out
a decider whose flip the substrate can itself represent. It says nothing about a decider
standing \emph{outside}, and an outside decider can exist for the very same property, correct on
every program. The line between inside and outside is the boundary of the sentence, and the boundary is
Richard's lesson: the language you talk about a system in is a different language from the one it
talks in.

\subsection{What this does to the book}

It does two things. It keeps me honest: nothing in what follows claims that a system with a
record can check its own shortcuts on autopilot, because that's a wall, the same wall, and I
showed you the bricks. And it tells you what a record \emph{can} do, which is the thing Part~II
has been about since the counter: it can carry a shortcut \emph{with its receipt}, so that the question
``was this earned'' is answered by an event you can point at. No decider has to exist for that,
which is lucky, because on a system with a recursion theorem no inside one can. The
diagonal says such a system can't automate the judgement from inside, for any behavioural property with a yes and a no. The latch
says you can record the commitment. Those are different jobs, and a record does the second.

The diagonal has a famous cousin that looks as if it ought to bite a record too, so let me walk
right up to it. Gödel's second theorem says a consistent system strong enough for arithmetic can't
prove its own consistency, and Martin Löb, a logician answering another logician's question, sharpened that in 1955: if such a system proves ``if this
is provable, it's true,'' it already proves the thing itself. So can a record vouch for itself, and
does Löb stop it? My first guess was that Löb stops it, since a record looked like a system talking about itself.
I landed somewhere else, and mostly it's a relief. Hold two things side by
side: ``there's a receipt for this somewhere,'' and the receipt in your hand. Löb's theorem is
about \emph{provability}, the bare claim that some proof exists, the receipt somewhere. A raised Boolean flag is not, by itself, the receipt in your hand. From a
clean start the earned-history theorem says there was a passing check,
commitment and certification in that order. The flag does not identify
the claim or the steps, and it need not store a proof of the checked claim.
The native table and channel carry more information; exporting a proof
requires an interface that actually supplies one.

Sergei Artemov's distinction between implicit provability and explicit
proof terms is useful here, but neither a flag nor the word ``receipt''
turns one into the other. The guarantee in this book comes from an external
proof about the checker, the clean start and every permitted operation.
It is not an internal proof of the system's own consistency, and does not
evade Gödel's or Löb's hypotheses.

Push on that and it gives, because a receipt is only as good as whoever wrote it. Its trust rests
on the checker meaning what it says, and that gets settled once, from outside the machine.
That's where I chose to stop this machine's chain of reasons. Gödel's second theorem does not
forbid a machine from checking a proof about a checker. What it limits is a system's ability to prove \emph{its own} consistency, when the system
is strong enough to do arithmetic and its axioms can be listed by a machine. Eliezer Yudkowsky and Marcello Herreshoff's 2013 draft on agents that trust their
own rewrites describes a related problem, the Löbian obstacle: how an agent can justify
trust in a successor's proofs. That's a cousin of this question, and it doesn't settle it, and it doesn't make
my design the only one possible. So I didn't get rid of the receipt somewhere. I moved it out of the
machine and handed it to whoever reads the record.

One more thing follows from the same picture, by a short argument. Can a record rest on itself, the way the sentence ``this
sentence is certified'' would like to? It can't if it's earned and permanent. The check behind the certificate that put the record up happened while the record was still down, because the record goes up only after that check passes, and once up it never comes back down, so it goes up only once. So no claim whose truth needs the record already up can be the claim the record went up on. (A later certificate, with the record already up, can stand on such a claim; it raises nothing.) Saul Kripke's 1975 theory of truth calls a sentence like
that, one that only ever leans on itself, ungrounded, and earned records are grounded in his
sense: every one bottoms out in a check that didn't lean on it. Caspar Oesterheld's 2019 work on
programs that cooperate by simulating each other needed a grounding step of the same kind to stop
an infinite regress. I haven't written this argument out anywhere else; the claim is exactly what this
paragraph says, and it's short enough to check by hand.

I want to draw one last distinction, because the two are easy to conflate and conflating them is the
easiest way to misread this book. There's a \emph{second} wall, nothing to do with the diagonal.
It's Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s kind of wall, a window with a colliding pair in it. Two states that differ in their
certification reading can look identical through a window that doesn't show that reading,
the stamp inside the closed drawer and the drawer opened and shut, and then no function of
the window recovers the reading (Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre}: a decoder has to give one answer on
everything the window lumps together). This wall comes from missing information. Nothing about it is undecidable; it holds for finite things with
nothing to compute; and it sits \emph{beside} Rice. None of Rice is underneath it. The property the diagonal uses (any behavioural property of programs with a yes and
a no) is a different kind of thing from the reading the window hides, and nothing here says
the two are the same. So there are two walls, on two different axes. The diagonal is about what no inside procedure can
decide. The window is about what no outside observer can see. I'll need both, and I'll try
not to call one by the other's name again. The machine I build later has a colliding pair of
exactly that kind (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-separation}).

\part{Established}
\clearpage

Part~III is step four, the sharpest case. A record that a claim was checked and closed is a
distinction that stays, so it pays what Part~I found keeping takes, and it's the case where you can point at the
kept 0 and at what it cost. It starts with what \emph{established} means, and why two computers
with the same bits can differ in it. Then it builds the smallest example I could find that meets the definition: a record with two
places, a flag that is the blank cell, over a flat part of two counters and a line number, six
kinds of instruction in all. Read through a window on the line and the two counters, it's a flat
case, a computer, run by its moves for the instructions and blind to the record and the ledger. The
step that raises the flag is the write of a 0, a merge in the record's part of the state, and that's why it's
charged; the order the step enforces, check, then commit, then certify, is what makes this
record's raise mean a claim held. That's what I mean by certification, and it's the layer this part adds to the bar
Part~II set. Then how far the example reaches, the real systems that already put a price on a write,
the thesis about which kept distinction is worth paying for, and what the example's counter has to do
with heat. Those claims are about the model; the example is where you can check them line by line. The flat part's own steps merge too (counting a counter down lands two states on
one), and their physical costs depend on the implementation; the ledger leaves them alone.

%===========================================================================
\section{What established means}
\label{sec:established}
%===========================================================================

Parts~I and~II were about any kept distinction at all. This chapter picks one: the distinction
between an answer that was checked and the same answer that wasn't. It's the case the first pages of
the book called the sharpest, and it's sharp because the two answers are the same bits, and everything that differs
is in what was kept.

\subsection{Two computers that end up the same}

You met these two computers in one paragraph at the start of the book. Now I'll take them slowly:
what an ordinary computer does about what Part~I found keeping takes, and why that matters to anybody who isn't a
physicist.

Put two computers on a table. Hand each of them the same list of a thousand numbers.

The first one sorts it. It compares, swaps, walks the list again and again until nothing is out of
order. Then it does one more thing: it walks the whole list front to back and checks that every
number is no bigger than the one after it. That check could have failed. It passes. Then it tidies
up after itself, wipes its scratch work, and leaves the sorted list in memory. (That check compares
neighbours, so what it settles is that the output is in order. That the output holds your
thousand numbers and no others is a second claim, and it would take a second check comparing the
output with the input. When I say sorted below, I mean in order.)

The second one never looks at your list. Somebody typed the sorted version into it earlier, same
thousand numbers, same order, and it puts them in memory.

Now wait until both are done and read the retained digital state we have
chosen to compare: the list, the working registers and the control position.
Arrange for both programs to finish at the same control point and clear the
scratch fields. Those endpoints can agree. The first compared the entries
and checked their order. The second loaded the same answer without doing
either. Wheel the boxes out, swap them and bring them back. From those fields
alone, neither of us can tell which run happened.

That is a construction with a specified observation. It does not establish
that every microscopic state of two physical computers agrees: the room,
heat, clocks or retained logs may carry other evidence. And ordinary computers
can keep a checked flag or a protected log. These two programs were arranged
to erase the distinction from the fields being read. That choice, and what
it prevents the next reader from answering, is the example.

Who cares? Anybody who's been handed a sheet that says ``all tests passed.'' Anybody who's looked at
an inspection sticker on a windshield: the sticker looks the same whether somebody checked the
brakes or somebody sold the sticker. An audit, a proof, a ledger, an AI that sounds very sure of
itself: every one of them is a pile of bits that could have come out of either computer, and the
question that matters is the one the bits can't answer. Did something establish this, or did it just
print it? I'll come back to every one of those later in this chapter and say which of them this
book actually helps with, and I'll warn you now that it's fewer than you'd hope.

I'm going to call the first run's relation to that answer \emph{established}: it
checked the order of this list. The second run has the answer without that relation.
The list's order is there either way. What can a machine keep of the difference
between the runs? The rest of this chapter takes that question apart.

It belongs in a book about a 0 because a record that the check ran would be a distinction that
stays, a 0 in some cell that says ``checked.'' These two computers did not keep that
record. A machine that does keep it gives you something more to inspect.

\subsection{Look harder}

The obvious answer is: just look harder. Don't look at the end, look at everything. So make the
computers as lookable as computers get. Scale them up to the size of a warehouse, every wire a
lamp that's lit or dark, every switch something you can walk up to and touch. Nothing is hidden in a
chip too small to see. Put both of them side by side and walk the floor.

While they run, sure, you'd see the difference. One has a whole wing lighting up, comparing and
swapping, and the other just copies. But they finish, and the comparing wing goes dark. Now walk the
floor and look at every single lamp. The sorted list is spelled out in lit and dark lamps in both,
the same pattern, and everything else is dark in both, because both cleaned up.

There is no lamp anywhere that says ``a check ran here and passed.'' It isn't hidden, and it isn't encrypted; it just
isn't there. You can see every retained digital field in this drawing, and none records the earlier check. Looking harder doesn't help, because the problem isn't that you can't see enough. It's that
nothing was kept.

The shape I want you to carry through the rest is that the problem was never visibility; it's keeping.

\subsection{So keep the trace}

Then the fix is obvious, isn't it? Don't let the run go. Keep the trace: every comparison, every
swap, the check and its answer, written down as it happens. Wheel the computers out on the cart and
back, read the traces, and you'll know which one sorted. Problem solved?

It's the right instinct, and it gets most of the way to this book. But take it apart, because
``just keep the trace'' has three things wrong with it, and each one is a piece of
what comes later.

First, a trace is bits, and bits can be typed in. Whoever typed the sorted list into the second
machine can type a trace in too: ``compared, swapped, checked, passed,'' a few thousand lines of
it, every one of them plausible. A trace written by a program is something the program produced,
unless some enforced rule constrains how the program can write that log. So keeping the trace doesn't
answer the question; it moves it. Did something establish this trace, or did it just print it?

Second, the way out of that is to take the pen away from the program. Don't let the program write
its own trace. Have something underneath it write the trace, one step at a time, as the steps
actually happen, so nothing a program does can add a line that didn't happen or erase one that
did. Airplanes do a version of this. Flight recorders go back to a prototype David Warren built in
Melbourne in the 1950s. He was an Australian scientist at the Aeronautical Research Laboratories,
working on jet fuel, and after a string of unexplained airliner crashes he wanted a box that would
hold the instrument readings and the voices in the cockpit for whoever came looking afterwards; I
know his story from museum and encyclopedia accounts, and I haven't read his own report. The
recorders that came out of that idea preserve instrument data and cockpit sound.
The sound can include a person's account, correct or mistaken. A recorded
sensor reading can also be wrong about the aircraft. What the recording
supplies is evidence of what those channels carried, subject to the recorder
and sensors working as specified. Crash protection helps that evidence survive. The flight recorder has the right shape, and that shape isn't mine. Later in
this chapter it gets its name from computer security, a reference monitor, and I'll say outright
that a machine built that way would be doing what this book describes. What the book adds is
narrower than a rulebook for everything underneath. It's about the records that go up and never
come back down: what that something has to keep for good, and what keeping it takes.

Third, a fixed memory cannot retain every possible history of unbounded
length with exact recovery. Give the run one independent yes-or-no choice per
tick: after $n$ ticks there are $2^n$ histories to distinguish. A fixed number
of bits eventually runs out. A completed finite trace can fit, and a predictable
trace can compress. The obstruction needs unbounded independent possibilities,
not just the word ``trace.''

Flight recorders make a practical choice about the history to retain. A voice
recorder loops, replacing older sound when its capacity is reached. Thirty
minutes, two hours and twenty-five hours are different retention windows;
the applicable requirement depends on the aircraft and rule. The FAA's
\href{https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-02-02/pdf/2026-02110.pdf}{2026 final rule}
extends twenty-five-hour recording to specified newly manufactured aircraft.
Whatever window is chosen, it is a window. It does not imply that no other
machine can store an entire finite run.

The fingerprint is the sharpest reply, so take it seriously. Fold every new line of the trace
into a fixed-size scramble of everything before it, and you've got a hash chain. The timestamps of
Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta, two cryptographers at Bellcore whose story comes later in this
chapter, work that way; so do the audit logs the cryptographers Bruce Schneier
and John Kelsey designed in 1999; and so do the measurement registers in the security chip a lot
of computers carry, the TPM. For the PCRs and lifecycle under discussion, an extend folds a measurement
into the previous value. Reset permissions depend on the register, platform
and locality; some PCRs are resettable during operation. A claim about an
unbroken history must specify which resets and writers its policy permits. That really does keep something about the whole trace in a few dozen bytes. But look at
what it keeps: it keeps a binding, and the content isn't in it. To read the history you still need the trace
stored somewhere, and the fingerprint only tells you whether a copy somebody hands you is the one
that went in. The binding holds only because nobody knows how to find two traces with the same
fingerprint, which is a bet on how hard a search is. No law of nature backs it. That part isn't only my opinion.
The computer scientists Moni Naor and Guy Rothblum proved a sharp version of it in 2005, and they even call the thing a
fingerprint: keep a small private fingerprint of a big file somebody else stores, check the file
by reading only a little of it, and against an opponent with unlimited computing the size of the
fingerprint times the amount you read has to be on the order of the whole file. Do even slightly
better than that against an opponent with limited computing, and you've shown that one-way
functions exist, which is the hardness bet in its barest form. Their setting is a stored file. A
growing trace is a different setting, but it's the same bet, with its terms written down. And squeezing traces that keep
growing into a fixed number of bits has to land many traces on one fingerprint, and that's a merge, hidden behind how hard it is to find which traces land on the same fingerprint. It's the
same merge as in the example of Part~I (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}) where four people have to sit in three chairs. Fingerprints are great, but they're not a way out of forgetting; they're a very clever way of
forgetting.

So the real question was never ``save everything.'' The real question is:
what's the smallest thing worth keeping for good, and what does keeping it take? The answer this
book ends up with is the commitment, in the database's sense, a question closed, and the trace
drops away. (The cryptographer's sealed envelope also goes by the name commitment. It's a different
thing, and both come up later.) What's kept for good isn't every comparison the sort made, just the
one fact that a check of this very claim passed and the question got closed. And the part
that matters most is that keeping even that one fact for good takes something on every machine. It's paid by
forgetting something somewhere else or by taking fresh states the machine never gets back, and on a
finite machine the fresh states run out, so it's the forgetting. That's Part~I's counting of states again, and Part~I
counted the fresh states.

So the premise was never that computers can't keep records. They keep records all day. It's that
nothing in the rules of an ordinary computer makes the record paid for, permanent, or earned, and
those three come in at different places, so I'll say where. Paid for is the model's one rule: in the
Thiele Machine, the step that raises the record has to cost something. Permanent is a premise, the
one Part~I's counting of states needs, and one of the conditions Part~II puts on a record. Earned, meaning a check
of this very claim passed first, isn't in the model's core at all. It's what the step of the small
machine in the next chapter enforces, proved for that machine and every program on it run from a clean start. One more word rides
along with permanent, and it'll come up when I line my record up against other people's: dated. A
record that goes up and stays up went up at one particular step of the run and not another,
even though the record doesn't write down which step. So dated, in this book, means it has a
place in the run's history. Carrying a timestamp is something else, and my record doesn't do it. A machine that charges one for every step it takes meets the first rule, and the charging does
nothing toward
the others, and I'll keep pointing that out.


\subsection{Computed, stored, established}

Three words get used like they're one.

\emph{Computed} is about the steps. The first machine computed the sorted list. The second didn't.

\emph{Stored} is about the bits. Both machines stored it.

\emph{Established} is neither, and that's the whole problem. It isn't the steps, because they're gone. It
isn't the bits, because they're identical. It's something like this: the first machine has a right
to lean on ``this list is sorted,'' because it ran a test that could have failed, the test passed, the
test was about this very list, and then the question got closed. The second machine has the same
sentence and no right to it. That's a true fact about the two of them, and it's written down
nowhere, in either one. (Whose right, strictly? A machine doesn't lean on anything, any more than a
filing cabinet does. It's the right of whoever reads the first machine to lean on what it says, and
the machine is where the grounds for that right would have to be kept. ``The machine has a right''
is shorter, so I'll keep saying it, and now you know what it's short for.)

I'll hold four words still from here on. A \emph{check} is the test, the thing that could say no. A
\emph{commit} is the closing, the question shut for good, about that edition of that thing. The
\emph{record} is whatever stays behind to say so. And \emph{established}, in the sense a machine can
carry, is all three, about one thing. The first machine had the check and the closing and kept no
record of either, which is the problem above. Where the closing and the record are one act, as in a
database's commit, writing the record is the closing. The small machine keeps them apart, a
commitment the next one replaces and a certificate that stays. The book cashes this working sense at three depths: a paid closing in the bare model; an
object with a checked relation and a paid event, in Part~II (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}); and the
whole chain on the small machine, in the next chapter. Each place says which one it means.

That raises a fair question: what if the second machine, handed the typed-in list, runs the check
on it? Then it has what the first machine had, and if it closes the question and keeps the record,
it has established that the list is sorted. It didn't do the sorting and it
doesn't need to. The line I'm drawing is between checked and unchecked. Whether the list was
computed or copied doesn't enter into it, and ``without doing either'' up there was about the copier that never looked. So whatever this
book ends up counting, it isn't how hard anybody worked.

People say ``a right to lean on it'' about a lot of things that turn out to be vibes, so I had to find
out whether this one was anything. I went looking, and I'll go through what I ran into.

\subsection{The clerk who forgets everything}

The picture of a computer I used in Section~\ref{sec:structure} is a person with a pencil, a
strip of paper and a short list of rules. So I went back to the source, Alan Turing's 1936 paper, to see how far he actually
takes it.

He takes it a long way. Back then a ``computer'' was a job, a human doing sums by hand, and Turing
modelled that person. He's careful with the person's mind: whatever the clerk knows, beyond a
handful of states, has to go down on the paper. Then he goes all the way. He imagines the clerk
getting up, walking off, forgetting everything, and coming back later. To pick up where he left
off, the clerk leaves himself ``a note of instructions,'' and Turing says that note \emph{is} the clerk's
state of mind, as far as the computation is concerned. Marks on paper and a note are the whole
state.

My two computers are sitting right inside that. Suppose the clerk didn't write the note. Somebody
slipped it under the door, in the right form, with the right instructions. He comes back, reads it,
carries on, and every mark he makes from then on is exactly what he'd have made if he'd written it
himself. Turing's model can't tell the clerk who did the work from the clerk who was handed a note
saying he did. It was never asked to. Turing wanted something you could check without crawling into
anybody's head, and a note on a desk is about as checkable as it gets. That's why the paper still
works ninety years later. The chosen note omits its provenance. A Turing machine can retain additional provenance fields, and its transition rules can restrict how those fields are written. The omission belongs to this note, not to the reach of the model.

So the founding picture of computing is a man who leaves his desk, forgets everything he was doing,
and trusts a sticky note. I relate to him deeply.

And now the question nobody needs answered to follow the argument, which is exactly the kind I
can't leave alone: who were those clerks? They were real people. In the late 1800s the Harvard Observatory hired rooms full of women to
do the arithmetic of the sky, cataloguing stars by hand for a fraction of a man's wage, and some of
them made discoveries of their own, Henrietta Leavitt's way of telling how far away a star is among
them. (I took the wages and the discoveries from Dava Sobel's history of those women, and from the
historians at the American Institute of Physics, who put the men's hourly pay at nearly five times
the women's.) Rooms like that ran artillery tables in both world wars; that part I took from David Alan Grier's history of human computers. So when Turing modelled ``the computer,'' he was modelling somebody's actual
afternoon. That doesn't change the argument a bit. It changes the picture, though, for me anyway: the
sticky note was always a person trusting another person's work, and the question of whether the
work behind it was really done is older than any machine.

\subsection{Information doesn't have it either}

My next guess was information: one machine got some, the other didn't. That one died fast. Claude
Shannon, who turned information into a number in 1948, says on his first page that the meaning of a
message is ``irrelevant to the engineering problem.'' His entropy depends on the probabilities of the possible messages. With an
even spread it is the logarithm of their number; with an uneven spread the
number alone is not enough. Fix the same distribution and the same message
and the information assigned to that message agrees for both computers.
That calculation has not included which history produced it.
He'd give them the same number if one of them got hit by lightning and came out right by luck.

Fine, forget the set and look at the one message. In the 1960s three people, separately, worked
out how to measure the information in one string: Ray Solomonoff, an American who was after a theory
of guessing what comes next from what came before; Andrei Kolmogorov, the great Soviet mathematician; and Gregory Chaitin, an Argentine-American mathematician who later worked at IBM. Their measure is
the length of the shortest program that prints the string. The same two computers hold the same string and get the same number. And
then there's the thing in that theory I keep going back to and standing on, to see if it creaks.
Running a program can't add this kind of information. What comes out can't hold more than what went
in plus the program, give or take a little. Leonid Levin, who studied under Kolmogorov in Moscow and
later left the Soviet Union to teach at Boston University, proved a general version of this, and he has
a one-liner for it that's too good not to repeat: you can torture an uninformed witness all you
want, you won't get information about the crime.

The bound says that an effective sorting procedure does not create
unbounded algorithmic description complexity from that input. It does not
say that sorting tells a person nothing. A person with limited time may now
see the smallest entry immediately. Description length, useful access and
a record that a particular check ran answer different questions.

Logic says the same thing in a different coat. The standard logic of knowing, the
one the Finnish philosopher Jaakko Hintikka worked out in 1962, has a property people call logical omniscience: if you know
some facts, you automatically know everything that follows from them. So by that logic, once you
knew every number on your list, you already knew whether it was sorted. Hintikka flagged the problem
himself, in the same book, and people have been trying to fix it since. The fixes read like a pile
until I asked each one the same thing: when it lets you write \emph{known} next to ``sorted,'' what
does it make you write in the margin? Hintikka's margin is empty. Each fix writes one thing there.

The fix that comes closest to me is from 1995, by Sergei Artemov, a logician at the City University of New York
who studied under that same Kolmogorov (the 1995 report came out of Cornell). He wanted a logic that could
name the proof itself. What I think he's saying: you only get to know a thing if you've built an actual
justification for it, and the justification rides along with the claim. That's a reason traveling with the claim, which is almost a record, but only almost, because it's a way of writing things down and reasoning about them, and nothing in his margin says the reason was ever run, or when.
People have taught it to count, too: Ho Ngoc Duc, a logician at Leipzig, in 1997, made knowing
take reasoning steps, and Artemov and Roman Kuznets, a logician then at Bern, in 2014, asked how big a justification can get before knowing by it
stops being feasible (Part~II weighed both properly, in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}). I took those for rivals at first. As I read them now, Duc counts the
steps the knower takes and Artemov and Kuznets weigh what you'd hand somebody to check it, one
distance from two ends. It has a computational side, too: Francisco Bavera and Eduardo Bonelli, two Argentine computer
scientists who work on what programming languages mean, in 2018 turned justification logic into a lambda calculus whose terms carry, and can inspect, the
history of the computation that made them, and Samuel Bucheli, Meghdad Ghari and Thomas Studer, three logicians, Studer the head of the logic group at Bern, put justifications on a time line in 2017, where they persist and change.

Line that up against the margin this book wants: earned, paid for, permanent, dated. Artemov's
reason is nearly earned, the steps and the sizes are prices, the time line is a date. Their
time line keeps its dates. Mine is dated only in the execution history: the raise happened at a
definite step, and the record doesn't keep the step number. What none of it has
is the closing of a question as a step with a price. Their prices are on reasoning, and the Bern
justifications change, the one thing a closed question doesn't do. Push on mine, though, and it gives twice. Artemov's margin holds the reason itself, and mine only
says a check passed. And their prices grow with how hard the thing was to know. This book charges the
step that raises the record, and how long the checking took never enters it, so for a measure of
effort, read theirs.

So the two most careful accounts I could find, one about bits and one about knowing, say the same
thing: the sort added nothing.

And yet you know something after the sort that you didn't before. You can read the smallest number
off the first slot. You can stop worrying. Something happened, and that's the clue, the first
solid thing I've got: whatever
\emph{established} is, it isn't new bits. It's the same bits, \emph{settled}: a question sorted into yes and no, with yes made to stay. It's the 0 again, about a claim.

\subsection{Statues that walk off}

If it isn't in the information, maybe it's in the knowing, so I went and read the philosophers.
And there it was again: people had been arguing about the difference between having the right
answer and knowing it for a couple thousand years.

Plato's version is a joke about statues. There was a story that the sculptor Daedalus made statues
so lifelike they'd walk off if you didn't tie them down. Plato says true opinions are like that:
they wander off, and they're not worth much until you tie them down with the reason why. Once
they're tied down, they're knowledge, and they stay put. Knowledge tied to a reason, and knowledge that stays: of everybody I'd have bet on to hand me that shape, Plato wasn't on the list.

Then in 1963 Edmund Gettier, whose trap Part~II played with cups (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}), broke the tidy version in three pages. Smith and Jones are up for the same job. Smith has good reason to think
Jones will get it, and he's counted the coins in Jones's pocket: ten. So Smith figures, with good reason, that
the man who'll get the job has ten coins in his pocket. Then Smith gets the job, and, unknown to
him, Smith also has ten coins in his pocket. Smith had a belief that was true and backed by a reason, and it still wasn't knowledge. He
was right by luck, because his reason was about the wrong pocket.

Gettier's case is the push that matters for a machine. Checking one pocket and committing to a claim about
another is right by luck. So whatever a machine commits to, the check underneath has to be about
\emph{this very claim}, and I'd better say exactly what that means, because it carries a lot of weight
later.

A check is about this very claim when four things hold. It tests the same property the commit names.
A cousin of that property won't do. It tests that property on the same thing the commit names, and
the thing next to it won't do either. Nothing has written to that thing between the check and the commit, so it's still the same
edition the check looked at. And the check is honest: it says yes when the property is true and no
when it isn't, on every value it could ever be handed, this one and all the others. Break the first three and
you're Smith with his ten coins. Break the fourth and the check is just a rubber stamp. The next
chapter builds a machine whose step won't let a commit through unless the first three hold, and whose
checks come with a proof of the fourth.

Two notes on those four, because they matter later. The fourth asks for more than it needs. To rule
out luck, a check only has to never say yes when the property is false; saying yes every time it's
true is a bonus. And the third is a very old bug in computing wearing Gettier's coat. Security people
call it time-of-check-to-time-of-use: check a file, use it, and something swaps the file in between
(Matt Bishop and Michael Dilger, two computer security researchers at the University of California,
Davis, wrote up how to hunt for it in 1996). Databases guard against the
same thing by making sure, just before a commit, that nothing they read has been written since;
H. T. Kung and John Robinson, two computer scientists at Carnegie-Mellon, called that optimistic concurrency control in 1981. A philosopher's
pocket and a sysadmin's race condition are the same bug. One limit, said now: a machine can only promise
``nothing has written to that thing'' about its own memory; for brake pads or a voter roll the
third condition becomes a premise about whoever measured (Section~\ref{sec:models}).

At this point I went further than this chapter needs, because the obvious next question is:
does anything fix Gettier? People tried for years. The first patch is ``no false steps in the
reasoning'': Smith's mistake was believing Jones would get the job, so rule that out. Then a
philosopher named Alvin Goldman came back with barns, and he credits the barns to Carl Ginet,
another philosopher working on what it takes to know something. You're driving
through a county that, unknown to you, is full of fake barns, just painted fronts propped up to look
like the real thing. You look at the one real barn in the county and think ``that's a barn.'' It's true, you believe it, you have a good
reason, your own eyes, and there's no false step anywhere. And still you were lucky: if you'd glanced at
the next one over you'd have believed the same thing and been wrong. Every patch gets a new barn,
and as far as I can tell the arguing hasn't stopped. That tells me something I'll keep: whether a
check was good isn't only about this one case. It's about what the check would have done on the
cases next door. Hold on to that, because it's the next section.

\subsection{What ``could have failed'' means}

I keep saying the first machine's test \emph{could have failed}. Take that apart, because it's the
piece everything else hangs off.

The machine is deterministic. Given your list, the check was always going to pass. So in what sense
could it have failed? By ``could have failed'' I mean this: hand the checking stage an out-of-order
candidate output and it says no. I do not mean hand the whole sorter an unsorted input; putting
that input in order is its job. The relevant counterfactual is a defective candidate reaching the
checker. An ordinary unsorted input reaching the sorter isn't it. Chance has nothing to do with
it. The copier that never checks has no corresponding rejection.
