shares that tape with the guest, any of that code can flip the bit without paying, because the
host's step has no opinion about it. So an ordinary programmable computer, as built, doesn't enforce the toll for its
programs; that comes from how it's built, and it could be built to enforce it. A host whose own
step mirrors the guest's bit and charges for its crossing enforces it, and the universal programs $U$
and $U_P$ are fixed tables that go one better: they earn their own flag, by their own check,
commit and certificate, exactly when the guest's would rise, and pay on their own ledger what the guest pays, $U$ exactly and $U_P$ to within
a surcharge of at most two when the guest's reading starts at no (Theorems~\ref{thm:u34-U-earned}, \ref{thm:u34-U-flag}, \ref{thm:u34-presented} and~\ref{thm:u34-presented-surcharge}). That's a statement
about which reading a step rule prices, not a claim that Turing machines can't price one.

Computing ran into this exact gap in hardware, and how it got out is worth the detour. In 1974
two computer scientists, Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg, asked when a machine can run guests, a whole operating system
inside another, efficiently and safely. Their answer is one sentence you could check against any
instruction set. Call an instruction \emph{sensitive} if it reads or changes the machine's own
settings, the things the host has to keep for itself, and \emph{privileged} if running it
outside the host's own mode makes the machine stop and hand control to the host, which is
called a trap. For the kind of machine they modelled: if every sensitive instruction is
privileged, a host can be built. The guest runs at full speed, and whenever it touches
something that matters, the machine itself stops it and lets the host decide, and a host like that
is one whose step has an opinion.

Then the obvious next question: did the machines people actually bought pass the test? The most
common one didn't. In 2000 John Scott Robin, an Air Force officer, and Cynthia Irvine, a
computer-security researcher at the Naval Postgraduate School, went through every instruction
of Intel's Pentium and found seventeen that are sensitive and not privileged; POPF, which loads
the processor's flags, is the one usually pointed at. A guest could run them and the host would
never hear about it. The fixes came two ways: VMware rewrote the guest's code on the fly so the
troublesome instructions never ran as written, and in the middle of the 2000s Intel and AMD
added hardware support so they'd trap. Does that change anything here? It doesn't change the theorems. Popek
and Goldberg were after speed and isolation. A record and a price weren't their question, so their result isn't
mine and mine isn't theirs. It changes the picture, though. The universal programs sit where
they'd want a host to sit: the host's own steps collect each guest's toll and earn each guest's
record again. And an industry learned the same lesson the expensive way: a rule binds the guest
only if it lives in the step underneath.

The smallest version of ``a ledger beside an ordinary machine'' is a Turing machine
configuration with a counter next to it, where each step adds one, plus one more if it writes
a nonblank symbol. The counter doesn't disturb the machine.

\begin{theorem}[A counter beside a Turing machine changes nothing]\label{thm:u19-tm-lift}
Let a Turing machine with transition table $\delta$ step a configuration $c$ to
$\mathrm{tm}_n(\delta, c)$ after at most $n$ steps (stopping when $\delta$ has no entry). Pair
each configuration with a counter, and step the pair by stepping the configuration and adding
the step's charge. Then for every $n$, $\delta$ and pair $(c, m)$, the configuration part
after at most $n$ steps of the pair is $\mathrm{tm}_n(\delta, c)$. In particular this holds
from $(c, 0)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put the ordinary run and the run with the counter side by side. Both start
with configuration $c$. Whenever their configurations agree, they look up the
same entry in the same transition table. If the entry is absent, both stop.
If it is present, both take the same next configuration; only the paired run
also changes its counter. Their configurations therefore agree again, ready
for the next comparison. This covers every step up to the chosen limit $n$,
as well as a stop before that limit. The counter's value never enters a lookup.
\end{proof}

The pair is a Turing configuration with a number riding beside it, and nothing more. Its counter
is kept in the state, and a ledger kept in the state isn't a price on the move:
Definition~\ref{def:certsys} puts the cost on the move's name, and this counter's charge depends
on what the step writes. This theorem therefore does not supply exact accounting for the basic
instruction-price signature, or a reading with an earned-history meaning.
It does not rule out equipping the same state space with other instruction
prices and a Boolean reading satisfying the basic toll. The projection
claim is simply that this additional count leaves the tape computation alone.

One limit on all of this needs saying, so it isn't read as more. Certification is one event. If you wanted
a machine to carry some other kind of reading, you'd need an event for it, evidence for it and
a price law for it, and nothing here supplies any of those.

\subsection{The small machine's merges}

And the whole small machine isn't the eight-state piece it runs. It merges some states without
adding anything to the ledger.

\begin{theorem}[The small machine's merges]\label{thm:frag-merge-split}
(1) A move of the small machine that takes the flag from down to up is CERTIFY; CERTIFY merges two
different full states into one (a state with the flag down and the same state with the flag up land
on the same state), and it costs at least one. (2) DEC $A$ 2 also merges two different full states,
and it costs nothing. So it is false of the small machine that every move that merges is priced.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Only CERTIFY changes the flag, and it costs one. The two states with the flag down and up, and
a committed claim, are the same state after CERTIFY. (2) Take a core at line 1 with $A$ at 1 at
version 0, and the same core with $A$ at 0 at version 1. DEC $A$ 2 takes the first to $A = 0$ at
version 1, line 2, a write; it takes the second to line 2 with $A$ still 0 at version 1, because
DEC on zero is no write. Same state, zero cost.
\end{proof}

The theorem puts names to the last item on the list of what this machine doesn't do, near the end
of this chapter. Part~I's counting of states wants a finite machine that puts a price on every merge. This
machine has counters with no top, and it prices the three record acts and leaves its counting
merges at a price of zero, so Part~I's counting of states doesn't reach it whole, and that's why the eight-state piece
is a piece. The record's part of the state closes the rest: asked only of merges between states with the same
line and counters, the merge premise holds for this machine's own prices and forces the toll on
it with no finiteness premise (Theorem~\ref{thm:record-merge-toll}).

\subsection{Reading the instruction rules}

The instruction rules settle some concrete questions about running this machine. Follow
them through a check, a zero decrement and a trapped trace.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{The check price is flat.} CHECK costs 1 whether it's asking ``is this 0'' or ``is this at
least a billion.'' The property language is fixed and each property is one evaluation, so
``pays for its work'' here means that flat price, the same however hard the
question was. A machine that charged by the difficulty of the check would be a different
machine, and I haven't built it.
\item \textbf{DEC on zero isn't a write.} It doesn't change the counter, so it doesn't change the
version. That's the right call for versions (nothing changed), but it means DEC on zero is
a way to move the line number that adds nothing to the ledger and leaves no trace in the record. The idle run in the
subsection on the window, earlier in this chapter, uses exactly that.
\item \textbf{After a trap, a trace still pays.} On programs, a trap stops the run. On arbitrary
traces, instructions after a trap are each charged their cost and none of them changes the
core. That isn't a separate choice. A price belongs to the instruction, the same from every state
(Definition~\ref{def:certsys}), so a CERTIFY on a trapped machine costs what every CERTIFY costs, and
the ledger adds it; Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}
has no exceptions for that reason. The choice is one level up, in putting the price on the instruction and
not on the instruction at a state, and what it brings with it is that a trapped
machine is still charged for instructions that change nothing.
\item \textbf{``Checked'' means what the property language can say.} On this machine that's \emph{is
zero}, \emph{is even} and \emph{is at least $n$}, and a live fact means one of those holds of one counter's
current value. It doesn't mean the program is correct, or that anything follows from the
property, or that the property was worth checking. So can a proved machine of this kind check
``sorted,'' the claim the sorter-and-copier table of Section~\ref{sec:established} runs on? It can, through an encoding. A copy of
this machine, instruction for instruction, with its property language left open, has provenance,
checker soundness, no forging and the floor of three proved once for every property language that
comes with an exact equality test and a checker proved equal to its meaning. Give it ``the list
this counter encodes is sorted'' as a property and it certifies a sorted list for three and
refuses an unsorted one forever. The instruction rules are those already given, with the chosen property language in place
of the three original properties. For sorted lists, decode 0 as the empty list and
$2^h(2t+1)$ as the list with head $h$ and tail decoded from $t$.
Every positive code has $t$ smaller than itself, so decoding terminates. The checker
returns yes on an empty list or singleton, and on $a,b,\ldots$ exactly when $a\le b$
and it returns yes on $b,\ldots$. Induction on the list proves that this is exactly
adjacent nondecreasing order. The provenance proof uses only equality of properties, and soundness only that the checker's yes means the property holds, so the same instruction-by-instruction argument applies. What makes that a check of
the list is the proof that the checker means sortedness. Without that proof, ``sorted'' would be a number
some unconstrained code wrote into a counter, and the record would be honest about the counter
and silent about the list.
\item \textbf{The certificate is historical.} Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY, the counter can
change, and the flag still goes up. The flag says a claim was checked and committed about
an edition. It says nothing about whether the claim is still true.
\item \textbf{One latch, and a channel that moves on.} The flag records that an earned chain
happened, once. After that it stays up, and later CERTIFYs change nothing. The channel is the
part that names a fact: with the flag up from a clean start, it names a fact that some earlier
passing COMMIT committed. But a later commitment replaces it, so at the end
it names the last earned commitment, which needn't be the one the flag rose on. Two runs from
$\mathrm{start}(0, 0)$ show it, worked from the instruction table. First run: CHECK \emph{is zero}
$A$; CHECK \emph{is zero} $B$; COMMIT \emph{is zero} $A$; CERTIFY; COMMIT \emph{is zero} $B$.
Second run: the same five instructions with the last two swapped, so COMMIT \emph{is zero} $B$
comes before CERTIFY. Both end in the same state: both counters 0 at version 0, both facts in the
table, the channel holding (\emph{zero}, $B$, 0), the trap down, a ledger of five and the flag
up. In the first run the flag rose at step four, on the commitment about $A$. In the second it
rose at step five, on the commitment about $B$. So the flag is an ever-certified latch: it says
an earned chain happened at some step, and the end state doesn't say which claim or which step.
A receipt naming the claim the flag first rose on would need that claim kept where nothing can
overwrite it; a receipt with a time on it would also need the step number kept; and several
certifications that each last would need a record richer than one flag. The publication file constructed earlier in this chapter keeps the set of
claims certified at least once. That extension shows exactly what the native
state left out. It still does not record which certification came first or
at what step; those questions would need their own retained answers.
\item \textbf{Sixteen checks per run, ever.} Facts never leave and the table holds sixteen, so a run
gets at most sixteen passing CHECKs in its whole life, and the seventeenth traps. A
certificate needs only one, so this costs nothing for the theorems, but it's a hard wall
for any program that wants to keep checking forever, and it's this machine's small version of
``you can't keep all of it'' from Section~\ref{sec:established}. A CHECK that repeats a claim already in the
table, same property, same counter, same edition, passes again and takes another entry. So the
wall is sixteen passing CHECKs, and sixteen different claims is a different count. Removing
duplicates, evicting old facts or collecting dead ones would each be a different design, and each
would need its own invariants proved.
\item \textbf{The clean start matters.} Provenance, soundness, no forging and the price of three are
all stated from a clean start. Hand the machine a table pre-loaded with facts nobody
checked, and of course none of that follows. The theorems are about what the machine
produces. What you smuggle in at the door is outside them. The door is narrower than clean for some of them: a commitment's provenance and checker soundness use only the table, and hold from any start whose table holds nothing but facts about older editions; the empty channel and the lowered flag come in for the flag's provenance and the price of three. Spell the door out once: the theorems
cover any list of instructions anybody can issue, from a clean start, on a step that runs as
written, with nothing else writing to the machine. They say nothing about whoever sets or
restores the start, about a reset, about a device that misbehaves, or about whoever carries the
flag's value to you.
\item \textbf{The universal programs have stated guests.} $U$ (Appendix~\ref{sec:universal-host}) runs every one of this machine's
programs from every clean start $\mathrm{start}(x, y)$, with halting, answers, flag and ledger matched (the flag over the whole run, the ledger at matching points). $U_P$ (Appendix~\ref{sec:presented-universal}) runs every
computably presented Thiele machine, with its reading decided by a program, its record carried as
a latch, and its ledger matched to within a surcharge of at most two when its reading starts at
no, and of three when it starts at yes. When the guest certifies with a ledger below three, no program on
that host, run from a clean start, matches its ledger exactly. A
machine outside that class, with a reading no program decides, isn't covered by either. The
host with a guest step built in, charging one per guest step whatever the step was, would have a
ledger at least the guest's and usually more; $U$'s is exact, and $U_P$'s is exact up to the
surcharge.
\item \textbf{Encoding and running time.} The universality result takes its inputs already
packed into the counters. Getting there from an arbitrary Turing machine goes through
Minsky's exponential packing, and that packing is
what it takes to reach two counters this way. Anyone who wanted this to run fast would have to
start the analysis over.
\item \textbf{The step charges for the act, not for what the claim is worth.} CHECK \emph{at
least 0} passes on every value, so CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY on it raises the flag for three from
any fresh loaded start (the note after Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-tight}), and that's by design. The
step checks order, aboutness and an honest checker. What a claim is worth is the entitlement
count of Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}, a number computed over the rivals a run narrows. A
step sees one state, so it cannot compute that count. A check that cannot fail narrows nothing
and costs three, and the book keeps both numbers, apart.
\item \textbf{The toll on this machine comes from the record's part of the state, with no finiteness premise on the whole machine.}
Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s counting of states forces a toll on a finite machine that prices
every merge. This machine is neither. Its counters have no ceiling, as a machine that runs every program has to have, and its editions can't have one either (the version rule says why), so it's infinite. And, by design, its unpriced instructions merge states: take a core at line $\ell$ with $c$ at 1 and version
$w$, and a core at line $j - 1$ with $c$ at 0 and version $w + 1$, everything else alike, and
DEC $c$ $j$ sends both to line $j$ with $c$ at 0 and version $w + 1$, at a price of zero. A price of zero
doesn't mean the hardware pays nothing. Any physical heat belongs to the implementation's account. A positive floor
requires the thermal premises and an input distribution with entropy loss;
merely taking a step establishes neither. This ledger does not measure that heat. The
ledger leaves those merges out on purpose. It counts the keeping in the record, not what computing
spends. Computing doesn't have to merge; a reversible base computes by paying in fresh states. On this machine
full merge pricing would charge DEC, an ordinary step, and clause (c) asks for computing to cost
nothing. Charging every move would instead give a clock's schedule. Its total counts moves, rather than isolating
record acts. The machine can still retain a record; this total alone does not
say which acts established it. So
merge pricing on this machine applies to the record's part of the state only: a move that sends two different
states with the same line and counters to one state costs at least one. This machine's own prices
meet it. The endless counters would allow a raise that merges nothing, and the flag
doesn't take it: CERTIFY lands a state with the flag down and the same state with the flag up on
one state, a merge of exactly that kind, in plain view. So every price list that meets the premise charges the flag-raising step at least one, with no finiteness premise, and through the trap it charges every CHECK and COMMIT at least one too, so a certificate from a clean start costs at least three on every such list (Theorem~\ref{thm:record-merge-toll}). That's a price I assume for losing distinctions in the
record, and assuming it is all it is. Turning it into heat takes the physical conditions of
Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}; a unit on a ledger isn't heat on its own. The exact price of one, the least the premise allows on each of the three acts, is still a design choice.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{What this chapter adds up to}

So this chapter has one machine, and it isn't the model. It's a Thiele machine in the opening's sense,
a Thiele machine with the toll proved (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-instance}), and
its toll charges the blank cell's 0: raising its flag is a merge in the record's part of its state
(Theorem~\ref{thm:record-merge-toll}). Its flat part computes whatever a Turing machine can, under Minsky's
$2^n$ encoding, done outside the machine, its computing adds nothing to the ledger and can't touch
the record, and, from a clean start, its record is earned.

If you ever find yourself wondering whether a property of this machine is the model's or just the
machine's, hold it up against Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s definition of a Thiele machine, the latch of
Section~\ref{sec:latch}, and the four things certified asks for (Section~\ref{sec:layers}). What follows from those holds of
every machine that meets them; the rest (a table of sixteen facts, three properties) is this machine's choice. The flat price of one is the third of the four, and at least one of it is what the record's merge premise asks of each act on this machine. There are six instruction kinds, and a seventh, PAY, for a host that has to charge
somebody else's prices (Appendix~\ref{sec:presented-universal}). If the model needs more than the five parts and the toll, this is where it will show.

%===========================================================================
\section{How far it reaches}
\label{sec:reach}
%===========================================================================

The small machine earns its flag, and pays for it, on its own programs. Everything in this chapter
asks how far that carries. Every statement in it is proved, and the runs are reported as runs. I
give each statement here and leave the constructions to the appendices, because they're about the reach of the case, not the case.

\emph{Other machines as guests.} One fixed program, $U$, written in the small machine's own six kinds
of instruction on a host with more counters, runs every program of the small machine as a guest,
from every clean start. It fetches, decodes and carries out each guest instruction itself, the way
Turing's universal machine does; nothing in the host means ``run one guest step.'' It halts exactly
when its guest halts, with the guest's answer in its counters; its flag goes up during its run exactly when the
guest's goes up during the guest's, by its own check, its own commitment and its own certificate; and its ledger equals the
guest's at every point where the two runs match. The host is a certified Thiele machine, and whether $U$ halts
is undecidable. Add one move, PAY, that costs one and does nothing else, and the same kind of
program, $U_P$, runs every Thiele machine whose next move, step, prices and reading are computed by
programs that always answer: it halts when the guest's run stops, its flag goes up exactly when the
guest's reading is yes at some state of its run, on a chain whose check is the guest's own reading,
and its ledger is the guest's prices plus a surcharge of at most two at the raise when the guest's
reading starts at no, and exactly three when it starts at yes, a surcharge that no program on that host, run from a clean start, can always avoid. Appendix~\ref{sec:universal-machines} has both.

\emph{Other flat cases.} Lay the toll over a register machine, a Turing machine or the
lambda calculus and none of them computes one function more; what each gains is a record and a cost.
Each is the flat case with its price column put back (Section~\ref{sec:latch}).

\emph{Machines from parts.} Wired side by side, end to end, or one inside the other, a Thiele machine
stays a Thiele machine, and the tolls add the way money adds. What breaks, breaks for reasons you
could name in advance: a single flag for two claims costs two claims' worth, a clock is still a clock,
a shared value without a version can't be trusted, and a hand-off that costs nothing can't be allowed
to carry a certificate (Appendix~\ref{sec:parts}).

%===========================================================================
\section{Five small models}
\label{sec:models}
%===========================================================================

So far there's been a toll, a counter, two kinds of wall and a latch, every one of them shown on paper, on
cups and cards and dice I made up, and then a small machine to run them on. That is the model on paper and on one small example. It's time to go and look at what people actually do. I picked five systems that keep
records other people rely on, with real money or real security behind them, and asked each
the pricing question from the paper models: \emph{is there a price on the moment the record is written?}
The question isn't about the work around the write; it's about the write, the moment the 0 goes on the page and stays. I'll tell you the answer first, because it's a
single sentence and it surprised me: of the five specifications, read through the
transcriptions I made of them, only one takes a fee at the moment of the write, and that one has a leak at exactly
the place Section~\ref{sec:counter} said a counter leaks, where it goes down.

``Price'' needs one meaning for all five, or the answer is whatever I want it to be, so I'll fix
it here, and every system below gets classified by it. A specification \emph{prices} an event when it
attaches one of three costs to it. A \emph{fee}: something taken at the event itself, whatever
happens afterward. A \emph{bond}: value put at risk by the event and lost only if some later event
happens, a contradiction, say. A \emph{budget}: a finite allowance the event draws down, so that only
so many such events can ever happen. A wall isn't a price under this definition. Nobody pays a
hash; reversing one is just infeasible. Neither is work a protocol needs and never charges for.
The table at the end of the section has a column for each of the three kinds, and what it shows
is a finding about the five, because the definition came first.

Three things are easy to blur in a section like this, so I'll name them now and keep them
apart all the way through. There's the \emph{real specification}: the document real money and
real security run on. There's my \emph{transcription}: one mechanism copied out of that document
into a mathematical model, small enough to examine. And for some of the five there's a \emph{wrapper}: a tiny
abstract model that takes one premise as given and says what follows from it. A claim proved
at one level isn't a claim at the level above it. Near the end I'll walk one system, gas,
through all three, so you can see exactly where each claim stops.

For each system I isolate the mechanism the question concerns: a \emph{fragment} with its
own states and operations, transcribed from the system's specification where one was
available. I will put that mechanism on the page, state the guarantee it carries, and show
how the argument follows its rules.

\subsection{Proof-of-stake finality: the price is on going back}

Ethereum and chains like it decide which blocks are final by having validators, people who've
locked up money (their \emph{stake}), vote on checkpoints: blocks picked out at regular numbered
rounds called \emph{epochs}. A vote isn't for one checkpoint. It's a \emph{link} from a checkpoint the
validator already trusts, the source, to a later one, the target, and every chain starts from
one first block, its \emph{genesis}, which counts as trusted from the start. In the design Vitalik
Buterin and Virgil Griffith published in 2017, called Casper, a checkpoint is \emph{justified}
when validators holding two thirds of the stake vote a link to it from a justified source,
and \emph{finalized} when it is justified and a two-thirds link runs from it to its direct child. The record is
``this checkpoint is final.''

Two rules carry the price: don't vote for two different targets in the same epoch, and don't
cast a vote whose span, source to target, surrounds the span of another of your votes. Break
either and your deposit can be destroyed, which is called \emph{slashing}. The
theorem they prove, called accountable safety, says that if two \emph{conflicting} checkpoints
are ever both finalized, at least a third of the stake broke a rule and can be slashed. So
the price is on \emph{reversal}, on making the record contradict itself. The write itself,
finalizing, need not incur a slashing penalty. This is not a claim that
running validators has no operating costs or other protocol charges. In the
terms from the start of the section, Casper's price is a bond. The deposit stands behind every vote, the finalizing votes included, and it's taken only from a validator whose own votes contradict each other, which is what making the record contradict itself takes from a third of the stake.

Do it with three validators of equal stake. Draw genesis at epoch 0, two competing
children at epoch 1, and one child of each at epoch 2. Let A and B vote both links
on the left branch, from genesis to its first child and from that child to the
next. Let B and C do the same on the right. Each link has two of the three votes.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth,every node/.style={align=center,font=\small}]
\node (g) at (0,0) {genesis\\epoch 0};
\node (l) at (-2,-1.8) {left\\epoch 1};
\node (r) at (2,-1.8) {right\\epoch 1};
\node (ll) at (-2,-3.5) {left child\\epoch 2};
\node (rr) at (2,-3.5) {right child\\epoch 2};
\draw[->] (g)--node[left] {A, B}(l);
\draw[->] (g)--node[right] {B, C}(r);
\draw[->] (l)--node[left] {A, B}(ll);
\draw[->] (r)--node[right] {B, C}(rr);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
B appears on both branches at each target epoch. A and C do not.
The diagram records votes; it has no step deducting a balance.
Both epoch-1 blocks are justified and have the required link to their child, so
both finalize. B voted for different targets at the same epoch, which makes B's third of the stake slashable, while A and C have broken
neither voting rule. The votes supply evidence for a penalty; this example
does not execute the transaction that collects it, and Theorem~\ref{thm:u13-casper-instances} below has exactly this instance, so the theorem's premise isn't vacuous: forks of that kind can be
built, and the theorem fires on them.

The fragment is a reconstruction of the published casper-proofs argument from Runtime Verification
and the University of Texas at Austin, based on Yoichi Hirai's proof, with validator sets and
quorum intersection as a premise. A \emph{quorum} is a set of validators big enough to act, here
two thirds of the stake, and \emph{quorum intersection} is the arithmetic of the three-validator
example: two thirds plus two thirds is four thirds, so any two quorums share at least a
third. The fragment takes the overlap as given; it doesn't do that arithmetic. It has no deposits,
no rewards, no fork choice (the rule for picking a branch to build on), and no connection to
anything else in this book. A finalization fork implies that a set of
validators the size of that overlap, at least a third of the stake, has
committed a slashable offence. A one-validator chain finalizes without
any such offence, which
is the ``write costs no stake'' sentence, proved here in a degenerate setting.

The fragment is small enough to read in one sitting, and every name below is from the transcription.

\begin{definition}[Casper setting and votes]\label{def:u13-casper}
A \emph{setting} has a type of validators, a type of block hashes with a parent relation and a
genesis hash, and two classes of validator sets, the ``two-thirds'' sets $Q_1$ and the
``one-third'' sets $Q_2$. It carries two premises: \emph{quorum intersection}, for any two sets in
$Q_1$ some set in $Q_2$ lies inside both; and \emph{at most one parent} per hash. A \emph{state} says,
for each validator, target hash $h$, target epoch $t$ and source epoch $u$, whether that
validator voted the link $(h, t, u)$. A link from $p$ at epoch $u$ to $h$ at epoch $t$ is
\emph{justified by} $q$ when $q \in Q_1$, every member of $q$ voted $(h, t, u)$, $h$ is the
$(t - u)$-th descendant of $p$, and $t > u$. Genesis is justified at epoch 0, and a block
reached from a justified block by a justified link landing at epoch $t$ is justified at $t$. Block $h$ is \emph{finalized} at
epoch $v$ with child $c$ when $c$ is a child of $h$, $h$ is justified at $v$, and the link
from $h$ at $v$ to $c$ at $v + 1$ is justified. A \emph{finalization fork} is two finalized blocks
$h_1 \ne h_2$, neither an ancestor of the other. The transcription calls a validator \emph{slashed} when it voted two
different targets with the same target epoch (a double vote), or voted links $(h_1, t_1, u_1)$
and $(h_2, t_2, u_2)$ with $t_1 > t_2$ and $u_2 > u_1$ (a surround vote). The state is
\emph{quorum-slashed} when some set in $Q_2$ consists of such validators.
These names describe offending votes, not a balance deduction: there are
no account balances in this state.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Accountable safety]\label{thm:u13-accountable-safety}
In every setting, every state with a finalization fork is quorum-slashed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let the fork be $h_1$ finalized at $v_1$ and $h_2$ at $v_2$. If $v_1 = v_2$, the epoch is above 0, since genesis is the only block justified at 0, so the links that justified $h_1$ and $h_2$ there are each voted by a set in $Q_1$; quorum intersection gives a set in $Q_2$ that voted both, and their targets $h_1$ and $h_2$ differ. That set double-voted. If
$v_1 \ne v_2$, say $v_1 < v_2$, walk down the chain of justified links that justifies $h_2$. Every block on that chain is an ancestor of $h_2$, so
none descends from $h_1$. (So $v_1 > 0$: the only block justified at epoch 0 is genesis, an
ancestor of every justified block.) Some link in the chain starts at or below $v_1$ and lands above
$v_1$. If it lands at $v_1 + 1$, it and the finalization link of $h_1$ have distinct targets at
that epoch, and the intersection set double-voted. If it starts at $v_1$, its source is a
justified block at $v_1$ other than $h_1$, and the links that justified those two blocks give
a double vote the same way. Otherwise it starts below $v_1$ and lands above $v_1 + 1$, so it
surrounds the finalization link of $h_1$, and the intersection set made a surround vote.
\end{proof}

Everything the fragment promises stands on the overlap, and with the overlap taken away it promises nothing. The one parent is in the setting because the original proof uses it, and the proof above never does.

\begin{theorem}[The premise can hold, and the write costs no stake]\label{thm:u13-casper-instances}
(1) In the three-validator setting where each validator has stake 1, $Q_1$ is the sets of
stake at least two thirds and $Q_2$ the sets of at least one third, the state where A and B
vote one branch and B and C the other has a finalization fork; B is slashed, A and C are
not, and $\{B\}$ is in $Q_2$. (2) In the one-validator chain setting, one vote finalizes
genesis and no validator is slashed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Both are computations on fixed finite data. In (1) every link carries two of the three
votes, so stake two thirds, so both epoch-1 blocks are justified and each has a justified link to
its child at epoch 2: both are finalized, and as siblings neither is an ancestor of the other.
B voted two different targets at epoch 1, which is the double vote; A's and C's votes are one
link at epoch 1 from source 0 and one at epoch 2 from source 1, which neither double-vote nor
surround. In (2) the one validator's vote from genesis at 0 to its child at 1 is a justified
link, so genesis is finalized, and a single vote can neither double-vote nor surround.
\end{proof}

For the record itself, one thing that means is that finality is
revocable at a price, the price is named, and a final block can hold a false statement.

The obvious next question is whether the 2017 design is what Ethereum actually runs. The answer is partly, and the
paper's own title is the clue. It's called \emph{Casper the Friendly Finality Gadget}, and its
first sentence says it's a finality system that \emph{overlays} a chain still choosing its blocks
by proof of work, so it's a gadget, bolted on top. In 2020 a larger group, Buterin among them, wrote up
\emph{Gasper}, which joins Casper's finality to a fork-choice rule called LMD GHOST, and on 15
September 2022, in the switch people called the Merge, Ethereum stopped choosing blocks by proof
of work at all and went over to proof of stake. So the checkpoints and the two slashing rules
above are one part of a system that holds real money today, and the transcription is of that
part's safety proof as the 2017 design states it. Everything between the two, the fork choice
and the rest of the running protocol, is the gap between my transcription and the running system, which I walk
through near the end of this section with a photocopied recipe and a kitchen. None of that moves the price: finalizing still costs an
honest validator no stake, and what costs is contradicting yourself.

\subsection{Gas: the one that charges a fee at the write}

Every operation on Ethereum costs \emph{gas}, paid in ether by whoever sent the transaction. The
yellow paper, Ethereum's formal specification, gives the reason in one line: every computation is fee-bearing so the network
can't be abused and halting questions are sidestepped. The record I care about is a nonzero
slot in the shared storage, which every full node in the world (every computer keeping its own complete copy of the
chain) has to keep until it's cleared. Clearing a slot is allowed, and the refund rules below exist to reward it.

Writing a fresh storage slot from zero to nonzero costs twenty thousand gas,
by the table in the paper's appendix, plus twenty-one hundred for touching a \emph{cold} slot, one
the transaction hasn't touched yet (after the first touch it's \emph{warm}). As I read it, the point
is to discourage storage growth, since storage grows every node's database.
That charge is a fee on the write, at the moment of the write, and it's the only fee in the five. Gas
has a budget too, in the sense from the start of the section: every block has a gas limit, and the
gas its transactions use can't exceed it, so only so many writes fit in a block.

Where does a number like twenty-one hundred come from? Somebody picked it, so the obvious next
question is who, and why, and the answer has a date on it. In September 2016, just as Ethereum's
developers were gathering in Shanghai for Devcon 2, their developer conference (the third one,
since they started counting at zero), attackers started filling
blocks with an operation that was cheap in gas and expensive in fact: it sent every node off to
read data from its disk, and nodes fell behind the chain. The first repair, a fork that October
called Tangerine Whistle, raised the prices of the operations the attack had leaned on. The
cold-slot charge came later, in a proposal by Vitalik Buterin and Martin Swende called EIP-2929,
switched on in the Berlin upgrade of April 2021, and the motivation it gives is still those 2016
attacks. So twenty-one hundred isn't a law of nature or a measurement of anything deep. It's a
scar: a price set after somebody found the place where the old price was wrong. That doesn't
change the argument; the write is still priced at the moment of the write. It does change how I
read the rest of that table: some of its numbers, at least, are somebody's answer to ``what did
this cost last time,'' which is a record of a different kind.

Now for the leak, which is Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s leak. Set a slot and then clear it \emph{in the same transaction} and
you get a refund. Count it through: first write twenty-two thousand one hundred; clearing it
costs a hundred and credits a refund of nineteen thousand nine hundred; net, twenty-three
hundred. The other half is that if you
leave it set, you pay at least twenty thousand. The write is priced, and
the \emph{revoked} write nearly isn't. But I have to add what the fragment leaves out, because twenty-three hundred
on its own misleads: the realized refund is capped at one fifth
of the gas the whole transaction used (that's the 2021 change from Section~\ref{sec:counter}, the one that ended
the refund-hoarding token's advantage). So a real set-then-clear pays a lot more than twenty-three
hundred. As for how much more, the cap is a fifth of everything the transaction used, and that
includes the twenty-one thousand every transaction pays just for existing. Take a
transaction that does nothing but set and clear the slot, and count only that base and the two
stores (the instructions that load their arguments add about a dozen more): it uses 43,200 gas, so the cap is
8,640, so it pays 34,560, which is 13,560 on top of the base. (Look at the slot alone and
forget the base, which the rule doesn't do, and you'd get 17,760.) Either way it's far above
twenty-three hundred. The counter-level net is twenty-three hundred, and what the transaction pays is not.

The arithmetic below is the way the specification has it, so you can redo it with a pencil.

\begin{definition}[One slot in one transaction]\label{def:u13-slot}
A slot run records the slot's value at the start of the transaction (original), its current
value, whether it has been touched (warm), the gas charged so far, and the refund counter.
A store of a new value charges 2100 if the slot is cold, plus 20000 if the slot still holds
its original value, the new value differs, and the original is 0 (2900 if the original is
nonzero), and otherwise 100. If the value is unchanged, the refund does not change. Otherwise add together
these applicable adjustments: add 4800 when the original and current values are
nonzero and the new value is zero; subtract 4800 when the original is nonzero and
the current value is zero; and, when the new value restores the original, add
19900 if that original is zero, or 2800 if it is nonzero. Store the new current
value, mark the slot warm, and keep the original value unchanged. The run starts
fresh: original and current 0, cold, gas and refund 0. The \emph{net} charge is gas
minus refund.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Pricing the persistent write and the revoked one]\label{thm:u13-sstore}
(1) For every list of stores from a slot whose original and current values are 0, warm or cold, with gas and refund 0, if the slot ends nonzero then the net charge is at least 20000, and from a fresh slot, which is cold, at least 22100. (2) Storing 1 then 0 leaves the slot at 0 with net charge 2300; storing 1
alone has net charge 22100.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Keep two lines on the sheet: ``current value zero: net at least zero,''
and ``current value nonzero: net at least 20000.'' The starting slot meets
the first line. I will check that every store leaves it meeting whichever
line describes its new value. The original value remains zero throughout,
so there are only four changes to check. Zero to zero adds 100
to net; zero to nonzero adds 20000; nonzero to nonzero adds 100; and nonzero to
zero adds $100-19900=-19800$. The last case starts with net at least 20000 and
so ends at least 200, still nonnegative. So every store leaves the appropriate line true. Carry the two-line test
through the list of stores: if the final value is nonzero, the net charge is
at least 20000. A cold access adds another 2100, once, on the first store.
Keep that extra charge in a separate column; later updates are exactly the
ones just checked and do not depend on the accumulated total. A nonempty
run from a cold slot therefore pays that 2100 on top of the bound, giving
at least $20000 + 2100$ when it ends nonzero. (2) Direct
computation: $2100 + 20000 = 22100$ for the first store, $100$ for the second, refund
$19900$, and $22200 - 19900 = 2300$.
\end{proof}

The fragment covers one slot in one transaction, with the gas and refund arithmetic copied out of the
Ethereum execution specification's storage instruction and gas table, at a named commit. It has no stack, no call context, no other
slots, and \emph{no refund cap}, the one-fifth rule applied at the end of a transaction.

Then comes the wrapper, which is a different kind of object, and the walk near the end is about
exactly that difference. It's a \emph{gas schedule} in the abstract: any states, any steps, a cost
per step, a yes/no commitment flag, and a charge predicate saying which steps get charged. It
formalises no EVM (the Ethereum virtual machine) at all. It is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s result
with the whole-run ceiling, the one that pins the amount as well as which steps pay, under a new
name. Its two halves are worth reading separately. Leave one
committing step uncharged, and a one-step run commits at no charge, so the floor fails outright; one missed commit
is enough. Charge one step that doesn't commit, and the schedule charges more than the number
of commits on that one-step run, so the ceiling fails. And
the class isn't empty: in any system, the price that charges one exactly on a step that raises
the flag and nothing on any other meets both halves (Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s step price).

The wrapper itself is the cleanest thing in this section and has the least
Ethereum in it.

\begin{definition}[A gas schedule]\label{def:u13-gas-schedule}
A \emph{gas schedule} has states, instructions, a step, a cost $c(s, i) \in \mathbb{N}$ that may
depend on the state, a Boolean commitment flag on states, and a Boolean charge predicate
$\chi(s, i)$, with two premises: a charged step costs at least 1, and an uncharged step costs
0. A step \emph{commits} when it takes the flag from false to true. For a run $t$ from $s$, let
$c(t)$ be its total cost and $n(t)$ its number of committing steps. The schedule has the
\emph{floor} when $c(t) \ge n(t)$ for every run, and \emph{no overcharge} when $c(t) \le n(t)$ for every
run. It has \emph{unit pricing} when $c(s, i) = 1$ if $\chi(s, i)$ and $0$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Gas schedule exactness]\label{thm:u13-gas-exactness}
For every gas schedule: it has the floor and no overcharge if and only if $\chi(s, i)$ holds
exactly when the step from $s$ by $i$ commits, and it has unit pricing. Moreover, (1) if some
committing step from an uncommitted state is uncharged, that one-step run costs 0 and the
schedule fails the floor; (2) if some charged step does not commit, the schedule
overcharges.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The equivalence is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s characterization with the whole-run ceiling, under another name. From right to left, each step's cost is 1 on a committing step and 0 otherwise, so a
run's cost counts its commitments. From left to right, apply the floor and no overcharge to
one-step runs: a committing step must cost at least 1, so it is charged; a charged step costs
at least 1 and may not exceed its commitment count, so it commits and costs exactly 1. Parts
(1) and (2) are those one-step runs read the other way.
\end{proof}

Gas prices storage growth and computation. It says
nothing about whether what's stored is true.

\subsection{Attestation: hash chains, and a quote about the past}

A trusted platform module keeps platform configuration registers, or PCRs.
An extension hashes the old value together with a new measurement digest.
A quote signs selected PCR values and challenge data supplied by the asker;
the verifier must check the signature, challenge and expected measurements.
That can establish a fresh report of those values. It does not establish
that every relevant fact about the machine was measured.

PCR reset permissions depend on the register, locality and platform rules.
Some reset at startup; some support permitted resets during a boot. Thus
``you can only extend'' describes an interval with those resets excluded.
Intel SGX uses enclave measurements and attestation reports for a related
purpose, but it does not use this PCR-extension interface.

What does the specification price on the registers? Nothing: no fee, no bond, no budget. Within the stated reset and access restrictions, forging a different
measurement history that passes verification relies on defeating the
cryptographic assumptions or trusted components. Authorized resets are a
separate operation, not an attack that requires breaking a hash. Expensive against infeasible is the difference between a price and a wall, and
it's easy to blur, which is why the definition at the start of the section leaves walls out.
What stands behind a cost can come in three currencies. It can be economic, a fee or a deposit
the protocol takes (Casper and gas are here). It can be cryptographic, a reversal made
infeasible by a hardness assumption, which makes it a wall with no exact price on it (attestation and
transparency are here). Or it can be physical, energy spent or hardware worn, which none of these five
specifications charges as a fee or a bond; the nearest thing is the chip's write budget, below. And the record's permanence is only as long as the register lives: a
register's continuity lasts only through the interval allowed by its
reset rules, not necessarily an entire boot.

Why the registers, then, when something that lasts would make a better record? Because the quote is what a remote asker
reads, and the registers are what it signs. The same chip has longer-lived records, and they're
closer to the latch than anything else in this section. Version 2.0 of its specification has
storage slots of a kind it calls a bit field, changed only by a command that ORs new bits into the
old value. During that index's lifetime the command can set a bit and
cannot clear one, the OR rule from Section~\ref{sec:latch}. Deleting and
redefining an index is governed by separate authorization and policy; it
must be included in any claim about persistence across that lifetime. It also has counters advanced by an increment command. On first use,
a new counter starts above the values previously held by counters on that
TPM, so deleting an index and making a new one does not restart the count
at zero. This is a guarantee of the specified chip, not protection against
replacing it with another chip. And those slots are rationed. Bryan Parno and his
coauthors, building a system called Memoir in 2011, noted that the specification of the day only
required a counter to be able to tick once every five seconds, and that the chip's storage was
expected to survive about a hundred thousand writes in its whole life, so writing once a second
would wear it out in under twenty-eight hours. Memoir writes to it twice per boot. Those figures describe the hardware assumptions discussed in Memoir, not
a universal write quota for every TPM. Endurance and throttling constrain
real use, but an expected endurance figure is not itself an enforced
protocol budget. The quoted PCR interface supplies no such numerical price. On the bit field it's the budget of Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-growing}'s chain
of $k$-bit words, which can only climb $k$ times. Phones and small controllers go one floor further down,
to fuses like the PROMs in Section~\ref{sec:latch}: a version number kept as a row of fuses, one
more blown at each security update, and boot code that refuses anything older. An industry guide
on it, Rob Smart's 2021 explainer for PSA Certified, a security certification scheme for chips and
devices, tells designers to make sure there are enough fuse bits to last the number of updates
expected over the device's lifetime, which is part (5) of that same theorem, written as a design
rule.

What all of this is for is \emph{rollback}. Memoir's example is a password checker restored to an
old saved state to undo a user's password change, and in 2017 a system called ROTE did the same
job for Intel's enclaves by having several machines vouch for each other's counters, with the
stated result that the only way left to break it is to reset every one of them to its start.
In 2016 Raoul Strackx and Frank Piessens's Ariadne got that job down to flipping a
single bit of non-volatile memory per state update, which they call the theoretical lower limit.
Notice who the attacker is in every one of these: whoever gets to put an old state back. A bad
program doesn't come into it. A record kept by the step can't see that attacker. Every guarantee the small machine gives about a record's earned history (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}) is stated from a clean start; put back a state the machine really reached and each one still holds of it, through the run that reached it first, and none of them can say that nothing came after it. The per-step toll still holds after a restore; it just can't tell you what happened before it.

Replicated services put the same kind of record somewhere else: inside each replica, where a
replica that's been taken over still can't make it say two different things. Byung-Gon Chun and
coauthors' attested append-only memory (A2M, 2007) is a log a replica can only add to; Dave Levin
and coauthors' TrInc (2009) shrinks that to a trusted counter; MinBFT (Giuliana Veronese and
coauthors, 2013) uses a trusted counter to reach agreement with $2f+1$ replicas when $f$ of
them can lie, where the usual count is $3f+1$; and Damysus (Jérémie Decouchant, David Kozhaya, Vincent
Rahli and Jiangshan Yu, 2022) has a small trusted service, the Checker, that keeps a monotonic
counter of where the protocol is. Allen Clement, Flavio Junqueira, Aniket Kate and Rodrigo
Rodrigues (2012) worked out, with proofs, what such a record buys, and as I read their result it's
a good warning for this book.
On its own, stopping a replica from saying two different things doesn't lower the $3f+1$ bound
in an asynchronous network at all. Add signatures that a third party can check, and it turns any
protocol that survives crashes into one that survives liars, with no extra replicas. The way I
read it, a record helps the others only as far as they can check what it says, which is
Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s point from the other side.

There's a fourth currency under those three, the logical
kind, and it's the one every permanent record on a finite chip pays in: Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s counting of used and fresh states applies to any of these records. With only finitely many states holding the record on, a step that switches it on somewhere, and never switches it off anywhere, forgets something.
Forgetting alone doesn't single out a record write: any step that overwrites a field able to hold
two values forgets something too. What singles it out is where the forgetting lands. Take the
states the record already reads yes on, together with the one the step switches on. The step
sends every one of them to a yes state, and it can't keep them apart, so what it destroys is a
distinction on the record's own yes side: two states it already vouched for, or the state it just
raised and one that was up already. Any overwrite merges states somewhere; a permanent write is
forced to merge them on that side.
That needs no premise about money, keys or heat. The economic, cryptographic and physical
payments each need a premise of their own about their kind (a fee rule, a hardness
assumption, Landauer's principle), and they hold exactly where that premise holds.

\begin{theorem}[A permanent write forgets on its own yes side]\label{thm:u13-logical-payment}
For any states $S$, instructions $I$, step and Boolean reading: suppose a duplicate-free list names
every state, the instruction $i$ never turns the reading from on to off, and $i$ turns it on
at some state $s$. Then the step by $i$ is not injective. More: the step by $i$ sends every state
that reads on, and $s$, to a state that reads on, and it is not injective even on those states.
\end{theorem}

Count the on-states and call their number $K$. The list of all states is
finite, so this count is finite too. The instruction keeps each of those
$K$ sources on, and it also sends the additional off-state $s$ to on.
That gives $K+1$ distinct sources with only $K$ on-states available as
landing places. Two sources must land together. Both came from the stated
collection, so the failure to keep sources apart already occurs there.
Permanence of any other instruction was never needed.\proofclosed

What the quote can do is say what was \emph{measured}.
It can't say the measured code is correct, and it can't say anything about runtime state
that was never folded in. A correctly measured buggy program attests beautifully. The
fragment proves that exact limit: one register, a hash about which nothing is assumed, a quote as a pair, and no
function of the quote decides a runtime flag the quote ignores, which is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s cube again. And a second small result shows
that a sign-and-verify interface \emph{alone} gives no authenticity (a scheme where verify always
says yes passes the interface), so a cryptographic premise has to be added; the fragment
doesn't model signatures, formats, or a freshness check (the nonce is just a field the
verifier fixes).

The same limit, turned outward, is the honest edge of the four conditions of Section~\ref{sec:established}.
Every one of them is about a thing the machine holds: same property, same thing, same edition,
honest check. For a claim about the world (the oven is hot, the parcel arrived) there's no edition
the machine controls. Whatever reads the world is a window onto it, and ``nothing changed between
the check and the commit'' stops being something a step can enforce and becomes a premise about
the sensor. So a record can establish claims about the machine's own state, and claims about the
world only through named premises about whatever measured them. A correctly recorded sensor
reading establishes what the sensor reported. Whether the oven was hot
still depends on the sensor and the connection between its report and the world.

\begin{definition}[Platform and quote]\label{def:u13-quote}
Fix any functions $H: \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ (the extend hash) and
$\delta: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ (the digest); nothing is assumed about either. A
\emph{platform} is a measurement log (a list of numbers) and a Boolean runtime flag. Its register
is the log folded from 0 by $H$. The \emph{quote} with nonce $n$ is the pair
$(\delta(\text{register}), n)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The quote cannot attest unmeasured state]\label{thm:u13-quote}
For every nonce $n$ there is no function $D$ from quotes to Booleans with
$D(\mathrm{quote}_n(P)) = \mathrm{flag}(P)$ for every platform $P$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take two platforms with the empty log, one flagged true and one false. Their quotes are
equal, since the quote never reads the flag, so $D$ would have to return both values on one
input.
\end{proof}

Anything that depends only on $\delta(\text{register})$, the quote can answer; that's what it's
for. And the second result is the one I mentioned: a ``signature'' scheme whose check always says yes
fits the sign-and-verify interface perfectly and accepts a signature no key ever made, so the
interface on its own promises nothing.

\subsection{Certificate transparency: visible, unpriced}

The certificates that make your browser show a padlock are issued by hundreds of
authorities, and a bad or compromised one can issue a certificate for a domain it shouldn't.
Certificate Transparency puts certificates in public append-only logs built
as Merkle trees. An inclusion check ties a certificate to a particular root;
a consistency check ties a later root to one the reader already has. It was specified in RFC 6962 in 2013 and revised as
RFC 9162 in 2021. I went looking for which one the running logs follow, and it's still 6962:
Mozilla's reference for web developers says browser implementations are based on 6962, and as late
as November 2025 Chrome's team was only proposing to drop its rule that every certificate carry a
timestamp from at least one 6962 log. The fragment I
transcribe is 9162's. A Merkle tree is Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s hash chain folded into
a tree: hash each certificate (those are the \emph{leaves}), hash the leaf hashes in pairs, hash
those in pairs, and so on up to one \emph{root} hash. To prove one leaf is in, the log hands you
only the few hashes sitting beside the climb from that leaf to the root, the \emph{path}, and you
redo the climb yourself. A second check, \emph{consistency}, shows that a bigger tree is a smaller
one with leaves added on the end and nothing rewritten. The record is a leaf in the tree.

The data structure has a history of its own in security. The computer scientists Scott Crosby and
Dan Wallach, at Rice University, built tamper-evident logs on the same kind of tree in 2009, with
a proof that an entry is in the log and a proof that a later version of the log extends an earlier
one, each a logarithmic number of hashes. A rewrite that fails to extend a
previously witnessed root is caught by the consistency check.

The RFC prices nothing, and it says in its first section that logs let interested parties \emph{detect} misissuance
afterward. They don't \emph{prevent} it. And a log that shows different views to
different people (a \emph{split view}) can defeat the auditing, so logs are still trusted parties.
What it buys is visibility.

Which raises the obvious question: if the specification prices nothing, why does any authority bother logging?
Nothing in the RFC makes it. The answer is a browser. Chrome's team set the rule, enforced from
Chrome 68 in July 2018, that every certificate issued after 30 April 2018 had to meet its
transparency policy, and a
publicly trusted certificate that doesn't is simply not trusted by Chrome: the visitor gets a full-page warning in front of the site. So there is a price after
all, though it isn't anywhere in the specification: it lives in one vendor's browser, and it's the price of being shown to that
browser's users at all. Is that the bottom? Not quite, because it means the strongest lever on
this record is a policy one company can change, which is a fact about who holds the stamp. The
tree has nothing to do with it. That policy changes nothing in the table at the end of this section, which asks what
each specification prices. But it's worth keeping two sentences apart: ``the specification
prices nothing'' and ``nothing is priced.''

Do the inclusion proof by hand. Lay out seven cards $d_0$ through $d_6$,
each standing for one leaf hash.
Join neighbours with paper brackets: $a=\nu(d_0,d_1)$,
$b=\nu(d_2,d_3)$ and $c=\nu(d_4,d_5)$. The last card stands alone.
Next join $a$ to $b$, giving $L=\nu(a,b)$, and $c$ to $d_6$, giving
$R=\nu(c,d_6)$. The root is $\nu(L,R)$. Here $\nu$ means ``put these two
expressions, in this order, inside one labelled bracket.'' Equal symbolic hashes
must have exactly the same bracket structure.

To check $d_3$, keep only that card and the three siblings $d_2,a,R$.
Combine $d_2$ on its left to recover $b$, then $a$ on the left to recover $L$,
then $R$ on the right to recover the root. You never needed to open the cards
inside $a$ or $R$. Those three siblings are the inclusion path.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}cll@{}}
Step & What is supplied & What is rebuilt \\ \hline
Start & card $d_3$ & starting leaf hash $d_3$ \\
1 & $d_2$ on the left & $b=\nu(d_2,d_3)$ \\
2 & $a$ on the left & $L=\nu(a,b)$ \\
3 & $R$ on the right & root $=\nu(L,R)$ \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Swapping left and right changes the bracket. The path has to carry the
correct order as well as the correct siblings. The hashes here are brackets, not numbers,
so what you just checked is how the tree is put together; a real log uses short hashes, and
``two different trees can't give the same root'' is then a separate promise from the
cryptography. Nothing in this fragment signs anything, no auditors talk to each other, and no
log misbehaves.

\begin{definition}[Inclusion check, RFC 9162 section 2.1.3.2]\label{def:u13-inclusion}
Given a leaf index $m$, a tree size $N$, a leaf hash, a root hash and a path, the check
rejects unless $m < N$. Otherwise start counters $f=m$, $s=N-1$ and an accumulated hash $r$ equal to
the leaf hash. For each path element $p$, reject if $s=0$. If $f$ is odd or
$f=s$, replace $r$ by $\nu(p,r)$; in this branch, while $f$ is positive and
even, halve both counters with rounding down. In the other branch replace
$r$ by $\nu(r,p)$. After either branch halve both counters once more. At the
end accept exactly when $s=0$ and $r$ is the claimed root. A \emph{symbolic hash}
makes a leaf hash $\ell(x)$ and a node hash $\nu(a,b)$ distinct constructors:
two hashes are equal only when their entire constructions agree.

The consistency check used here takes old and new sizes $M,N$, roots $u,v$ and
a path, and rejects unless $0<M<N$. If $M$ is a power of two, prepend $u$ to
the path. Reject an empty resulting path; otherwise its first element seeds
two accumulated hashes $r_\mathrm{old},r_\mathrm{new}$. Start $f=M-1$, $s=N-1$,
and halve both while $f$ is odd. Process each remaining path element $p$:
reject if $s=0$; when $f$ is odd or $f=s$, put $p$ on the left of both
accumulated hashes and halve both counters while $f$ is positive and even;
otherwise leave $r_\mathrm{old}$ alone and put $p$ on the right of
$r_\mathrm{new}$. After either branch halve both counters once. Accept exactly
when $s=0$, $r_\mathrm{old}=u$ and $r_\mathrm{new}=v$. All halvings round down.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The RFC's own examples pass]\label{thm:u13-ct-examples}
With the symbolic hash, in the RFC's seven-leaf tree with leaves $d_0, \dots, d_6$ (writing
$d_k$ also for its leaf hash $\ell(d_k)$), the inclusion check accepts leaf 3 with path $[d_2, \nu(d_0, d_1), \nu(\nu(d_4, d_5), d_6)]$, and
likewise leaves 0, 4 and 6 with their paths; the consistency check from size 4 to size 7
accepts. For every input with $m = N$, the inclusion check rejects.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Use the brackets $a,b,c,L,R$ built above. For leaf 3, the counters start at
$(3,6)$: put $d_2$ on the left, leaving $(1,3)$; put $a$ on the left, leaving
$(0,1)$; put $R$ on the right, leaving $(0,0)$ and root $\nu(L,R)$.
Leaf 0 has path $[d_1,b,R]$ and three right combinations. Leaf 4 has path
$[d_5,d_6,L]$: right, right, left. Leaf 6 has path $[c,L]$:
left, then left; its first branch shifts $(6,6)$ to $(3,3)$ before the ordinary
halving, which accounts for the unpaired last leaf. Each reconstructs the same root.
For consistency from 4 to 7, the old root is $L$ and the supplied path is $[R]$.
Prepending $L$ seeds both hashes with $L$; shifting the initial $(3,6)$ gives
$(0,1)$, so the sole remaining element leaves the old root alone and makes the
new root $\nu(L,R)$, with final counters $(0,0)$. The boundary case $m=N$
fails the first test $m<N$.
\end{proof}

And the append-only part of the fragment is as plain as it sounds: the history is a list,
and adding to the end of a list leaves every old entry where it was.

\subsection{Proof-carrying code: no price, no permanence}

Necula's idea, from Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}, is to ship untrusted code with a proof that it obeys the host's policy; the
host computes what would need to be true and checks the proof with a small checker. The
record is the checked proof or the result of checking it. An implementation
may retain either. Proof-carrying code does not by itself require a permanent
latch or assign an abstract toll to acceptance. Producing and checking the
proof both take computational work; that work has not been identified with
the unit charge in this book.

\subsection{The same table, five ways}

Lay them out by the one definition of price from the start of the section. Casper puts a bond
behind the write and takes it on \emph{reversal} (slashing). Gas takes a fee at \emph{the write} (and refunds the
revocation, capped), and rations writes with a gas limit per block. Attestation prices \emph{nothing} on
the registers the quote signs, and puts a budget on its longer-lived slots and counters.
Transparency prices \emph{nothing}. Attestation and transparency make reversal
infeasible or visible. Proof-carrying code prices nothing and keeps nothing.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.15\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.16\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.16\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.19\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.21\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{System} & \textbf{Fee at the write} & \textbf{Bond} & \textbf{Budget} & \textbf{What the transcription proves} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
Casper finality & none & the deposit, taken on a contradicting vote (slashing) & none & a finalization fork means a slashable third \\
Gas & 20000 for a fresh slot, mostly refunded on revocation, up to a cap & none & the gas limit of each block & a persistent write to an empty slot nets at least 20000 \\
Attestation & none; reversal is infeasible & none & none on the registers; a write budget on the non-volatile slots and counters & the quote can't decide what it never measured \\
Transparency & none; misissuance is visible & none & none & the RFC's own inclusion examples pass \\
Proof-carrying code & no required persistent latch & none & none & the checker is the verification condition \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

Each row proves what its own transcription says, and no more. To read a row as a claim about
the running system you'd need evidence from that system, and no row shows that certification
is the one event every model has to price.

So the thing the toll charges for, the moment the record is written, is charged a fee in one of the five
specifications I read, and in that one the designers had to patch the place where the charge
could be clawed back. I find that neither a vindication nor a refutation. It's a fact about
what people built, and what they built was mostly walls (hash chains, signatures) and
penalties for contradiction. Tolls on commitment were rare. Whether a toll on commitment is a
\emph{better} design than a wall is not something I can prove, and I won't pretend the five say
so. What I read in them, and it's a reading of five fragments I chose, is that each has a condition treated as a record, though the conditions differ in durability, and that the price axis is
mostly empty. With one definition of price fixed before the survey, that last part is a count:
of fifteen cells in the table, four are filled (one fee, one bond, two budgets), and only gas
takes a payment at the moment of the write.

That leaves the question Section~\ref{sec:latch} raised and Section~\ref{sec:pointer} has to face. The five systems have five different
events chosen as ``the record'': finalized, committed, attested, logged, checked. Is there
anything that picks out one event as \emph{the} one worth recording, or is it an unforced choice every
time? The pointer thesis is my proposed answer, and the next section gives the evidence it asks for.

%===========================================================================

\section{The pointer thesis}
\label{sec:pointer}
%===========================================================================

Everything so far leaves one choice open. A permanent record driven by the machine is a
latch on an event, and the event is yours to pick (Section~\ref{sec:latch}, the two
cups on one die). Five real systems each picked a different one
(Section~\ref{sec:models}), and for the machine in this book I picked certification.
So I owe you an answer to the obvious question: is that just my choice, or is there
something about how people and machines lean on records that picks this event out?

What I have is a thesis, in the sense the Church-Turing thesis is one
(Section~\ref{sec:structure}): a claim tying defined things to the world, which no proof
can settle. Whether it stands or falls is what decides whether the choice of event has a reason behind it.
Nothing before it depends on it; the latch, the windows and the counting arguments hold
whichever event a system records. What follows is the claim, where I got it, and how its terms apply to the systems being described.

\subsection{The claim}

Of all the events a machine could put on its ledger, the ones its price list charges for and
its counter adds up, certification is the one whose records
get \emph{copied and relied on by parties who didn't produce them}: checked, stored, and acted on
across independent places that share no other state. Copying alone can't be the test. A
replicated system copies everything it holds to every node, the gas used in a block header as
faithfully as the word final, so rival events get copied too. Reliance does not
automatically separate them either. In Ethereum, the previous block's gas use
helps determine the next block's base fee: another party reads it and acts on
it. That is an explicit rule in \href{https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1559}{EIP-1559}.

So the examples cannot establish that certification alone is copied and acted
on. The thesis asks whether a separately justified class of reliance selects
it, and whether that selection gives a reason to charge its establishment.
The formal toy below fixes its readers and actions in advance. It can test
those choices, but it cannot choose the real readers for us. Both the claimed
selection and its connection to prices remain to be justified.

There's a second handle on the same question, and it comes from Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}. The permanent-certificate
theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges}) never uses the word certification for anything special: given Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s rule that
forgetting is charged, it prices any reading that, once up, stays up, on a machine
with finite memory. So it points at a narrower
candidate: the events to price are the ones that write a record no later step can take back.
Certification is one of them. As an exact answer that candidate is false, because a merging
step can also revoke (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s three cards). Whether the records that are copied and relied on are the permanent ones, and
whether being copied and relied on picks out anything the merge criterion doesn't, is what the two handles
have to settle between them.

I can see two holes in that from here, so you don't have to find them for me. The first
is a missing premise. Even if the world copies certification records more than any other kind,
``copied'' doesn't give you ``priced'' on its own. Something has to connect them, and the best
candidate I have is a premise about incentives: a record that many independent parties copy and
lean on is exactly the record worth forging, so it's the one where a price buys the most
protection. That's a reasonable premise, but it's still a premise. The thesis's second half states the
connection as a claim to be tested; it doesn't explain it, and nothing in this book supplies the explanation. The second hole is a circle. If ``certification'' just means ``the record other
people rely on,'' then of course it's the one that gets relied on and copied, and the claim says
nothing. So the event has to be picked out without mentioning reliance: here it's a reading going
up for good right after a check of the same claim passed, which you can find in a run without
asking who reads it. Whether the world copies \emph{that} event more than its rivals is then a real
question, and it could come out no.

The thesis says no more than that, and what's left is the rest of what a thesis owes you.

\begin{thesis}[The pointer thesis]\label{conj:u14-pointer}
Let $C$ be the class of ecosystems with reliance that faithfully model deployed record-keeping
disciplines, each with its reachable states, its observers reading independent carriers, its
certification event, and the records its discipline prices. Then for every member of $C$: (1) the certification event is the pointer on
the reachable states, so it is copied and relied on by parties who didn't produce it, and every
event copied and relied on in that sense holds
wherever certification does; and (2) every record the discipline prices is copied and relied on
by parties who didn't produce it.
\end{thesis}

The thesis leans on two notions with no precise mathematical definition: what it is to
``faithfully model'' a system, and which systems count as ``deployed.'' Those two tie the
definitions to the world, the way ``computable in the plain-English sense'' does in the
Church-Turing thesis, and no definition can do that job, so the claim is a thesis. The other
term it needs, independent carriers, has an exact definition: each observer's view depends only
on its own part of the world, and any two observers' parts can be set independently of each
other. The schema takes the class, the reachable states, the certification event and the priced
records as inputs; it proves nothing about which real systems satisfy them.

\subsection{The end of the logic}

The logic that started in Part I ends here. Part I found what keeping takes: anything kept is paid in a merge or in fresh states, alongside the model-dependent thermal bounds (Section~\ref{sec:what-a-chair-is}), and a toll on raising a flag is forced by three premises
(Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}). Learning doesn't have to merge anything, so it owes no floor; it
borrows a blank page, which is a supply of fresh states, and can hand it back. Committing on a finite supply of fresh states has to merge
(Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}). Part II earned the rest. The counter is arithmetic once the schedule is
fixed (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). A window with a colliding pair in it can't price the flag exactly (Section~\ref{sec:windows}). Entitlement is an object,
a check, and a paid event, and, given lists, a tree and a covering that someone supplies, and a run that
paid for the tree's depth, it
costs at least the index bits it commits to (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}). Insight is a distinction made to stay, and a committed relation is that at its best (Section~\ref{sec:insight}).
A feeling doesn't qualify.
Over any base a record that is driven by the computation and never comes
down is a latch, with two unforced choices, the price list and the event
(Section~\ref{sec:latch}). With more than two places, a record that is driven by the computation
and climbs a partial order is a
row of cups, each one a latch; the toll over the whole row charges at least one on any step that
turns up some cup, and a
straight line of stages needs exactly one cup fewer than it has stages, cups that only turn up (Section~\ref{sec:direction}). When the
machine has finitely many states, its record only grows, and the
ordinary machine forgets nothing, the toll prices crushing two states of one fibre, and a window
can price exactly by seeing the cups move (Section~\ref{sec:shadow-exact}). No inside procedure whose flip a substrate can represent decides a shortcut property,
given a recursion theorem. What a
record can do is carry the commitment (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}). This part made ``established''
a record that a check of the claim passed (Section~\ref{sec:established}), and the small machine earns
one by a check, a commitment and a certificate, one unit each (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). Of
five specifications, read through my transcriptions, one charges a fee at the write (Section~\ref{sec:models}).
For the choice of event, the pointer thesis proposes certification and lists how
that proposal could fail (Section~\ref{sec:pointer}).

One question about the price itself is still open: do the requirements I've put on a price
pick out the toll and nothing else? If a short list of them left only one price standing,
that would settle it. The lists I tried don't, and
the no is small enough to check on three states. Call them blank, once and twice, with once and
twice reading yes. The flip takes blank to once and leaves the other two where they are. The
smooth takes both once and twice to twice and leaves blank alone. The smooth forgets something, so
the price on merging from Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} charges it one unit. (The flip forgets too, blank and once both land on once, so the price on merging charges it as well, as the list requires.) It raises nothing, so the toll
charges it nothing. Now try requirements that name no reading: no charge on a move that changes
nothing, none on a move that forgets nothing, the same cost when you rename the states, a total
that adds up along a run, a cost that looks only at the step, and a cost of one on the flip from blank. The toll, read as
